Input: I see more than a few people have had problems with setting up this printer on their networks. I think I know why.

Personally, it took me about 1 minute to install this printer via my wired network. And it worked flawlessly... for two weeks. Then the network card appears to have spontaneously died - while sitting on the floor, unmolested, happily printing a document. It will work with usb cable, but will no longer be recognized by the network, despite performing a clean reinstall of the drivers. Both of my computers stopped recognizing the printer at the same time. I suspect that those with problems setting up the printer probably had a dead ethernet card in theirs.

I owned the 2070N before this one, and other than longevity (lasting only 1 year) I had no complaints about it. Same goes for this one. But a 2 week lifespan is plenty to complain about.

** edit:
Found a fix! After speaking with support, I found a way to revive my wonky printer. Turn off the printer. Press and hold the blue button while turning it on. Then press it seven (?) times, IIRC. I had to do this a few times over the years, and it always worked. Then I killed my printer by putting something through that I shouldn't. My fault.

For some reason, I decided to buy another one of these. I guess the main reason I went back is the printer install is very, very easy. My latest 2170W has been working fine for over a year, now. No networking issues. Considering my experience with alternatives, I'm more than happy with this printer.

In France, Siemens phone systems are the rage my wife just returned from her trip...but it must be something with the Euro models.  In the US, they are junk.

Replaced the Siemens system with a Panasonic 5.8ghz KX-TG5100M system for about 2 years now and have had nothing but fantastic success.  The only negative/problem we encountered was the system used the NiCd 850mAh batteries and a year ago during a week long power outage (hurricane) the $25 batteries drained and would not recharge no matter what.  On a hunch, I called Panasonic customer support and explained my situation and they sent me new 1000mAh NiMH batteries for all my phones at no charge. Input: Okay, first things first:
This kit includes everything shown (INCLUDING CYMBALS)

Includes: frame, snare pad (dual zone for rimshots), 3 tom pads, 3 cymbals, hardware for mounting everything, module, kick pedal, kick drum, hi-hat pedal (module has different sensors for open/closed hi-hat so both register), even drum sticks, all cables needed to hook up the kit.

Not included: Throne, cables to hook into a speaker/PA/amp, etc. (but those usually come with your amp anyway).
THAT'S IT. Everything you need to actually get sound out of all the components is there.

That's the main reason I would rate this kit high.
Most other kits I looked at prior to purchase wouldn't correctly advertise if it includes cymbals or not. HUGE ISSUE, but have no fear for this kit.

Okay about the product:
Haven't gotten to play it much since the Holidays just passed, but the sound is nice. Customization of the kit sounds, recording, trial to some software... (All this is is the product specs I think.)
Got to play it more since (*This is an update*) then and things work well in general. See the cons for the bad stuff.

All in all, a good product. Probably not the best you can get but for the price, a good entry level kit and you can get some good use from it before you move to a more expansive kit.
I'd recommend this kit to anyone who is beginning or has more use for an electric kit than an acoustic kit. If you're more experienced, I'd say this would work, but I know I'd like something more high-end.

Some cons:
FIRMWARE ISSUE. Easy patch if you google the kit and firmware update. All you need is to unzip the folder and have a cable to connect the module to your computer. (This is the reason why I'd rate it 4 stars.)

So far, I have had my kit a bit off balance, but I'm sure I can get it adjusted the more I play it. Just haven't gotten that far yet. Careful you don't tip the kit and break something (I don't think this is really a problem with all kits, but I'm letting you know that it's possible for it to want to tip over)
Its difficult to keep balanced sometimes because the frame is loose on mine. I figure I can tighten the frame a bit. But I'll probably just strip the screws in the plastic mounters. So try adjusting the feet position a bit.

That's about it. Hope this was helpful for you.

Input: The Alesis Q49 is about the best choice you can make if you are looking for a compact budget priced keyboard controller that you can play with both hands.

The Q49 is very spartan in its feature set - 49 full size keys, full size pitch & mod wheels, octave up/down buttons, sustain switch input and just 1 dedicated data entry slider - note that it has no assignable data entry knobs or controller (drum) pads.

It can be powered either by a USB port on your computer (there is a USB cable included - it's tucked into one of the foam endcaps in the carton) or it can be powered by a 9V power adapter (NOT included). As most people will probably be using this device with a computer, please be aware that the Q49 USB connection may not work with a USB hub - i.e., you may have to plug it directly into a free USB port on your computer - Alesis mentions this in their trouble shooting guide, and that was my experience.

That said, I really like this keyboard - First, it's pretty much plug & play - you don't have to mess around with loading a pesky hardware driver (although of course, you do have to configure your software apps to recognize it - I got it to work with Reason 4, FL Studio 9 and all my stand alone software synths with no problems).

It's fairly lightweight and doesn't have a lot of excess plastic, so if you want, you can kick back in your easy chair and rest the Q49 on your lap. The keys do not have aftertouch, but they respond well to velocity changes. Pitch and Mod wheels are the same size as what you find on full-size controllers.

The octave up/down buttons light when they are activated, a nice little feature.

Note that if you are into editing/designing sounds or tweaking parameters on your soft-synths while you play, then this keyboard probably isn't for you because there are no assignable rotary controls - this is where those little two-octave units come in.

As an added bonus, you also get a "Lite" version of Ableton Live.

Input: Overall, I am really pleased with the Scarlett. The physical interface itself is beautiful and it's intuitive to use. I like how the ring around the gain will light up red if it detects you are clipping. Most importantly, with a good microphone, a decently quiet room, and a simple audio recorder, the audio quality is really superb. I am very happy with this purchase.

I want to clarify a few things for future buyers, though, and don't take this as a warning to stay away from this product. It is excellent if you can set it up right.

#1 - MICROPHONES V. INSTRUMENTS. The Scarlett has a very nicely designed combo jack, which allows you to plug in both an XLR connector and a 1/4" TRS jack plug. The Scarlett is automatically configured to recognize any XLR connector as a microphone and any 1/4" TRS jack plug as an instrument. So if you intend to use microphones I urge you to get an XLR cable to connect them. It is basically necessary you use XLR for condenser microphones to utilize the 48V phantom power. Even with a dynamic microphone, I really recommend you use an XLR connection. A dynamic microphone using a 1/4" TRS will be much quieter than one using an XLR, and can hardly be heard through a headphone monitor even with the gain turned up 100%.

#2 - MONITORS. If you intend to use headphones as a monitor (to listen to yourself as you record), you will need headphones ending in a 1/4" jack (6.35mm). Most headphones rarely end in anything other than a 1/8" jack (3.5mm), so it is 99% likely you will need an adapter. Get yourself a 1/8" female to 1/4" male TRS adapter if you want to use headphones. You can find these easily at Wal-Mart, BestBuy, etc. As a side note, on the back are two line outputs that also require 1/4" TRS jack plugs - these are for loudspeakers, not headphones. There is only one jack for one pair of headphones. (I am pretty sure you can use a headphone splitter if you need more headphones.)

#3 - DRIVERS. The package insert for this product will tell you to register your product on their website so you can download a USB driver. Go ahead and register because there are other free downloads, but DO NOT install the USB drivers from focusrite.com if you are using Windows. If you already installed it, you must uninstall it by going to Control Panel > Uninstall a Program. Go to http://beta.focusrite.com/releases/focusrite_usb2_drivers/ and download/install the latest USB2 driver (last I checked, there was only one available). You will know the driver is working if Line Output and Line Input appear and are enabled in Control Panel > Sound when you plug in the interface.

#4 - Find, download, and read the manual for this product. It will save you from any disappointment or surprises.

Input: The Yamaha MD-BT01 is a well-engineered product that works mostly as advertised, with the exception that you have to jump through a few hoops to get it working at all on iOS device.  I should start out by saying that this a $50 Bluetooth adapter that functionally performs the same task as a $10 5-pin DIN MIDI cable...it just does it wirelessly.  Therefore, I consider it more of a convenience item than a true necessity.  One exception to that argument might be that you can have several of them running at once (five, I believe).  So you could imagine having an interface with only 1 MIDI connections, and now you could have MIDI running (wirelessly) to several different hardware units, which is pretty cool.

The two important "issues" for you to be aware of before buying the MD-BT01 are: (1) It requires MIDI power and both the IN and OUT jacks; and (2) iOS Bluetooth doesn't recognize it natively, so Yamaha has engineered a software workaround.  The device runs off the power of the hardware you plug it into IF your device offers MIDI power.  There are more units than you'd think that do not have MIDI power.  This would include all of the Korg Volca series, which only has a MIDI in jack.  By contrast, the Korg Minilogue and Roland Boutique series do provide MIDI power to run the device.

Once powered up, you can't just go to your Bluetooth menu in "Settings" and find the MD-BT01.  You have download Yamaha's utility app to find the device and connect to it.  You can also rename the unit or do firmware updates from that utility.  As several reviewers have pointed out, I think you also have to identify it as a MIDI destination in an app that supports it.  There are several of these, but I found that if I skipped this step, I couldn't just load up a sequencer app (like Inifinite Looper or Xequence) and make the connection.  But once it works, it generally works.

I should point out that my primary concern prior to buying the device - latency - really isn't much of an issue at all.  The latency seems pretty minimal, and if you're just using the MIDI connection for sequencing or to mess with control parameters on a synth, it's basically a non-factor anyway.

The device is a little bulky, and maybe a little expensive for what it does.  I suspect that this is the type of device that will seem archaic in 5-10 years, but then again, MIDI is still with us, and has been since around 1983.  The primary reason I like and wanted the MD-BT01 is to connect my iPhone or iPad to a hardware synth with needing to use a MIDI interface.  If you're willing to deal with a few steps along the way, it works pretty well for that objective.

Input: I'm very happy with my G3X. It's definitely built really strong and feels like it can stand quite a beating. The sound quality is great and doesn't have that digital computerized 'fake amp' sound. I also own a Line6 PodXT (which is still one of my most favorite modellers), a BOSS GT-8, Digitech GNX3 (which sounds very digital). So i have a lot of different references to compare it with. This little baby does an outstanding job at amp modelling and the various FX. It's very easy to operate this device and finding the sound you're looking for shouldn't take you long at all.

Operating the G3X with a set of Eneloop rechargeable batteries offers you many hours of running it without the need of the (included) power brick. I prefer the Eneloops since they will hold their charge for a much longer time than regular rechargeable batteries when leaving it in the device without using it for an extended period.

The LCD screen is nice and bright and the foot switches and knobs feel very solid and work very responsive and smooth.

I decided to get the version with the expression pedal. Even with the pedal it's still really nice compact and less than half the size of my other full size (floorboard) modellers. This thing is great for traveling for sure and will easily fit in a small case or backpack.

The sound of the built-in rhythm patterns isn't bad at all. I like it a lot better than the sound of the drums in my Digitech GNX-3 or my Boss DR-5 drum computer. The looper works great too, it has a nice long recording time and operates easy and smooth. I only wish it would record and playback the guitar sound in stereo instead of mono.

Hooking it up to a PC with USB is super easy as well. It's great that the computer will power the device through USB when you don't have the power hooked up to it or no batteries inserted. And using the included library software on your computer makes presets even easier to (re)organize. The visual representation of all the built-in amps and stomp boxes makes it a breeze to set up a preset real fast.

I have the G3X for a few months now and am very impressed and happy with the overall value of this product. I would highly recommend this for the traveling musician but also for the beginning player that just likes to play in the privacy of his own room and try out many different sounds and effects without breaking the bank. This bad boy is an absolute joy to play around with.

Two metal horns way up!

Input: What a lame name and color for such a unique pedal. Oh well.  This thing should cost more than $100 so I won't complain.

It really boils down to a set of DS-1 and SD-1 circuits tied together with the "color" knob to blend them along with other essential tweaks too lengthy to go into here.  I've owned a Boss Blues Driver for a while now and have found it limited for creamier tones.  It's a great pedal don't get me wrong but it really just sounds like a blackface Fender cranked.  I'm currently running a modded Blues Jr. with a Cannabis Rex which gives me good basic blackface tones.

Here's where this pedal shines IMHO.  i.e., PROS

With a Tele with Fender OV pups and the pedal tone @ 7, drive @ 9, and color @ 2 o'clock, respectively, this thing sounds almost exactly like a Vox AC-15 on the top boost channel with the gain and master at around 10 o'clock.  I actually tried this pedal with the above settings on my brothers AC-15 and couldn't believe how similar it sounded.  That chimey natural sweet breakup is here in spades, pretty amazing since I wasn't necessarily looking for a Vox simulator! This tone sounds like nothing you'd get from a DS-1 or SD-1.

With a Les Paul studio and pedal tone @ 9, drive@ 3, and color @ 2 o'clock, respectively, this thing sounds similar to a cranked Marshall.  Crazy pinch harmonics and chunky fatness and sustain for days.  It handily slapped the Rat 2 all over the room with the sheer gutsiness of harmonic complexity and killed it in dynamics as well at lower gain settings. Think of the raspy guitar tone from GNR's Paradise City and you'll get the idea.  This tone sounds like nothing you'd get from a DS-1 or SD-1.

CONS

1. The tone knob seems pretty useless to me anywhere above 9 o'clock.  I haven't played it on stage or in a band though so maybe it would be useful in such scenarios.

2. It's not a transparent pedal but nowhere near as bad as a lot of other stuff out there cheap and/or expensive.  In a live situation I doubt you'd notice it but sitting in front of the amp in a quiet room you'll hear some of your highs go bye-bye.  I bet the tone knob could be tweaked to adjust the top end sparkle but honestly the pedal is so fun to play you'll get over it..

3. The color knob is tricky.  I could not find a use for it anywhere below 12 o'clock.  It started to sound a lot like an SD-1 which isn't a terrible pedal.  I guess if you were recording you'd find this useful for getting compressed singing lead tones.

4. It's an ugly orange/yellow pedal that looks like it was marketed by the engineering department.

Manager: Hey you Mr. Smart Engineer with mismatched clothes. Come up with a name and look for the pedal by next week.  I was slacking off reading articles about golf clubs so you need to hurry up and get this done even though you've designed a totally awesome and unique sounding pedal in the minimal time/budget we provided you.

ENGINEER: Call it the Overdrive / Distortion because that's what it is.

Is it?  I don't think so. But what do I know? I'm just an engineer who loves to play guitar and build pedals sometimes.

Input: I ordered this package because I wanted a playable violin with all the necessary accessories at the lowest price.  I was able to open the case, rosin the bow, position the bridge, tune up the violin and start playing.

If you buy a violin from a shop, they will set it up for you.  Setting up is the process of making final adjustments to the violin so that it functions smoothly and suits the musician.  Those of us who buy online have to either complete the setup ourselves or find someone to do it for us.  The Merano violin comes with an instruction sheet called "How to Set Up a Violin".  It tells how to install the bridge, how to tune the violin, and how to rosin the bow.  At the very end, the instructions mention that you might also want to sand the bridge down one millimeter at a time until you are satisfied with the way the violin plays.  The instructions also mention that you can put rosin on the tuning pegs to keep them from slipping.

If you're not comfortable and happy with the way the violin plays after the basic setup, you need to go back to the Internet and find out how to do the more advanced adjustments.  You may want to adjust the string height above the fingerboard, the separation between strings, and the curve of the top of the bridge.

The default setup of the Merano violin didn't suit me.  The strings were too high for my taste, which means extra force must be applied by the fingers to press strings down to the fingerboard.  Also, the strings were set too close together for my big blunt fingers.  The default setup might be okay for someone with long thin fingers.  I lowered my strings by sanding down the bridge and filing down the nut of the violin.  I increased the separation between strings by filing new notches in the nut with a triangular file.  It took me about two hours.

One thing I really like about this inexpensive violin is that if I drop it or make some mistake adjusting it, the maximum possible damage is still less than $100.  My other violin is a professional grade instrument and I'm afraid to do any adjustment on it myself for fear of making a mistake.  I think the Merano will probably become my favorite violin for casual playing.

Update: After six weeks I'm still pleased with the violin.

Input: I love this! Before purchasing this, I had been researching and reading so many reviews of different guitar humidifiers. This is the only guitar humidifier I could find that did not have any history of it leaking inside guitars. This was very important to me. I would be devastated if it were to leak inside my guitar. I currently own a single unit humitar, as well as a humitar/humireader package. I really do trust that this will not leak into my guitar. It is very simple, all you have to do is soak distilled water into the sponge every week. The sponge holds a lot of water! I recommend purchasing the humitar/humireader package first. The humireader is pretty accurate, I have another humidity monitor in my room, and they are about 1-2% off. The humidity in the guitar case is going to be different then the humidity inside the guitar. It is a good idea to monitor the humidity levels because you do not want to over or under humidify your guitar. There have been a few instances where the humireader in my guitar read 65%, which proves that this product is effective but that is way over the recommended humidity level. I would not have otherwise knew I that the humidifying levels where too high without the humireader. It is cheaper to buy the humitar/humitar package together, rather than buying the only the humireader. The only thing that would make this product better is if it didn't stretch the guitar strings so far apart. Just would like if the product was a little thinner. I hope this was helpful. Definitely recommended!

Input: This contents of this review are based on that fact that this keyboard costs under $200.  Just knowing that it costs under $200 should tell you right off the bat this is not for a professional musician, nor will it have professional quality and tone.
However,  if you are like me and just beginning or even perhaps an intermediate musician looking for a practice keyboard, this is probably the keyboard you want to buy.
I tried out many many keyboard in the $200 price range and this is the ONLY one I would buy.  If it were not for this keyboard, I would have spent over $500 on a Yamaha.
What I like about this is the keyboard has a semi-weighted feel to the keys and the piano tones are very lush and nice. The organ tones as well are awesome.
After using it for a few months the keys are starting to 'crackle' a little and realistically this keyboard could probably only stand about 3-4 years of use before it breaks down.
I have no regrets at all about purchasing this.  If I continue to play and enjoy playing, I will probably go out and buy a $700 range professional digital piano or keyboard down the road and sell this one or give it away.
Also, you do need to purchase an a/c power supply (so add another $20) and probably a simple stand ($25).  So make sure you factor in another $45 for accessories.
If you are the type of person who likes to buy once and have a product for life, this may not be what you are looking for.  I would recommend a higher quality instrument.
If you just want to start playing right away and don't have a big budget, this is the ONE keyboard to get.  Quite frankly, almost any keyboard under $200 is a piece of junk!

Input: NOTE - I bought these headphones from Status Audio direct during the Black Friday sale and received them a couple days ago, hence why this is not a verified purchase.
These are definitely the best closed back headphones I've owned to date [you can just my head-fi username conquerator2 for a complete list of gear that I've owned and tried]. They are a bit V shaped, with a deep punchy bass response and a broader 5.5 - 7K treble rise but they aren't nearly as recessed in the midrange as most V shaped headphones. On the contrary, these headphones are surprisingly detailed, with very good soundstage and imaging and a surprisingly open sound, without hints of a closed-in feel, which closed back headphones usually have. They are pretty comfy too [great pads] and the build quality is surprisingly decent! You can use any slim profile 3.5mm or 1/8' cable with these; I wasn't a big fan of the tangly straight or coiled cables that were included, so I use a nuforce cable. In conclusion, I am fairly impressed at what these headphones can achieve, considering the price. I enjoy listening to music on them and they can be a good commute headphone too, and why I wouldn't say they'd be my first pick if I were looking for a completely flat monitoring headphone [open headphones usually have an edge here], these will find a permanent staple in my productions as a great closed back for testing aspects like soundstage, bass and highs. These absolutely trounce Beats and would be my current recommendation in this price range.

Input: I recently purchased an LPB-1 because I had a need for a straight "booster" on my pedal board.  Boost pedals, as a concept, are an extremely straightforward concept, but the way they impact tone through an amp depends quite a bit on placement in the signal chain, settings, and the type of amp.  With these issues in mind, I struggled a bit to decide between a 4- or 5-star review, since the LPB-1 has some limitations conveying clean, "transparent" boost.  But given that EHX has made it extremely affordable ($40) and it functions very well for a particular type of boosted sound, I decided that there was enough "function for value" here to warrant 5 stars.

Boosts raise the amount gain in your signal, so the assumption by many is that this makes the audio "louder".  While this can be true, particularly if the boost is used later in the signal chain, boosts can just as much increase the saturation of the input signal, and hitting the preamp of a tube amp (or perhaps some modeling amps) may also cause it to overdrive.  The EHX LPB-1 has a single knob for adjusting the amount of added gain - there are no tone controls or additional parameters.  But, used with other pedals (and the settings on your amp), tone control in a booster is more of a luxury than a necessity.

Choosing between boosters can be difficult because you really won't know how they function until you use them with your own rig.  I opted for the LPB-1 instead of the MXR Micro Amp (itself a single-knob industry standard) because the LPB-1 tends to be warmer and fuller sounding.  On a large, bassy amplifier, this may not be desirable.  But on a 10" bright combo amp, such as my Fender Super Champ X2, this is a desirable quality.

Some critics of the LPB-1 have noted that the LPB-1 will get "dirtier" more easily than other boost pedals.  Some have even noticed that there is a mid boost with overdrive, almost like a Tubescreamer.  However, this was a sound I actually wanted, and if you have a amp that can stay clean at high enough volumes, the LPB-1 should add additional saturation and "fullness" to that tone, without making it sound like an overdrive pedal.

I think the LPB-1 may make sense for a lot of players who use smaller, brighter amps since it is affordable and pairs well with that type of sound.  If your are looking for a boost to stack in front of other overdrive pedals to emphasize for lead work, you could consider the Micro Amp, or something with tone controls like the Micro Amp+ or Blackstar LT Boost.  In my case, I have the Soul Food (also made by EHX), which offers a lot of clean boost at low overdrive settings, but is considerably brighter than this LPB-1.  Between the two, I should have most of my needs covered.  The LPB-1 is a tested and proven classic and a great value for a blues/crunch sound, or to emphasize other pedals by giving them "just a little more".

On the plus side, I love the sound quality of these headphones.  While they are not sound cancelling, they are noise isolating.  My music sounds really good through these; I'm hearing all sorts of new layers in songs I thought I knew like the back of my hand!

Overall, the headphones sound great, but are not constructed all that well.  They're not worth 30 dollars, but I'm not regretting my purchase of them either.

Input: I purchased this guitar because it had a Telecaster body and was cheaper than a Fender or the Squire version of Fender. A guitar's a guitar right?
Well, the reason it's cheaper is because cheaper parts were made to put it together.

The black paint on the body picks up the slightest scratch. Picture a cheap paint job on a car compared to a really well done paint job on a car. The well done paint job is going to cost more.

The pickups are adequate. I changed the pickups to Fender pickups and there was a significant difference in tone and volume.

I like the guitar for the reasons I purchased it, it wasn't expensive and had a Telecaster body. But I dislike the guitar because, well, it's cheaply made in comparison to the Fender or Squire models. If I had to do it all over again, I'd invest $80 more dollars and get the Squire.

If you're not a guitar fanatic and just want a cost efficient Telecaster body, this is an adequate guitar but if you're looking for a guitar to gig with or actually take it outside of your house, you'll need to change the pickups and expect the paint to be lacking in quality.

I am not deducting points for this, as obviously, the dimensions are available and I should have looked into it more closely before ordering - but I still think it's fair to warn you, it's oddly large, garish, and frankly just not very nice to hold or look at in person.

Aesthetics aside, I would have liked that the mic head could be panned vertically as you really need to lean down to speak directly into it when having it on a desk. The design of the mount and the stand that accompany it don't allow for this. Prepare to stoop a bit to get good vocal contact. The lack of a mute button, or an off switch of any kind was also disappointing.

Janky Construction: The LED light in mine that sits front and center is mounted about 20 degrees off of flush. The silver band that divides the axis of the orb is a sticker made to simulate the look of brushed metal. Because mine was sloppily applied and has air bubbles in it, the effect is ...not achieved. The small desk stand that ships with it is made of a very cheap alloy, the lock threads on the telescopic function barely work, and the black rubber feet are also prone to marking up your desk if you move it around. The "Blue" logo front and center is a horribly chromed plastic. All in all... a major bummer quality wise. Assembled in China, and without care or oversight from anyone with an eye for detail.

The design eccentricities (large size, garish chrome grill) might have worked if the materials used had been quality. Then again, maybe I'm asking too much of a 100 dollar piece of hardware. Still, based on this experience, I don't think I will buy a mic made by Blue again. They should have toned down the ambitious design flourishes if they didn't have the money to execute them with good materials.

Input: So this is my second review of Gibson Melody Makers. I am completely satisfied with my first Les Paul version. I ordered 2 more of the SG version and will describe what I recieved.

The first one was perfect. No issues, but it was noticeably heavy. More about this later.

The second one had some of the same issues that sgbuyer describes. The pick guard was warped or had bubbled up in the exact same spot as his, near the bridge and jack. Mine also has lifted up at the point near the bottom cut away. Some of the pick guard screws are install at an angle and not perpendicular to the guitar surface. It looks sloppy. The headstock, fingerboard and frets also show a lack of attention. The back of the headstock where the serial # is stamped was not finished completely. It was not sanded flat so the first and last number of the serial number are very faint. The "made in" stamp is barely discernable. Yes these are cosmetic, but it show a lack of quality control for this guitar. How hard can it be to sand it flat and not have the surface have "rolling hills" which prevent the stamp from working properly. The fingerboard is missing a chunck at the nut in the first fret at the bottom e string. It looks like the corner edge splintered off. The surface between frets show unsanded wood blothches, that would have disappeared had a hair more wood been sanded off. The frets have some kind or residue on the sides, corrosion or wood stain which will not scratch off.

I find it weird that one instrument can have so many issues especially in light of the personally signed quality inspection check list Gibson provides with the guitar. One of these cosmetic issues would be acceptable to me. All of them together is just not right.

These guitars may have a wide spec variance because of the cheap price, understandably. The SG model had the lighter colored maple fingerboard, the les Paul I bought has a darker wood with a different grain. Another example of this variance is the difference in weight between the 2 SGs. One felt as heavy as a real Les Paul when I pulled it from the box. One weighed 6.4 lbs (as did my MM LP). The other weighed 7.4 lbs! A full pound heavier. Both sound and play fine though.

EDIT: I also contacted Gibson. The Customer service guy was not very patient but did issue me a RMA#. He said they might just send me another if it can't be repaired. I was told I would need to pay for return shipping. That was the deal breaker. I just returned it to amazon.

Input: To give you a bit of background, I bought this product about 6 months ago when I started building my recording studio and was very excited about the build quality and the looks of the thing. It is built like a tank and looks gorgeous. It was going to be the centerpiece of my studio.

Then I kept running into issues with pops and crackles even on my incredibly fast computer (4.5 Ghz overclocked with 8 gb of ram and no bottlenecks). I thought it must be some sort of issue with how windows 7 is dealing with this usb audio interface because latencymon kept telling me that my computer was unsuitable for real-time audio. So I went on several google marathons trying to figure out the issue and played with every setting imaginable both in windows and in my bios. I updated every driver and opened my pc countless times trying to reconfigure hardware.

I kept being defeated by this little box, but I noticed the vast amount of forum threads where people were having problems with this product on windows computers. And it seemed Native Instruments was just completely ignoring the community. So today I ran across a thread that just had a lot of information pointing to the fact that this might just be a faulty product with bad drivers for windows. It made so much sense because I tried disconnecting the device and running latencymon, which showed a totally health system and right after I plugged it in the problems immediately came back. I cannot believe I wasted 6 months of my time to figure this out!

http://www.native-instruments.com/forum/threads/komplete-audio-6-clicks-dropouts-cpu-spikes-every-15-seconds. 217813/

I will be getting rid of this product as fast as I can and buying the cheaper focusrite scarlett 2i2, which nobody is having problems with.

TL;DR: Don't buy this product if you own a windows computer. All the optimization in the world will not fix the faulty drivers that come with this audio interface and you won't be getting any help from the manufacturer.

Input: I wrote a review of the Mix5 in February and gave it 3 stars. After playing with the Mackie mixer for a few months, I've decided to knock it down a star. Even my little Behringer Xenyx Q302USB auxiliary mixer sounds nicer than this Mackie unit, in spite of the fact that the Behringer mixer doesn't have balanced jacks (except for the single mic input).

I suspect the preamps in the Behringer mixers are just better than these Mackie Mix-series preamps. If you want to go for sound quality, and can live without balanced main outs, I think you should go with the Behringer Xenyx 502. It has the added benefit of being cheaper than the Mix5.

I have never used any of the Mackie high-end project boards, meaning the VLZ series, so I can't make any comparisons to those, unfortunately. Some people absolutely swear by them. I'm not knocking them. But if you don't want to spend $100 on a 402VLZ4, I'd recommend going with the Behringer Xenyx 502.

Its not a bad idea, but they could have made the transmitter smaller or made it so it plugs into your guitar and the transmitter clipped on your guitar strap. I think I'll be modifying mine to do that... Would have been nice if they gave a Y adapter for charging both units at the same time. So in short , yes it is too good to be true.

Input: I am a big fan of sennheiser products and have several headphones and cardioid and lavalier microphones from the company, but the MKE 400 is a let-down for the entire brand. First, it's poorly titled, because this is not a shotgun microphone in the most remote definition of the term - it catches just as much audio from in front of you as it does beside and behind you. Furthermore, if you happen to be recording anywhere that has any sort of HVAC system, even if it is barely noticeable to the human ear, this mic will pick it up, amplify it and make your audio absolute garbage. Sure, you can try to remove the hiss with a high pass filter in various applications, but the hiss is so incredibly strong that, in order to remove it all, you end up garbling up the dialogue you intended to record. Ultimately, this is not really any better than your in-camera microphone, and there are significantly better options out there from other, better manufacturers. To sum up:

Pros
-shock mount hasn't broken and doesn't noticeably transfer rattling to the microphone
-battery life is good, but it won't tell you when it's out
-plugs straight into the camera

Cons
-sound quality sucks like a vacuum (and sounds like one is running too!)
-no built-in high pass filter
-captures sound around the subject, rather than just the subject
-no live monitoring option
-looks, feels and is flimsy
-everything else

Buy a Rode or step up to an NTG2 or other alternative. Almost anything is better.

Input: Peavey used to build fine PA equipment, As I have owned Peavey PA gear since the early 1980's, but if their XR8600 and this P.O.S. The XR8600 I purchased a few months back had a cheap feel to it, the knobs feel like they are going to come off if you so much as look at them, plus, the XR 8600 replaces older "wood box" models like the XR 696F, which was I.M.H.O. a far superior, professional-grade product, with more bands of master EQ and a ninth channel. At least they've corrected that design error on the XR8600D.

Now, regarding the PVI 4B:
It was defective right out of the box.  Two of the volume pots were binding, and channel #2 had a loud hiss, even when nothing was plugged into that channel.  How did this get passed Peavey Quality Control?  Maybe they should return to manufacturing their products in Meridan, Mississippi and stopped exporting the build (and jobs) to China.

Input: really wanted to love this one. it was $180, and the look is just awesome. but, in studio and on stage, i am pretty disappointed and here is why...

other amazon reviews suggested that it is pretty good about plosives / pops, but it's really not. even in the video demonstration one of the top reviews posted here, you can hear it popping almost immediately.

as for live settings - with any sort of louder rock band - it picks up a lot of the drums, no matter where you're standing. it seems to get excited by the highs of cymbals in a way that it doesn't for just your voice. it's also not super directional, so you really have to eat it on stage.

i also don't recommend it for anyone using any vocal processing (compressor, delay) unless you are using in-ear monitors. this thing feeds back way too easily.

after giving up on it, i went for a completely uncool looking mic - the EV 967 - which has brighter highs, deeper lows, an all around more "studio" sound on stage - and seems to pick up my voice and only my voice, even when i'm right next to my drummer.

the Super Deluxe 55 seems to be much better about anti-feedback and side rejection. might be worth the extra money if the style is super important to you. but remember that while you are committing to this look, you are buying a microphone that you NEED to be RIGHT AGAINST to pick up properly, covering a huge chunk of your face in an unflattering way.

PS i kinda hate that this is labeled "The Elvis Microphone", but i guess that's what it is.

Input: I've never felt compelled to submit a review for any of my Amazon purchases, but this expereince with Fender warranted some comments.

I ordered this guitar package from Amazon and received it in 3 days even with super-saver shipping. Great service from Amazon.

I opened the kit and was prepping to plug it in and try it out when I realized there was no guitar cable included - pretty useless without a cable. I contacted Fender and they mailed a cable at no charge, but it took them a week (7 days) to do it. Once I was able to actually test the guitar, there was no Volume control knob, only three Tone control knobs. Obviously the top control was for the volume and it had the wrong knob assembled to it. I also realized there were no "setup/adjustment sheet" included. I contacted fender about these additional errors and they said they'd send them. I received the paperwork with no Volume knob. At that point, I cut my loses (and headaches) and I returned the package for Fender to deal with as there were simply to many quality control issues with the package I received, and the Fender rep seemed rather "slack" about the whole deal, calling it a "simple error" and didn't consider it "poor" quality.

The guitar and amp themselves seemed okay (I guess), but I received the impression that Fender has some quality control/assurance issues that they're not real concerned about addressing, which lead me to wonder what else may be wrong.

Great price, shipping and return policy for Amazon, poor quality control and slacker attitude from Fender.

Input: I have five cats and managing the litter boxes has become...interesting. This box is just what the doctor/vet ordered. I do wish they made a version of this that had the scoop holder portion lopped off, since it is really only necessary to have one of those if you have a location dedicated to multiple litter boxes and it would make fitting a second one in a lot easier. The depth of them is very nice since little gets tracked out of the box and "digging" rarely spills over the sides for my cats. For the two non-laundryroom litter boxes I have in the house, at other locations, I use two of the dome covered Boodabox litter boxes, which work well in a less traditional litter box setting (once the cats get used to entering them). Do grab  a forty pound box or two of litter though, since it takes about 30 pounds to fill this mammoth box to a decent depth with litter.

Update: I cut the scoop stowage portion, using my Bosch scroll saw, off one of these boxes quite some time ago to make it a better fit, it was easy to do and has worked out very well in the shorter space I had for it.

Input: All three of my cats LOVE this scratcher! I should have gotten more since they are constantly chasing each other off of it. It's sturdy and at 3" thick they won't be destroying it anytime soon. I love that it can be recycled after they destroy it and that it's sturdily assembled and arrived right in time! It comes with a bag of very finely ground catnip which I sprinkled on the scratcher.  Now comes my only complaint, I noticed when one of the cats moved the scratcher the catnip had gone through the spaces between the cardboard and onto the floor. Maybe the bottom should have been solid to prevent that, but then we wouldn't be able to flip it over when/if one side begins to wear down. Not a big deal since 2 of the cats and the dog love catnip and cleaned it up right away. Regardless the cats are leaving the furniture alone and when one of them isn't scratching it, then one of them are laying on it and purring like the happiest kitties in the world!!  I will update in a few months to see if their love affair lasts and if the scratcher holds up well. So far though this meow mommy loves seeing her fuzzy children so happy!

So it hasn't even been a month yet, and I have ordered a second one.  Not because there is anything wrong with the first one, but because my cats fight over it constantly!!  So far the first one is holding up well, but with three cats in the house there was always someone who wanted to scratch while someone else was taking a nap on top of the scratcher and then one would end up pummeling the other!  Now with two in the house there seems to be some semblance of peace restored in my home!  Who knew some cardboard would make them so happy!!  As long as it continues to hold up well and make it worth the list price of $34.95 I will be ecstatic!!

We have had both of our scratchers for 4 months or so, and my furry children still continue to use them as both a scratcher and a bed every day. Granted the cardboard has shredded some but when I vacuum  every few days I just pick up the scratcher and knock it a few times over a trashcan and it's good to go again! The scratcher is holding up great even with 3 kitties constantly abusing it with their claws.

~* UPDATE -- 8/2016 *~
Yes Another Update! We ended up with 3 scratchers in our house - which worked great since there were three kitties in the house at the time. Sadly :( one had to cross the bridge, but he loved his scratcher, (yes they all seem to have assigned scratchers,) until the day he left us! Anyway - it has been over 2 years since we purchased our first one, and even though it is a little worse for wear, it is still going strong! We haven't even needed to flip it over yet! We just knock the loose cardboard shavings over the trash can a few times a week and call it good to go! It took a few weeks for the third one, that belonged to our old, fat cat to be used by the other two - but now it is being shared by both of them as a secondary bed/scratcher. So it is still definitely worth the purchase price as far as I & my fur babies are concerned!!

Input: I was excited to install this product, especially after reading the reviews. We have two large and very energetic dogs, and we wanted to let them play in the yard more often, until we have our property fenced.

Installation of the product couldn't be easier. Simply plug it in, then walk around your property with one of the collars turned on in beep-only mode.  This will help you find the boundaries. Adjustment of the boundaries is simple via the boundary adjustment wheel. Once you are satisfied with your boundaries, mark them with the included flags.

Training the dogs was simple, using the included training instructions. After 3 days, my dog was trained.

However, I did notice a "dead" spot in our boundary. The collar simply would not  indicate it had left the boundary. Sometimes, after walking a dozen or so yards, it would immediately start to beep and initiate a shock, with no warning. I did not try this with the dog, but it would have been very confusing for the dog to try to find the boundary at this point. Since he would have had no warning, this simply would not do.

I also noticed the boundaries were very inconsistent. Sometimes by a matter of 5' or more. I could not reliably place the flags because the boundaries would differ so much from test to test.

I called PetSafe technical support, after 4 days of tweaking the system and training our dogs. PetSafe them began asking me a series of questions about placement and devices I had in my home. None of this was included in the pre-purchase information, the manual, or any of the technical information on the site.

Here's what it boils down to:

Do not place your transmitter near electronic equipment, including stereo speakers. PetSafe states 3', but when I notified the tech that it was approximately 5' away, the tech stated this may still be an issue. This should be printed in pre-purchase information.

The transmitter may be affected by certain types of WiFi routers. They did not tell me which ones, but this is critical information for a buyer to know. Practically everyone has WiFi in their home these days. Since they are aware of these issues, this should also be printed in pre-purchase information.

Finally, these transmitters are not compatible with wireless security systems, at all. The operate on the same frequency and I was told by the tech that this was likely the source of my problems. This can cause the transmitter to become unreliable, even shocking the animal while they are inside the zone. Essentially, these units are useless to you if you have a wireless security system. This is important information for the buyer to know, and a very common scenario. Since they are aware of these issues, this should also be printed in pre-purchase information.

The product seems decent. Easy to set up, easy to use, and clear training documentation for your animal. However, the lack of pre-purchase and post-purchase support information on product compatibility is very poor, and unacceptable for a product in this price range, especially given the time commitment required to get the system up and running and your pet trained. Because of this, I am only giving two stars.

Input: This is not the marvelous deterrent I'd hoped it would be.

When I got the mat, I immediately added double-sided tape to the top of it as an extra measure against my cats.  They are constantly getting up on my kitchen counters and stovetop in search of food, or who knows what else.  I am a stickler for clean eating and food preparation surfaces, so the idea of nasty litter-box feet all over my counters was disgusting!

I bought the mat, and my cats pretty much ignored it.  They would stand on whatever piece of counter top wasn't covered by the mat, step over the mat, and be on their way. Several times in the middle of the night I'd hear it go off, and come downstairs to see that the cat is standing on the mat, not a care in the world for the ridiculously loud beeping going on.  I mean, if that sound could wake me up while I'm on an entirely different floor and sound asleep, shouldn't it bother a cat's sensitive hearing?  Apparently not.

That, or my cats are just spiteful jerks who are purposefully setting this thing off....

Anyway, really all it does is prevent the cats from LAYING DOWN on the mat, and that's only because of the tape.

I did notice that the mat really scares the bejeezus out of my dogs when it goes off, so I'm keeping it for those times when we don't want them in a certain area, such as on a patch of freshly shampooed carpet or somesuch.

Input: I thought with mostly high reviews that this item would be absolutely adorable and had high expectations for it. I've always spoiled my cat and she has lots of beds, but I thought this would be perfect for her and even though it was just under $27 plus another $15 for shipping, my cat was worth it, so I decided to spend the extra money (more than I've ever paid for with a bed for her) and get what looked like an adorable bed!

I was highly disappointed upon receiving it with the quality for what I'd paid for this bed. Upon opening the box, the frilly fabric on both ends had long strings loose EVERYWHERE, so needless to say, I had to cut those excess strings off so it did not become a hazard to my cat if she got hold of them and ingested them. Then I discover that the vinyl bottom was coming loose in MANY areas from the foam bed itself. I in turn super glued the vinyl to the bottom of the foam (which I should NOT have had to do) but contacted the seller (Rowland Direct Wholesale) as I only saw this as a temporary solution and really poor quality that I'd have to go to these lengths to "fix" a pet bed that I paid enough for that I expected A LOT better quality for.

The seller's reply to all this was to provide pictures. I told them that is kind of hard to do when, as I'd already told them in my 1st email if they would have read it, the strings were removed IMMEDIATELY before my cat even got the bed as it provided a hazard to my cat if swallowed, so I told them it's not possible to provide pics of that but since the vinyl was super glued back onto the foam, that too is hard to take pics of unless they wanted me to try to pry it apart where I'd super glued it and then have to either "fix" the bed again OR have a more damaged product than I had to begin with. Their response was something along the lines of they would check into the issues for the future and if I had further questions about the item to contact them back by email again.

So really the seller was of no help at all. At no time was it asked that I return the horribly made product to them in exchange for getting a different one sent and also a replacement was never offered.

I advised the seller I will NEVER order anything from them again if this is the quality with which things are made from them when I paid a significant amount of money and that for what I paid, I should have gotten a better quality product. In the emails, they never directly replied to that comment even though it was said several times.

My cat LOVES the bed- if you choose to purchase this product, I'd advise anyone about the pillow it comes with as there is a rhinestone on the pillow on the ribbon that could easily be chewed off and become a choking hazard - my cat is always trying to chew at it, so I have to keep the pillow facing down so she doesn't chew it off and swallow it and have it become a choking hazard. As I stated in my title for this review- cute concept, horrible quality!

I will NEVER order from this seller again with the lack of help and lack of good customer service, and would honestly never recommend this product. I know of someone else who ordered the same bed and got it around the same time as I did and they had the EXACT same issues with the quality of the product-- so knowing it was not just me that got a faulty, horribly made product, I would never recommend this product since you expect better quality when you pay this much or at the very least better customer care- the product and seller failed in both those areas.

Not dropping crystals on the carpet or in the entry to my apt building would be a plus too.  Amazon actually removed this item from their store for a while (according to the customer service rep I last talked to) and was supposedly investigating the packaging.  Well, it's back, and I just changed my litter today so I'll try ordering again and see if I can get an intact bag to me in the next 3 weeks.

Input: We rescue/rehabilitate/train Irish Wolfhounds.  About 20 years ago it would have been unheard of for new owners to give up their $1,000.00 plus dogs -- especially as puppies.  But now for various reasons, which can include buying something they've always wanted, not understanding what they are getting into, or because of a change in circumstances, younger IWH's are being put up for adoption.  This year we have rescued two hounds and refused two others, all under the age of 17 months.  Rescuing/adopting an IWH reminds me of Forrest Gump talking about his box of chocolates, you never know what you're going to get.

One of the first physical problems we notice is the tartar buildup (or yellowing) on their teeth.  Evidently many owners don't understand how important dental hygiene is for a hound's quality of life.  This is easily fixed by buying either raw femur beef bones or natural white knuckle bones.  Since we are usually trying to sort out their diets and/or food allergies, we always start with white knuckle bones.  We avoid the barbecued/colored bones since they stain just about everything they touch, especially since our IWH's live with us in our home.  Outside might be another story but any  flavoring could prove to be problematic as far as potential allergies.

It is really amazing how quickly these bones can eliminate any tartar build-up.  You  must exercise caution when giving any dogs something to chew.  Occasionally pieces can break off and be swallowed by an enthusiastic dog so it is very important to supervise your dog(s) when giving them anything to chew or play with.  Chew toys thought to be indestructible often aren't.  It never ceases to amaze me what strong aggressive chewers are able to accomplish once they put their minds to it.  Some Irish Wolfhounds are "shredders", tearing up rugs, doggie beds, boxes, pens, or just about anything within reach.

We've had good luck with these Redbarn Natural White Knuckle Bones.  Our hounds get to chew on them from 10-15 minutes every day before we pick them up.  Anything longer and they get bored with it so the bones typically live to see another day.  While we prefer to use raw bones instead, these are a good way to get your dog's tartar buildup under control.  After their food allergies are sorted out, feel free to give the raw bones a try.

Input: Posted this back on Feb 16, 2016. Happened to be updating some reviews and noticed that this was here anymore though the link to it was still available. Reposting.

We had a neighborhood stray cat and at the start of winter, I was really concerned at how she would do in the cold. At first we tried just creating a shelter for her. While searching Amazon for another option, I came across the K&H Outdoor Kitty House. It was close to perfect.

I've seen a lot of the questions people asked and I want to say that mine came with a plastic flap that attaches to the back with Velcro. This allows the cat to be able to enter or exit via either side. This is really important is places that may have predator's as you don't want the cat to be trapped inside.

The heated pad does work. You do need to put pressure on it to feel the heat. When I first plugged it in at home, it did not feel warm to me. I followed the suggested steps and put a throw pillow on it. Within minutes, I could feel the heat on the pad. After I set it up, I checked it after the cat stepped out and it felt warm inside the house, even before I put my hand on the pad. The construction of this house seems to do a good job of retaining the heat. Between the heat from the pad and the cat's own body heat, it seems pretty cozy. Not warm like if the cat was indoors, but that isn't aways an option with strays.

It did take a day to get the cat to go in the house. We had put out some blankets that the cat was sleeping on and I took one and put it in the house so that the cat's scent was there. That seemed to do the trick and the cat has lived there all winter.

The only reason for four stars instead of five is that I wish the cord was longer. I read different things about using an extension cord. After going to Home Depot to get an extension cord, I spoke with someone from the correct department and felt confident that using the proper gage extension cord would be safe. I also purchased a cord cover, Farm Innovators Model CC-2 Cord Connect Water-Tight Cord Lock - Green for some added safety and have had zero problems this winter. With this plugged in since about the second week of November, I have not noticed any different in the electric bill.

It is pretty good with rain and snow if you can put this in a spot that offers some protection from above. I also angled it so that the wind is never blowing directly in the opening. During the snow, it is easy to put this up higher.

When I purchased this in November, it was about half the price it is now ($77 as I'm writing this - $45 when I purchased it). I wish the cost wasn't almost double as I wish more people would invest in something like this to help make the lives of the local stray's a bit better. I do recommend this for anyone looking to help an outdoor cat who needs some help from the elements.

If this review was helpful, please click yes. Thank you.

Harnesses are not an option for most shelters due to disease control methods...we must unfortunately (for now) use the harsh nylon leashes we can bleach multiple times a day. Input: Last month my wife posted an ecstatic, five-star review about the toy, which she amended to one-star today. The original:

"Life was different when we had an indoor/outdoor cat. We didn't need this type of toy, but our neighborhood wasn't kind to our outdoor cat and we lost him to a coyote:( Eventually we adopted another cat from the local animal shelter. He's a big fluffy handsome boy who weighs over 15 pounds and he lives indoors full time. We wanted a toy to help him get some extra exercise.

"My husband purchased our first Cat's Meow from E-Bay. He purchased a second one from Amazon because our kitty got so much value from the first one. You will need rechargeable batteries if you have the toy on a lot. We sometimes leave it on all night for our cat to play with. It's not indestructible but still works with the tip of the plastic 'tail' chewed off and tears in the nylon 'skirt' that covers the 'tail'. It seems pricey for what it is, but for us the value was there".

Our kitty loves the Cats Meow toy, but it doesn't last. We have now returned three for refund (ordering a new one each time). Two were higher-quality models (one with multiple-speeds) from a warehouse supplier. All failed after about 7 day's use. The very first, purchased from eBay, went for a month. I now have a fourth toy that was lame out of the box -- spinning one direction slowly. That one stopped working after two days use. That's four for four dead, from three different Amazon resellers.

Our cat isn't overly aggressive playing with these toys. The problem is something else. I have one last one coming from Amazon, this supposedly from the official As Seen on TV Store. I'll amend my review, with a report. Our cat will do without if this one fails, too.

Input: This is a lovely video about the United Kingdom from *Families of the World,* and like the other films in this series, it's all about two kids, their families, and their daily lives. Jessica lives on a dairy farm in the west of England with her extended family on their ancestral lands, plus some they rent from Prince Charles. She is a cute kid who is almost overshadowed in her video profile by the adorable animals whom her family raises (primarily very young calves, at their most engaging). James is 10 and lives in Bath, an ancient seaside resort that is part of a modern city. The kids in our family were intrigued by James's narration about the freedoms that British subjects enjoy, which the kids recognized from our own Constitution. They were taken by the beautiful place where he lives and by the mix of the very old and the very new in his life and Jessica's.

Our kids noticed the differences in what people call everyday items (biscuits for cookies, orange squash for an orange juice drink, football for soccer) and were intrigued by the lives of two children who live surrounded by architecture and culture that seem much more storied than our own. This was a good issue to discuss after we all watched the video: What does it mean when we say a country has a culture? What does it mean if a country has a state church, but also has religious freedom? How do the freedoms of these English kids differ from our own, and how are they the same? The Teacher's Guide included with this video has other useful information about activities, history, and a complete transcript of the video narration, which is done by two kids and is in English. (My friends who are ESL teachers love these videos, because the narration is straightforward, interesting, and easy to follow.)

If you go on YouTube, two trailers are available from this video, one for Jessica's section of the film and one for James's: "Families of the United Kingdom (Families of the World)," Rural Trailer and Urban Trailer. Well worth watching, as is the full-length video. This is one of my favorites in this great series.

Input: Back in 2007,Robert Redford made a film about the Iraq War in which he starred and directed entitled "Lions For Lambs".Despite co- starring with Meryl Streep and Tom Cruise,it became both a critical and commercial flop as it was talky,verbose and lacks a central theme. Then he starred in a political thriller "The Company You Keep" and finally starred in a film as the lone cast member in "All Is Lost". This film written and directed by J.C Chandor is about a man who tries to survive after he finds himself trapped in the sea.

Redford,who is simply known as "Our Man",finds himself in the middle of the Indian Ocean. When his sailboat collided with a ship container,he finds the floor of his yacht flooded. This only requires him to abandon it and leave on a ship and try to survive many obstacles in the middle of the sea like a tropical storm,the absence of navigational and communication systems, and lack of food.

This triumph of this movie is the fact that Robert Redford at his age of seventy-six years when it was made has shown that he still has the ability to carry a movie on his own. Also,he provided a memorable performance - probably one of the best if not the best in his career - as the sailor trying to survive being in the middle of the sea considering the challenges he is facing. Despite the fact that there isn't much dialogue in it and many questions aren't answered like why is he alone in the sea,J.C. Chandor provides us an thrilling and entertaining movie that deals with survival in the sea. No question that Redford has gladly rebounded from Lions Of The Lambs and still has the talent to wow his viewers on the big screen.

Input: D.O.A. is a film noir drama film directed by Rudolph Mat, considered one of the best classics of the genre.  D.O.A. reflects the photographic roots of director Rudolph Mat. He compiled an impressive resume as a cinematographer in Hollywood from 1935 (Dante's Inferno, Stella Dallas, The Adventures of Marco Polo, Foreign Correspondent, Pride of the Yankees, and Gilda, among others) until turning to directing in 1947. The lighting, locations, and atmosphere of brooding darkness were captured expertly by Mate

 "Film noir" refers to a genre to refer to films that highlighted the seamy side of life and carried a cynical message.  It typically has certain stylistic (night shots, rain, shadow) and plot (good mix of shady characters. femme fatale, double and triple crosses, ordinary person makes a bad choice, & results in a fatalistic ending.
.
The frantically paced plot revolves around a doomed man's quest to find out who has poisoned him and why  One of the film's many ironies is that his last desperate search involves him in his life more forcefully than he has ever been before... Tracking down his killer just before he dies  discovering the reason for his death  turns out to be the triumph of his life

"DOA" starts with a bang. An accountant (Edmond O'Brien) shows up at a police station and reports a murder - his own! In flashbacks we learn the details as he tries to track down how he was murdered, why, and by whom. Along the way we meet his secretary (Pam Britton), a crooked businessman (William Ching) and his secretary (Beverly Garland), and a gangster (Luther Adler) and his chief henchman (Neville Brand).

Location shooting was just coming into vogue in the early 50s. "Side Street" (1950) gave us an up close noir look at New York and this film does the same for San Francisco.

This film is mandatory viewing for fans of film noir, and a pretty good mystery thriller for the rest.

SPOILER ALERT

The film begins with what a BBC reviewer called "perhaps one of cinema's most innovative opening sequences." The scene is a long, behind-the-back tracking sequence featuring Frank Bigelow (Edmond O'Brien) walking through the hallway of a police station to report his own murder. Oddly, the police almost seem to have been expecting him and already know who he is.

 Marla Rakubian threatens Bigelow when he comes to her for information  A flashback begins with Bigelow in his hometown of Banning, California, where he is an accountant and notary public. He decides to take a one-week vacation in San Francisco, but this does not sit well with Paula Gibson (Pamela Britton), his confidential secretary and girlfriend, as he does not want her to accompany him.

Bigelow accompanies a group from a sales convention on a night on the town. At a "jive" nightclub called "The Fisherman," unnoticed by Bigelow, a stranger swaps his drink for another. The nightclub scene includes one of the earliest depictions of the Beat subculture. The next morning, Bigelow feels ill. He visits a doctor's office, where tests reveal he swallowed a "luminous toxin" for which there is no antidote. A second opinion confirms the grim diagnosis, and the other doctor implies that the poisoning must have been deliberate. Bigelow remembers his drink tasted strange.

With a few days to live at most, Bigelow sets out to untangle the events behind his impending death, interrupted occasionally by phone calls from Paula. She provides the first clue: a man named Eugene Phillips had tried to contact him but died the previous day, purportedly a suicide. Bigelow travels to Phillips' import-export company in Los Angeles, first meeting Miss Foster (Beverly Garland) (whose on-screen credit reads "Beverly Campbell"), the secretary, and then Mr. Halliday (William Ching), the company's comptroller, who tells him Eugene Phillips committed suicide. From there the trail leads to Phillips' widow (Lynn Baggett) and brother Stanley (Henry Hart).

The key to the mystery is a bill of sale for what turns out to be stolen iridium. Bigelow had notarized the document for Eugene Phillips six months earlier. He connects Phillips' mistress, Marla Rakubian (Laurette Luez), to gangsters led by Majak (Luther Adler). They capture Bigelow. Since Bigelow has learned too much, Majak orders his psychotic henchman Chester (Neville Brand) to kill him. However, Bigelow manages to escape.

Bigelow thinks Stanley and Miss Foster are his killers, but when he confronts them he finds Stanley has been poisoned tooafter having dinner with Mrs. Phillips. He directs them to call an ambulance and tells them what poison has been ingested so that, in Stanley's case at least, prompt treatment may save his life. Stanley tells Bigelow he found evidence that Halliday and Mrs. Phillips were having an affair. Bigelow realizes that the theft was merely a diversion. Eugene discovered the affair and Halliday killed him.

Halliday and Mrs. Phillips used the investigation of the iridium as a cover for their crime, making it seem that Eugene Phillips had killed himself out of shame. However, when they discovered that there was evidence of his innocence in the notarized bill of sale, Halliday murdered anyone who had knowledge of the bill of sale. Bigelow tracks Halliday down and shoots him to death in an exchange of gunfire.

The flashback comes to an end. Bigelow finishes telling his story at the police station and dies, his last word being "Paula." The police detective taking down the report instructs that his file be marked "D.O.A."

Input: This made-for-TV (in the U.K.) film is an amazing tour de force on a small budget; the sensuous beauty of Florence and the Fiesole countryside, and the opulent grandeur of the scenes shot in Rome, evoke a great love of Italy and the awakening of love in the heroine.  Film scripts are not novels, please note:  they should be a reflection of the filmmaker's view of the essence of the source.  The intuitively clever casting of Timothy and Rafe Spall as the Emersons pere et fils added great authenticity to their depiction of a warm filial relationship.  And the real-life sensuousness and adult vitality of this version, and this Lucy, triumphed over the overstuffed Merchant Ivory film -- with that buxom little pixie Bonham Carter looking much too young to have an adult relationship with either of the men in her scope.  The fact that Andrew Davies did his homework and found Forster's late-in-life ruminations on what might have happened to Lucy and George after their marriage, is delineated in his beautiful coda to the film; and the creation of the long shot of the gorgeous dying light over the Arno transitioning to the light of death over the World War I battlefield is a stroke of cinematic genius. As for the viewers who wish for a happy ending -- Lucy and George lived on the brink of the most disastrous years of the war-torn 20th century, and what happened to them reflects the truth of the history of England's tragedy and triumph in those years. (Remember: Forster thought this film's coda would be a likely conclusion to his tale, too.)
This is a beautiful work of art and I highly recommend it for present and future viewing, especially for all who love Italy and the English countryside.

Input: I initially vowed not to watch this movie. The second had me so offended by everything that Peter Jackson had embellished, and truth to tell, I nearly walked out on the Fellowship of the Ring during the Rivendell sequence. The reason for this is I could give an hour long synopsis of the history and story of Middle-Earth ten years after I was dead, or so it seems, and I have memorized longer passages of the Lord of the Rings than I have of the Bible. (Yes, that is tragic.) That tells you how much of a geek I was.
It should also tell you how much I know of the story, and how important precision is to me, when we are talking of the Lord of the Rings. I hated the whole men-are-weak theme that was in this story from the first of Peter Jackson's films, nor did I care for the manifold other changes that the two movies preceding this one had, and I was, I admit, very angry at the end of the Two Towers, so angry that I decided not to watch this movie, and I will not purchase the Two Towers. After all, I know how the story ends.
This oath to myself, chiefly made to keep me from spending another seven dollars just to get angry, set off a long debate in my mind, a debate that also occurred in my circle of friends and family who have read the books/would be interested in this kind of movie. Their vote was unanimous: see the movie, they said. Yet the debate continued until this very week when I finally relented.
I am glad I did. This was the truest of all three films, and the dialogue was perfect, every signicant line being derived in one fashion or another from the books. The most drastic change from the written work was how the Paths of the Dead sequence was done in the film, and that change was easily forgiven. As I said of the first film, the film was editted for integrity, and this film was more so than the other two combined. Not to say that there were no differences between Peter Jackson's film and the written work, but they were forgivable, and none of the scenes were completely fabricated, or ripped out of the Hobbit, as I felt several scenes were in the second film, or changed excessively, unnecessarily, or counterproductively, as I felt several scenes had been in the first.
The best thing about this production, though, was the goal. For all his embellishments, Peter Jackson did not commit the travesty of trying to do anything different with the ending, nor did he try to add some message to it that was his own and not the intention of Pr. Tolkien. John Huston could not resist doing that with the made for television version released in 1980, and that production was just horrid. This production ended just exactly as it should have, and Peter Jackson's attention to detail was such that the last line of the film was the last line of the book. The entire movie was that true to the story, and Peter Jackson was entirely consistent with how he told it, meaning that he never contradicted himself. Four things only did I note about this production, and only people who have studied this series as much as I have would have even noticed (some of) them. First, the scene inside Mount Doom, once they reached it, was lengthened just a bit for dramatic effect. Secondly, the last time Frodo dons the Ring, he puts it on the wrong finger. Thirdly, the final conversation on Mount Doom's slopes makes no mention of Gollum. Finally, the Elvenship mentioned at the end is called the very last elvenship. Still, none of these detract from the story itself and I only mention them because to me they were incredibly obvious. After the second film, I had passed a death sentence on any possibility of watching the third, but the Lord High Executioner granted a pardon, and was not disappointed. Four and three quarter stars or even four....out of four.

Input: These kinds of movies can be great fun. They're mystery thrillers that can keep the viewer involved and on their toes if done right. This one is done very well.

It's like "The Cube" meets "The Exam" meets "The Killing Room." All these movies have essentially one set with a fixed group of characters all needing to figure out the big puzzle. "Fermat's Room", like "The Cube" is math based and here the characters' lives are at stake, so knowing your stuff is essential. All have been invited to a location for what they think should be a fun evening in a sort of conference. They soon realize they are in a sealed room which gets smaller each time they answer a question incorrectly or later than the time allotment afforded them. Though not all of these characters are mathematicians, they all have particular expertise which can help them from getting crushed to death.

This is a fun movie. The brain teasers come at a fairly regular pace via an electronic device. Everything is done electronically and mechanically so there is no "person" to appeal to. And as each participant questions why they have been included in this death game a lot of secrets come out and a nifty cat and mouse game ensues.

The director and D.P. do a nice job of handling the single set. The actors are all good. The story and secrets unfold and an even pace and the brain teasers are engaging. This makes for a good time. This will not change your life but it should keep you thoroughly entertained throughout.

They are full of the joys of relationships and the lows and go for the default hetro option and think Nate just needs to meet the right girl.

Meanwhile a new neighbour has moved in to another flat - this is Jonny and the two boys sort of hit it off. But Nate still thinks he can not come out to his friends and family (this is Manchester by the way where you have to explain if you are not gay sometimes). Anyway he is also an aspiring musician but just like his love life he lacks confidence in coming out with it all. As you can guess this story is all around the relationships and whether Nate will finally fess up to his true self.

Now this is a rather good indie effort; it does have production issues, the sound could be better and some of the acting is a bit staged. That said this has a great big heart and some funny and tender moments which bring it back from being barely ok. There is nothing new here in terms of plot - as we have all seen it before. And that is ok so long as it is done well and for the most part it is. It is supposed to star Jody Latham of `Shameless' fame but he is only in it for a few minutes of screen time. However, despite its flaws I still enjoyed this and would give a seven out of ten but I am rounding it to four stars as I always appreciate a good indie effort and it's made in Manchester too which is brilliant.
