Input: With all the negative reviews about third party inflation, most people have forgotten to review the actual figure! Yes, it's only $25 at the Disney Store or on their website, but enough about that.

People have given Disney so much grief about their SW acquisition, it's hard to see the GOOD things people are saying about it, this series being one of those good things. The Elite Series is a collector oriented line of diecast figures that really hits the mark and Captain Phasma illustrates that point very well. I have heard people compare some of the Elite Series figures to the Black Series figures, in this case it's really a moot point. Of all the TFA characters Phasma was the most perfectly suited to the diecast style, even though they didn't really use the properly reflective material for her armor.

All the masked figures in this series look great. As the description of the series says on the back, the makers of these figures have worked very closely with Lucasfilm to make the most faithful reproduction of these characters possible, and for the most part they have. I haven't (and probably won't) collect any of the figures outside of TFA without a helmet or mask. Main reason being if there is one shortcoming with this series it is that the paint and sculpt for the human faces aren't the best (especially if you're familiar with NECA).

All in all these figures are not expensive and fall somewhere in line between looking and feeling like a Sideshow Collectibles type statue and a great action quality figure. If you are a Star Wars fan I would highly recommend this series.

Input: I bought these thinking that it would be much better than good polished axles due to the fact that the graphite would last a while on the wheels.  When I installed them the day before the race, I found that the wheels were so snug that they wouldn't spin freely.  I put the axle into my drill and then used the drill to spin them while I held a washcloth tightly against it to remove some of the graphite.  Even after doing this the wheels would still not spin really well.  After a lot of work doing this, I finally got them to the point where they were OK.  Keep in mind that I also bought some of the wheels that were lathed and hollowed out on the inside.  My car actually weighed 5.09 ounces on my scale, but on the derby scale they didn't have hundredths and it weighed 5.0 ounces there and passed inspection.  I put all of the weight in the back of the car which is supposed to be best.  The car was amazing.  So here is how we ended up.

My son's car came in 4th place.  The car that came in first place was made from the same kit as ours.  They put the weight at the bottom in the middle.  His car had good polished axles and he added graphite.  His car was so much faster than ours that it blew me away!  The other two cars that beat us were no where near the quality of car - it came down to the speed of the wheels/axles.  HOWEVER, all this said, my son was proud to come in 4th and had a great time, so I didn't share my frustration with him about these axles.  Next year he will be old enough to help me more and I look forward to that.  I will just buy some good quality polished axles next year.  Hope this helps anyone looking at which axles to buy.

And you should see the stretch they did on the land from India to S.E. Asia. Bangladeshis will be very happy to learn their coast has been stretched to more than double what it is in reality. Perhaps they can ship some of the land back to the Azores as a humanitarian donation.

Input: THE BEBOP IS EASILY WORTH 5 STARS, but not in it's current condition - I will explain.

Background:
I am not new to flying drones. My first drone was the DJI Phantom 2 vision plus - a much more delicate and breakable drone when crashed then the Bebop, but it is also bigger, a lot more powerful, takes better video quality, and originally costing about $400 to $500 more then the Bebop with a Skycontroller.

Bebop Pros:
*The Bebop is very durable for a drone and can take a good amount of crashes without breaking parts. This is huge, because as a new drone pilot you will crash, period.- and probably quite a bit too. Where with other drones, like the Phantom 2 Vision plus, parts will break (like the gimbal) and camera and that alone costs, about $600. to replace.

*The Bebop's video is extremely stable and sturdy without a gimbal. This is huge too. No moving parts, less things that will break when you crash. Video quality isn't as good as say the Phantom 2 Vision plus, but it's well worth the trade to have a very smooth video - and I prefer the Bebop's technology for video stabilization then that of a gimbal.

*Drone is pretty small. Some might think this is a downsize, but I found it a lot more convenient then with my Phantom. It's easy to carry from place to place. I have more confidence using this around my smaller kids, then I do with the larger Phantoms. It's less spicuous to use  when out in public and in parks.

*Skycontroller - The Skycontroller really is the only way to use the Bebop. It has decent distance and makes the Drone much easier to use.

Cons - in this order:
*Price - This is the biggest concern.
With the introduction of DJI Phantom 3, they have set a new standard of quality and value for your money - like it or not. The Bebop with Skycontroller currently is $899.00. The Phantom 3 Advance is $999.00 and it is incredibly superior for only a $100.00 more. It's like buying a Moped for $899.00 or buying a Ducati for $999.00. Are you getting it now?

*Skycontroller \ Price.
The Bebop without the Skycontroller is really just a ridiculously over priced $500.00 toy. Sorry it's true. Without the Skycontroller you don't have the range or distance to really use the drone seriously.. Again, think of buying a Corvette but then being told you can never leave the  Cul-de-sac (dead end street) that you live on with the Corvette. Ya, it's exactly like that. And if you want to buy the Skycontorller separately it's $400 and stupendously expensive - so no win here.

*Cheaply made
For $899.00 I'd expect Parrot to make the Bebop drone feel like I was getting a block of gold, yet instead what I got feels very cheaply made as others have stated. 2 rubber landing gear lost on it's maiden flight. People have complained about this from the beginning and Parrot has done nothing to fix the wrong, at least with DJI, they came out with several versions of the Phantom 2 Vision Plus, in trying to correct problems and make a better drone, but not here with the Bebop. The battery connections has to be held on with a $0.25 Velcro strap. REALLY??? A $900.00 package and I am holding the battery to my Drone with a $0.25 Velcro strap. I would of respected Parrot more if they included a role of duct-tape, but then again that cost more then $0.25 and the price of the drone might of gone up another $50 bucks.

*Lastly Flight time.
With the stock batteries you're lucky if get 7 to 11 minutes of flight time. I'm sorry, $900.00 not acceptable for the price when Phantoms are hitting 16 to 20 minute flight times and the Yuneec Q500+ (you can now get at $999.00) can do 25 minutes of flight time. 7 minutes, 10 minutes, really not enough time to set shots you want to take video of and or pictures. It's just ridiculous .

Would I buy this product again? No, I just can't for it's price.
As much I like the Bebop and in many ways prefer it over DJI's Phantoms for everyday flying and want to give it 5 stars, good common sense tells me, no way - just not worth the money. If the whole package, (Bebop and Skycontroller) was $500.00 I'd still think twice in light of the Phantom 3 Advance, but at least it would be at a price point enough to temp me if I really didn't know any better and had no way of getting $1,000 to buy the more expensive drones. Remember, Moped or a Ducati. But then again, sometimes it just might still be worth the save $1000.00 for the Ducati then to buy a $500 Moped.

Personally, I would like to see what Parrot does with the next version of the Bebop. hopefully they will learn some lessons and, they will price more line with what they are offering in compareds to the competition and make the product with more quality so it can feel like a premium product for it's price.

Input: This is not the best for three reasons:  First, it's really hard to put together.  Second, the windshield is dark grey and not see through, so I couldn't even install it or my two year old wouldn't be able to see (he's still short).  Third, it doesn't get traction on most surfaces, and seems to need perfectly level asphalt.

Pros:
- Car is a good size with a good amount of power.  My 37 pound 4 year old could ride it fine.
- Theoretically, you only need a phillips head screw driver to assemble this.
- Battery comes fully charged, so you can get immediate gratification, by putting it together with your child (my two kids were excited about putting it together, and they handed me parts and held the screw driver for me) then driving it.
- Can tip up and rest on the back bumper, so it can store smaller leaned against a wall.  Storage is pretty big, but not as big as if it couldn't get stood up on its back bumper.

Cons:
- To get to the battery, like to be able to charge it, you have to unscrew two screws to take off a plastic battery cover.  Those screws can come all the way out of the battery cover.  You know how some toys, the screws come out of the toy, but the screw stays in the cover when it's all the way loose, so you can't loose the screw.  This is not like that. You loosen it, and you have to keep track of the two screws, for hours, while the battery charges.
- Assembly was awful.  For the front plastic piece under the windshield, there are two holes in it and two holes in the body of the car, and you screw it on there.  But, the holes did not line up.  The holes on the plastic piece under the windshield were too close together.  I had to get out a drill and move them to get them 1/8 inch farther apart.  Such a tiny little amount to widen the holes, and the factory should have had better quality control.
- Assembly was awful.  Each tire has a huge rubber band that you put on it for traction.  This is really hard to get on, and you need to put it on four times for four tires.  Yuck!  You need the rubber band too, or else the car will end up with the single drive tire spinning, digging a hole in your yard.  (It's one wheel drive, but that doesn't seem to affect performance once you have the rubber bands on.)  Instructions for these tires say put the rubber bands in hot water to get them easier to get on, and putting them in hot water did make them stretchy and easy to pop right on.  So now you need a bucket of hot water too along with your drill for the misaligned holes.  I really think they should have put these bands on in the factory, where some machine could just have stretched them and popped them on with no fuss.
- Windshield plastic is dark grey.  The product photo shows it clear, and the pic on the side of the box shows it clear, but really it is very dark grey.  My 4 year old is tall enough his head is over the windshield.  My 2 year old is short and he said he couldn't see through the wind shield, so I just didn't install the windshield.  This makes for a different look and feel to the car, so be aware.
- No traction on most surfaces.  Before putting rubber bands on, no traction anywhere.  After putting rubber bands on, traction only on perfectly flat asphalt.  No traction on grass, and when it gets to the middle of the road, where there is a small curve to the asphalt, it skids and needs to be pushed.

To drive, there is a button for forward and reverse that the child can push.  Then the child pushes a foot pedal to go.  The 4 year old had no problem driving around and liked it.  The 2 year old (maybe 2 years 2 months, so just turned 2 and is 25 pounds) understood how to make it go, but had some trouble.  Partly, he can't really steer.  Partly, he had some trouble pushing the pedal.  Partly, the car doesn't drive on most surfaces and is frustrating even for the 4 year old.  He was excited to sit in the car, though.  He'll grow into it, but be aware if that's your age/weight range, this toy may be old for them.

Instructions say up to 50 pound child.

I feel like this is a toy to where the quality control at the factory is bad and it's hit or miss if you get a dud or not.  Probably, a year from now, I will have forgotten the pain of assembly and maybe at that time I will look back and think how awesome a toy.  But right now, I am so upset about the misaligned screw holes.  If it's a gift, put it together ahead of time, and give yourself a full day.  If you are gifting to someone in another city and you won't visit to assemble it, then maybe look elsewhere if the parents are not too mechanical with a toolbox.  I think if all the holes had lined up perfectly, then I would have given a good review, and really it was just those two holes - other parts lined up fine.

Also, this is really key:  My husband thinks the alignment is off and that's why it's giving trouble driving and can't drive on most surfaces.  That fits with screwholes not lining up and steering column being hard to get in.  The steering column felt like it wanted to be almost an inch to the side and I had to force it into the hole in the dashboard where the steering wheel goes.  I am now thinking that the dashboard for my car was manufactured wrong and am thinking to disassemble and maybe mount it with totally new holes a bit to the side.  I really am good mechanically, and do most household repairs.  I think the way the Jeep I got was made is wrong, but not all the reviews are bad, so maybe the factory has ten production lines and nine are good but one is not and I got off the bad one.

Other reviews about the car not going say to add something to the wheels for more traction.  From googling that, I see that you can get bike tires and take the tread and glue it on the wheels.  Supposedly, according to online forums, this will burn out the motor faster with more friction on gears.  I dunno.  The bottom line is, with this unit I got of this Jeep model, I didn't get a functional toy and instead got some kind of expensive googling things and fixing up this project.

I also got another Power Wheels, the Frozen 2 seater Mustang, and that other one runs great on all kinds of surfaces.  I think skip this Jeep and instead get a different model with better quality control at the factory.

Input: Okay so I bought this to give as a Christmas gift to a child that loves things that light up.  The package arrived quickly as expected.  Putting the batteries in this thing is a real pain in the rear it requires a tiny screw driver (included in the package) and and multiple clasps and fasteners etc.  The ball itself once turned on plays a very loud obnoxious snippet of a song that lasts about 10 seconds and repeats it self over and over and over it tries your patience quite quickly.  The lights are colorful and the gyrating motion is strong really making it bounce and roll around the house. SInce the package came with 2 briteballs I let my dog chase one around the house at first she was terrified of it then she loved it chasing it and barking at it and then she killed it in about 3 days.  Now onto  the good stuff.  The way you turn this thing on and off is by depressing a metal pin that is quite small and almost impossible to find when its on and lights are blinding you and the thing is jumping around. So I get a panicked call from my husband.  He had delivered the toy to the child for Christmas and set it up for her but he said as soon as he pushed in the pin to turn it on the pin fell out leaving it stuck on.  He said he couldn't get the batteries out because it was gyrating and blinding him making it impossible to find the tiny screws and use the tiny screwdriver LOL.  He said it had been going off for hours and was so loud and obnoxious it was driving everybody crazy.  And he didn't know what to do so he threw it in his car to try to wait out the batteries.  So the thing is bouncing around his car crashing into things and shooting colored strobe lights out of the window.  HAHA so of course he calls me and is like what do I do?  He finally got it turned off by using the little screwdriver to poke through the hole where the pin had been to get it off.  Needless to say that thing went straight in trash.  Ohh if I could have been a fly on the wall.

Input: Ill give this kit 3 stars because its an awesome idea and I think with some practice you could accomplish some great papermaking, however I was disappointed in the kits initial performance. The package contains everything you would need to make your own recycled paper including shredded tissue paper (1 big bag of white and several smaller bags with bright colors) to get you started. Unfortunately the directions that come with the package are lacking. The enclosed pamphlet has pictorial directions which offer no recommendations on specific measurements/ratios for your project. Further, it tells the user to look up the Paper Factory Youtube video for more detailed instructions. After viewing this video several times I realized that this video is not for this version of Alex Toys papermaking kit! The tools used in that video do not match what is provided in the Eco Crafts Paper Making Kit and in fact belong to the Paper Factory kit which is different. I was able to locate a review video for the Eco Crafts kit and get an idea the measurements/paper mixture (we used majority white paper and added a little bit of colored paper to tint), and step by step instructions. We mixed our paper and water in a Ninja blender to be sure we got the finest pulp we could. The mesh screen was not tight the way you would need it to be to be able to squeeze all the water out and the plastic sheets provided for squeezing the water out don't fit inside the mesh screen which they should, to be able to adequately expel the water. What we ended up with was a really soggy sheet that had too much water in it. The excess water prevented the pulp from adhering together so the paper broke into pieces once dry. I may cut the plastic sheets to get them to fit the screen as I think this was our biggest problem. Overall my kids (8, 6, & 4) had fun with it and loved the paper once done, but not sure it was worth the effort. Hoping that after we practice a few more times that well get better and be able to produce something they can actually use for scrapbooking or other paper crafts.

Input: I've read David-Matthew Barnes before and I enjoy his young adult and adult fiction. This is the first poetry I've read of his, and I must say I enjoyed it. Each of the poems in this collection is very personal and tells a story. They're written with different styles, and though they all have similar themes, it's never redundant.

A few of the poems stood out to me and I highlighted them in the book. "Paper Boy" really resonated with me because I was a paper girl when I was younger, and I felt much the same way. The poem really captures that feeling of being alone and free and contemplating the future. I was twelve when I had my first paper route, and I remember biking along dreaming up what my life would be like, especially since I was "sophisticated" and had a job.

"Souvenir Boy," where the title I assume comes from, stood out to me because of the last lines "Although we've come close, there are more than hot white seconds between us - there lies a lost country or two."

"Look for Homer" felt so much like a fantasy to me, I wondered if this really happened. I got lost in the poem and placed myself there on Mylopotas Beach, and at the end I was sorry for the poem to end, and sorry for the poet to leave.

"Dear Mr. Sanchez" might be my favorite. I really loved the style this one was written in. As a letter, it's so effective in getting the meaning across and translating the poets emotions to the readers. I've reread it several times and have started my own poem using this form now.

"Celebrity Skin" felt like another fantasy to me, and I wanted to drop the book and email the poet right away and ask if it was real and if it were, who the person in question was. It was deliciously scandalous, like something you'd read in a novel.

Input: Dan Ames, who writes under both his own name and the pen name, Dani Amore, has concocted a delictiously twisted short story "Scale of Justice" with a surprise ending that seems to have come directly from "Tales from the Crypt." And, appropriately for a story involving a chef, author Ames seems to know that the proper recipe for this type of story is to let it simmer just long enough to maximize the flavor.

A chef who made the mistake of trying to rip off a Detroit crime boss is saved from literally becoming a meal for a group of hungry alligators by the big man himself and given a chance to win his and his son's life (the son has also made a drugged out mess of things). I did not use the term "big man" casually here, because the boss, one Diego Villanueva, is literally a huge man, weighing in at some 400+ pounds. Diego has a problem; his boss wants him to lose some weight rather quickly, and Diego knows that with his normal eating regimen that's impossible.

So, Diego informs the chef that if he takes over the preparation of Diego's meals and can create appetizing enough low calorie fare that enables Diego to stay on his diet and lose weight (almost a pound a day over the next month), then the chef's life (and his son's life) will be spared. That proves to be a task easier said than done. The chef has no problem whipping up delectable fare; the problem is that Diego doesn't seem to be losing any weight, and the daily weigh-ins are a grim reminder to the chef of what he's facing in a few more days.

Author Ames describes "Scale of Justice" as a hardboiled thriller, and the hardboiled part is certainly correct. Ames plays a truly bizarre scenario completely straight, and the first couple of chapters in the story (yes, even a 25-page story has chapters) are written in a blunt, matter-of-fact, hard nosed style. The later parts of the story, in which the chef desperately tries to figure out why Diego isn't losing weight, are played just as seriously. Plus, Ames is in no hurry to rush the ending; instead, he takes his time describing the chef's plight and how he tries to do something about it. It's only when Ames reveals the trick ending that the reader appreciates how truly warped (and darkly humorous) the entire scenario has been. And, because Ames has taken his time in telling the story, the impact of the ending packs an even greater punch. The story simply wouldn't have been as effective had Ames, as other writers might well have done, played the entire story for laughs. "Scale of Justice" only works because the chef's predicament seems quite real.

"Scale of Justice" is about as well constructed as a story of this length can be. You won't get much character development in a story this short, but you do get good atmospheric description, an interesting story idea, and a great ending. It's rare that I get through a story that packs a punch and doesn't seem to have a single paragraph that's not effective. Dan Ames has managed to write such a story here. The story actually brought back fond memoriesfor me, both in terms of plot and tone, of those that used to be anthologized in "Alfred Hitchcock's Mystery Magazine" (and often wound up dramatized on his TV show. "Scale of Justice" has exactly the right balance.

Gen's emotional involvement tampers both with her judgement and her responses, forcing her to assign the case to the cool and smooth Devlin, yet he wants her to be more than his sidekick. For Gen, a committed relationship was shaky ground; losing it means she's lost part of herself, and she has to fight for resolve on many fronts. Input: I really, really love alternative history, and having a fresh read in the "what if" genre makes Legacy a wonderful find for readers lusting after something newer than Man in the High Castle and/or Fatherland. In Sky's divergent novella we are introduced to Peter, the son of Hitler who has been raised in isolation and secrecy. He's brought out of hiding, dusted off, and groomed to follow in his father's footsteps by men who hope to see him pick up the pieces of a shattered nation, and attempt to restore what's left of a fractured ideology. The tone coerces a kind of sympathy that will sit uncomfortable with many readersbut it is in this aspect that I was totally sold on the writing. The moment you start *kind of* understanding an SS officer, my friends, is the same moment you know that the character development has been well executed.

It's generally pretty rare to find a whole lot of depth or dimension in a novella, but Legacy does a great job in the space it's been allotted. The style of writing is consistent with the subject matter, and while others might argue that the ending is predictable, I'd have to insist that the journey to get there is certainly a unique, engrossing commute. It's well worth an afternoon lost to intelligent escapism.

I'd like to thank the publisher, who furnished an ARC of this book.

When he and his friend Sam decide to break through a collapsed area in a Carlsbad, New Mexico cave, Nathan hopes to find fame, glory, and treasure. When he hears what he thinks is another spelunker trying snatch victory from his hammer, Nathan rushes in headlong.

Nathan describes the creature in the cave:

"It was as if a mad scientist took an octopus and placed it on a human body, in some insane experiment to create an aquatic version of Frankenstein. The creature stood over eight feet tall and the three tentacles sat in a way that made it appear as if the creature had some kind of crazy beard. He continued to fidget with the TV screen, unaware of my presence. The hands working the machinery were human-like, but with three fingers on its hands. The skin of the creature, illuminated by the large spotlight in the center of the room, was a denim-blue color like someone with poor blood circulation."

The creature severs Nathan's rope, his only link to safety and the outside world. The teen's life changes forever.

Using details and excellent characterizations, Mr. Gaydas expertly suspends our disbelief and allows us into the world he has created. Throughout his adventures, Nathan meets "creatures" with thoughts and feelings, an entity with an allergy to humans, a version of an intergalactic bureaucracy (Max Weber would be excited beyond belief), and stumbles onto a computer program which changes his outlook on life. He also learns enemies can be friends, things aren't always as they appear, and "alien" is a relative concept, even on earth.

While the book targets young people, readers of all ages will enjoy this wonderful science fiction adventure.

Input: Benjamin M. Baldinotti opens his debut book saying, Stress management doesn't have to be that complicated or hard to reduce, first of all, you have to understand stress in order to reduce it or avoid it completely. I know that you think stress isn't a choice and I know that, but I also know that stress can have a massive impact on your health, mood and overall your psychological and physical state.

In a very conversational manner and casual tone (setting the stage for paying attention to someone to whom we can relate) Benjamin divides his book into four sections - CAUSES of Stress, Stress SYMPTOMS, EFFECTS of Stress on your Health and Body, and How to AVOID and MANAGE Stress.

In each of these areas Benjamin makes note of situations to which we all can relate (causes or sources include not only work but home and finances and illness within the family unit, changes in home or job; symptoms include insomnia, chest pain, fatigue, GI problems, anxiety, depression, substance abuse; effects of stress as the cause of 85% of doctor visits; management includes meditation, exercise, positive thinking, breathing deeply, laughing, yoga, reading).

In typical Benjamin style he closes his brief session with us stating, We all think that we can live forever, no one thinks about life being just a short cycle of some ups and downs, so make sure to live it the way you want and the way you need it to be. Dont sweat over the little negative things in life because nothing good can come out of it except some additional completely unnecessary stress and believe me you don't need that in your life. Wake up and grab life by the neck and ride that thing like there is no tomorrow. You will be grateful to yourself later for taking matters in your own hands and don't let others to always look down on you, because in order to get respect you have to respect yourself in the first place.

Nothing terribly new here, but condensed in immediately accessible form that is easy to digest  and likely with allow some introspection. Grady Harp, May 16

Input: Okay, let me just get this off my chest. Sienna & Nick... I have an urge to punch things. I had a horrible feeling the first time that bitch showed up. I knew that I would hate her. I knew I would hate Nick. I almost thought that they would end up being connected somehow. I don't even have once ounce of pity for that skank.

Reckless begins just as Effortless left off. Kiera and Kellan had just symbolically married one another on the dance floor at Pete's. She is free of school, Kellan is getting ready to record an album and with nothing stopping them they are getting ready to start this new life...together....on the road.

But nothing seems to ever come easy for them. Joey returns and has her own plans of revenge for Kellan, but this first test of Kiera's trust and faith in him came much too quickly. I was not surprised by her reaction, I expected it. However, while the old Kiera was still there, the new Kiera was really trying to fight to make her way to the surface.

Kiera's character did show some growth in Reckless (finally), but for the first time I wanted her to be less reserved. I wanted the claws to come out. But she really did come into her own in this one, and she really did find that trust that her and Kellan never really had to start with. But as the D-Bags head off on tour, with Kiera along for the ride - for the first time it's not the fans and groupies that challenges their relationship. It's his dream, but so is she - could he throw away his band's dreams to ensure that he can hold onto Kiera? This is where Kiera's new found faith comes into place, she won't allow him to give up on his dream or crush the band's dreams either.

But when Kellan becomes the hot new star and is being tied to one of hottest singers Kiera is struggling to remain by his side, and remain invisible from Kellan's spot light - but that can all backfire as rumors spread and fans show how ugly they can be. Kellan's relationship is pushed along with his will. He has fought his whole life to be loved, to have a family and to mean something to anyone and his love for Kiera has suddenly become his dirty little secret. But some can only be pushed to far before they can't take anymore.

Although there are parts that had me completely twisted, Kellan's love for Kiera did not waiver one bit. They knew what damage could be done without trust and faith in one another. Although there are times when Kiera's private thoughts wander into dangerous territory, she does really try to think things out and there is just no faltering in Kellan's love for her.

This was a wonderful ending to this series. You get to keep all the boys and girls close to your heart and you even have your moments when you rather hug Griffin than slap him. This series was just a brilliant series. Between the ups and downs in the first book, the crazy stress of book two - Reckless for me was just icing on the cake. Yeah it had it's moments of stress and concern but you just felt this was going to be forever. That finally they have learned from their past and that they would make it. I don't want my time with Kellan to end, it was all summed up so perfectly that it just felt so final. Kellan has to be one of my all time favorites, I will miss him.

Input: 3 "More Than Your Past" Stars

After his introduction in Raleigh and Mia's book as the best friend, it's Pax's turn to face his past. In high school Pax first saw Gemma on one of the first night's she moved to town. Before the accident that hurt Mia and sent Raleigh to prison, Pax was part of the racing scene. His brief encounter with Gemma led him to wanting more until she turned up again dating his older brother Blake. But when Gemma accused Blake of rape, Pax wanted nothing to do with the girl who cried wolf.

Years later Gemma is back in town to help her dad who's in the hospital. Having been called names and accused of lying, Gemma has tried to run from the accusations. But being back in the small town brings up all the pain and suffering of the past since no one has forgotten and still no one believes her.

Running into Pax was the last thing she wanted but since he's now her dad's partner in opening a raceway, she sees him a lot even though he is still angry. But when the truth comes out, Pax becomes a partner leaving Gemma to wonder if she can heal old wounds and survive in a town that hates her so that she can be with Pax.

I was really excited to see where Pax's story went. He was a really interesting side character in book one. With such a tough subject, I expected more angst and more tension. In reality the book was overly sweet and a bit too easy. I didn't understand Pax's staunch stand behind his family when numerous times he was obviously the odd guy out for no reason and a recipient of his families terrible behavior. Pax was less bad boy and more follower which is fine just not what I was expecting. The story did keep me flipping pages and hoping that Blake got what was coming to him. Plus Gemma and Pax were smoking hot together.

ARC provided by publisher via Netgalley for honest review.

Input: First of all, I really like Dragos Roua's posts at his website. He's an extremely intelligent guy with excellent writing skills. However, His definition of "living off the grid," is not the standard definition. I hadn't caught up with Dragos lately and thought, based on this ebook title and subtitle, that he had truly gone OFF the grid. His definition is living without socially accepted descriptions of a regular job, basically just not following traditional social and work rules. He describes it as living, "...outside a normal grid of rules."

What does "Off The Grid" really mean? It's a pretty accepted definition. For example, from Wikipedia: "Off-the-grid homes are autonomous; they do not rely on municipal water supply, sewer, natural gas, electrical power grid, or similar utility services. A true off-grid house is able to operate completely independently of all traditional public utility services."

I was expecting to read about his life off the electrical grid, no public utility services of any kind - the traditional definition of "living off the grid." He doesn't do any of this. He's still comfortable, just unorthodox and definitely living an unconventional lifestyle.

The 3-stars are for what he wrote with HIS definition. Even though it's not the accepted definition, it was fascinating and I learned some interesting things. I obviously have an early Kindle version of the book and had to get past lots of grammar and spelling errors, but the content was fairly new to me and pretty interesting.

But, if you're expecting a book about someone truly living off-the-grid (as it's normally defined) and expecting ideas and tips for a real, nitty gritty life off the public electrical/utility/sewage/water grid, you might be very disappointed.

Input: Great title, great cover, and yet...

I came very close to not reviewing this. Why? Because I only review books I like and this teetered on the edge. But, I decided to review it because it had some really good points and I think a lot of people will like it.

What worked for me: This is so witty and fun, right from the first page. The voice is funny and captivating. If you enjoy quirky main characters and a story that hasn't been told before, this may be fore you. The futuristic world is unique and interesting. The different take on dragons was a blast. While our main character Myrna's sense of humor is a bit dark, I liked it for the most part. She started out spunky and independent and I instantly liked her. There is some great tension between Myrna and Trian that held a lot of promise. The romance took a very, very long time to start to take center stage but once it did it was well worth the wait.

What didn't work for me: The info dump all across the first fifty pages drove me crazy and nearly made me stop reading. All that information would have been much more interesting if the author would have 'shown' us with action and scenes instead of simply 'telling' us. I understand that this is a hard temptation to fight when writing in narrative first person, but it can be done and has been often to great effect. Unfortunately, the 'telling' instead of 'showing' never stopped. Then there is Myrna's odd, complete insensitivity to watching animals being devoured alive. While I'm an animal lover, I'm also a realist with a tough skin, but this callousness started to get to me after a few scenes of it. I get where the author was going with this, but it didn't exactly make me like that aspect of Myrna.

For the full review, go here:

Input: Not everything is what it appears to be. Amanda gets kicked down in the dirt by her ex-fiance Ross but won't let it keep her there. Deciding she needs to regroup and make some serious changes, she packs up and moves back home, finding a place that can be remodeled into perfection with just a little bit of elbow grease. What she didn't expect to find was the sinfully attractive contractor Brax who not only will help her rebuild her new home on budget, but happens to be her little brother's best friend. The connection is instantaneous but Ross has taught her to be more careful with her heart. Can she get over the past to move on to a brighter future, or will all of those doubts and fears hold her back from finding true love?

I'm pretty torn on this book. The premise was great, and it was easy to fall into in the beginning. Amanda is understandably cautious while Brax is an honestly sweet man with a gorgeous smile. The pacing between the two coming together was wonderfully done. It eased into the romantic aspects with tastefully down intimate scenes. But I felt the conflict was a little over played to keep the story on edge. After the first plot twist I knew immediately where things were headed and sort of dreaded reading the rest. Thankfully our woman Amanda has an amazing best friend Kara to defuse most of the problems and keep her head on straight. It really helped her to see that not everything is what it seems, and honesty is the best policy.

This story was well written and jumped from Amanda's point of view to Brax's- which was something I truly enjoyed. However the ending felt rushed and left me a bit unsatisfied. We never really got to see Amanda over come her personal demons. Maybe it was the epilogue that makes me feel this way. I don't really know for sure.

Getting down to it I did enjoy reading this book and I could see myself buying more from this author in the future.

Input: Heloise and William have danced around each other for a long time. As his bestfriend's little sister, William has tried to distance himself from Heloise while she has decided after once being rejected by him to protect her heart. They both have their share of scars, both internally and physically, but staying apart might be hurting them more than helping.
With Heloise in danger, William can't let her out of his sight. As they are forced together and their walls start coming down, it starts to become clear that the only way they can truly heal is with the love of the other.

"thou shalt not covet thy best friend's little sister."

Second in the Secrets and Spies series, A Raven's Heart can be read as a standalone. It's obvious that there is a continuous story thread involving the spy aspect but I never felt lost or confused, in fact it only made me curious about the first book in the series and future ones. I thought this started off very strong with the tension between our two leads. I will show up every time for the brother's friend, little sister trope and I thought that dynamic was portrayed very well here; a little less involvement with her brother's approval/disapproval and more shared history and emotional ties. As the story went on though, I thought the hero had disconnect between him continuously spouting (this was brought up a bit too much) about how he wasn't good enough for Heloise but still engaging physically with her. It was disorientating because I'm supposedly supposed to buy into his torment over not feeling good enough for her but at the same time he's constantly kissing on her and pushing their physicality. His reasoning for not feeling good enough for her was already a little murky, we are told he was kidnapped when he was younger and had to fight his way free but not given a clear enough picture to understand why he would demonize himself because of his actions. As the story goes on we learn he is a spy where he has to kill people occasionally, which fits better into the not feeling good enough narrative. If their intimate situations hadn't been ramped up so quickly in the beginning, I would have been able to follow along and connect with William's gradual breaking down and inability to stay away from Heloise.

"You want to pretend this scar isn't there, but it's what makes you you."

I was quite fond of Heloise as she was the little too smart for her own good, word loving, and scared bluestocking. Her personality quirk of etymology spouting was cute but I have read a heroine or two who could be her twin sister. Which is the main problem I had with this story, I've read it before. Again, I've read a ton of books from this sub-genre, which could maybe the problem in itself, but there was nothing new here. The writing is good and there are many crowd pleaser moments and lines, but maybe too many. It almost felt like the writer wrote what she thought a romance should be by taking good tropes, scenes, and lines and creating a story around that instead of having characters and story emerge from her. There was a kissing in the rain scene that should have felt emotionally powerful but all I could do was think about other scenes like that I have already read and compare them; this story was full of moments like that for me. Someone newer to the genre would probably not have the same problem I did. I've read Joanna Bourne's Spymasters series, which utilizes the same tropes and ideas as this but adds enough intrigue and emotion to distance itself from the similarities and be completely compelling.

She gave a watery laugh, "I might want to kill you, Ravenwood, but I'd never want you dead."

Heloise and William have a very back and forth relationship with them challenging each other that was fun to read. I just ran into the problem of having read it done better, I can read the same tropes over and over but I need fresh spins and/or deep emotional connections to the characters that I just couldn't seem to get here; there was a lack of "it" factor. Secondary characters stayed fairly close to the sides but there were a couple that I wouldn't mind knowing more about. This is also true for the spy ring the author has set up, there's enough there to grab your attention. I will say there were some comments made by Heloise regarding other women, former mistresses/courtesans and generally beautiful women, which felt mean spirited. There was a little bit of all those women are man hungry airheads; I could do without women on women hate and more female friendships. (Not suggesting Heloise would be friends with these women but less generalized superiority comments)

K.C. Bateman looks to be a newer author and I definitely see some promise in her writing, I would just like to hear more of her individual voice. There was good story plot progression and natural flowing interaction between the characters. I'll be going back and reading the first in the series and be on the lookout for the next in the series. If you're looking for a sweet "I'm not good enough for you but I can't stay away" with some road adventure, you might want to try this new author.

I received this book for free in exchange for an honest review. This does not affect my opinion of the book or the content of my review.

Input: Draw You Near #3 Savannah Sweethearts series by Jan Thompson

Over time they form a friendship of sorts and she lets her guard down a tiny bit. They actually share some things in common, their faith for one thing, which was surprising at first. However, something from the past may break that fragile friendship when Lars must leave Savannah suddenly and return to England. Will he return or is their budding love over before it really began?

Input: McKinsey & Company is a world-famous strategic consulting company, also known as "The Firm". Ethan Rasiel worked at McKinsey & Co. for several years and provides a quick, clear introduction into management consulting firm's problem solving methods. "I wrote this book with the goal of communicating new and useful skills to everyone who wants to be more efficient and effective in business. ... In addition, this book will give any executive woho works with management consultants, whether McKinsey or elsewhere, some insight into how these strange beings think."

The book is split up into five parts. In Part I, Ethan Rasiel explains the McKinsey-way of thinking about business problems. The author explains that the solution of the problem needs to be fact-based (facts are friendly), rigidly structured (MECE = mutually exclusive), and hypothesis-driven (solve the problem at the first meeting - the initial hypothesis). In addition, the author explains how McKinsey-ites approach business problems and apply the McKinsey problem-solving process to maximum effect. There is also a short introduction into a number of rules which McKinsey-consultants use for problem-solving purposes: the 80/20-rule, find the key drivers, the elevator test - sell in 30 seconds, make a chart every day, look at the big picture, say "I don't know", and don't accept "I have no idea".

In Part II, the author introduces the McKinsey-way of working to solve business problems. The author explains the selling process at McKinsey (the Firm does not sell, it markets), how to structure an engagement, and assembling of a team. Then the author comes to the most important part of the book, doing research, conducting interviews (the author insists on reading Chapter 8 - Conducting Interviews - "If you read no other chapter of the book from start to finish, read this one."), and brainstorming.

In Part III, the author, and the McKinsey-way of selling solutions. This part discusses the way McKinsey makes presentations, which is one of the strongest parts of McKinsey according to the author, displays data with charts (read Gene Zelazny (1985), 'Say it with Charts'), and the way to work with clients.

In Part IV, Rasiel gives some lessons how "McKinsey-ites" have learned for coping with the stresses of life at the Firm, and in Part V, the author recounts the lessons he learned at McKinsey and shares memories of various ex-McKinsey-ites. Both Part IV and V are 'a waste of paper' in comparison to the first three parts, but gives a little insight into what goes on behind the scenes at McKinsey & Co.

Yes, I can understand that some readers are disappointed by this book as it gives just an introduction into management consultancy (and McKinsey & Co). The author introduces the various problem-solving methods and tools, but does not discuss them in great detail. The author has responded to these criticisms by publishing The McKinsey Mind in 2002, which addresses this issue somewhat. However, for more details on the problem-solving methods and tools you will still have to read some other literature. I recommend you purchase The McKinsey Way if you want an introduction into management consultancy, and The McKinsey Mind if you want an introduction into problem-solving methods and tools.

Input: Tod Goldberg has skillfully written these three mind-blowing short stories which incite introspection, and draw upon submerged memories. He writes about places he has lived, descending deeply into his psychic to dredge up old emotions, sounds and tactile impressions of long forgotten, but deeply moving sensations. Sensations so deeply felt they must be hidden in a locked closet. Why do we do the things we do?

Tod carefully examines the stories and motives of convoluted lives. A golf pro, King of the Fairway, who cannot hit a straight ball, and cannot climb out of the sand trap of his own creation. Another, haunted by the ghost of his brother. Still another man, who is compelled to revisit the pain of his childhood home. How did these places affect their lives? Or, is memory simply a trickster lurking, designed to lead all down wayward paths? These are forceful interludes. The realistic characters linger to remind us of our own hidden mistakes, and agendas.

Tod Goldberg's rich voice is well known through the ever popular "Burn Notice" T.V. series. His darkly comic voice compels, and taunts, those prone to self-deception, and yes, self-destruction. This is a quick read. One you won't want to put down until the final pages is turned. The effects will linger. It is well worth your attention.

Input: Michael Shaughnessy's second novel (and I do recommend his first, The Archangel of Westminster, if you can find a copy) is a well-crafted page-turner that quickly hooks the reader into its `what-happens-next?' plot-line.  For the first two-thirds of the book, the situation confronting the priest-hero of the story, Fr. Michael Reilly becomes progressively more dire, and the reader wonders how it could possibly get any worse; which, of course, it unfailingly does.  I don't want to spoil the ending, but Fr. Reilly finally triumphs by means of a stunning gambit of humility and integrity.

The real strength of the book, for my money, is its character development - its depth of insight into the sundry and self-contradictory motives of each of the main characters kept me engaged, even more than the plot-line.  The Archbishop, stuck between concerns over public perception and pastoral care for one of his priests, and Adelia (the Red Madonna of the title, although by the book's end, it isn't yet quite apparent what, if any, significance attaches to the moniker), caught between concerns for Truth and Compassion, on the one hand, and her own vast ambition on the other, were the most intriguingly-drawn characters, for my part.

If the book has a weakness (and it is far from a fatal one), it is that the `good guys' are REALLY good, and the `bad guys' are REALLY bad - it could seem a tad `cartoonish'.  But that doesn't detract from the story itself; as far as it goes, Fr. Reilly gives a strong example of wrestling with his own conscience and choosing the right, even if he might prefer something easier.

The Red Madonna is the first book of a planned trilogy, which is good to know, because there's a lot of `unfinished business' by the end of the book.  Shaughnessy spends a bit of time on the marriage between Adelia and Jim; the twists and turns of the plot pull and tug on their relationship, in both constructive and destructive ways, but by the end of the book, their marriage and its future are still very much up in the air.  So I am left waiting for the next installment; and the one after that.  Well-played on that account, sir. . .

This is a book definitely worth reading, and all the more impressive, given that the author is basically writing in his spare time.

Input: This short piece was inviting and a lovely picture of ongoing romance in a young marriage. Loads of family in for the holiday can be stressful, and the way our Dark Hero supports his bride is ideal.

Two aspects of the story struck me particularly, the heroine has gone from cold, snowy winters in England to the tropics where she struggles to find her Christmas spirit in the midst of foreign holiday foods, island heat, and sand. This aspect makes Ms. Silver's story a good one for readers dealing with similar issues.

Second, Ms. Silver does an outstanding job of incorporating all that has gone before into the plot line without re-telling. Readers need not worry that they haven't read the previous title in order to enjoy this one. And fellow writers can study this piece as an exemplar for working on titles in series. She even leaves you wanting to go back and read the first book if you haven't.

Christmas at Ravencrest would also make a nice "Christmas in July" reading.

Input: Among the novels I usually read male authors are a rarity. So the single fact that Quarter Square was written by a man was reason enough to pique my curiosity and make me want to read this novel.

In the first part of the novel Joe (our protagonist) discovers a magic parallel universe which is accessible through the magic door in the century old theatre he's renovating and sleeping in. Through that hole in the wall one enters a Renaissance-fair-like magic version of Plymouth where dwarves dance and juggle, people sit around a bonfire and tell tales, others are singing, dancing having fun. A very colourful and enchanted alternate universe.

However, this haven is threatened by an evil who is after Joe, and the second part of the novel tells the story of Joe and Min (the heroine) being on the run and hiding from the evil werewolf with a neolite tribe, who live in huts in the desert, walk around barechested and loin-clothed.

What is interesting with Quarter Square, is that with this novel I felt the different parts of the novel (plot, writing, etc.) to be quite independent from each other: I found the writing of great quality, it was lyrical and exquisite.

"I rolled onto my back, gave my scalp and beard a good scratch and tried to concentrate on the noises and the smell of dry centuries. I preferred them to the sound of my thoughts and the stink of betrayal."

It set the mood and described the scenes while entertaining all senses of the reader and definitely making use of the reader's imagination:

"The air - heavy with summer smells of beer and cigarette smoke, diesel oil from the harbour, food from every direction and a hundred different perfumes and aftershaves - tasted like life and made me feel like even more of an outsider."

What made me pick up Quarter Square - the fact that its author was a man - didn't let me down. The difference in logic, perception and handling of events was refreshing and authentic. It was wonderful climbing inside the mind of a man and seeing and understanding why he does what he does. It was interesting to see Joe's reasoning behind his hurt of discovering his wife having an affair with his best friend and that it was mostly the sense of betrayal which infuriated him: that he doesn't begrudge his best friend for falling in love with his wife but for lying to him and making him lose his best friend. Reading a story through a man's perspective is fun and liberating: a man narrator is blunter, doesn't overanalyze things (even though he spends a fair time on exploring his emotions it definitely does not come off as mushy), and remains more realistic.

Though I was constantly enchanted by David Bridger's writing style, I didn't connect that well with the plot. I enjoyed the first part of the novel and reading about the "gipsy" circus of the insiders, but from the moment Joe and Min got on the run I felt the story lost most of its colours. (Though I still remember with amazement the description of Joe blending in a tree and David Bridger's description of what it feels like to live and breathe as a tree does.)

Joe is a great character, an ordinary guy next door, and his story is fantastic exactly because of him being so normal. Unfortunately I remained lukewarm and at times even antagonistic towards the heroine, Min. I didn't find her fleshed out enough, and then when she got together with Joe - though I can understand with their background why - it still irritated me that she didn't consider Joe her equal but treated her most of the time almost as a child. When finally Joe couldn't take that anymore and erupted in quite a monologue I read it with great satisfaction. It was good to see him finally step up and assume the role of the responsible man in charge of his own destiny.

Verdict: Quarter Square is very different from the usual urban fantasy novels. I would say it is more on the fantasy side than urban. David Bridger is a very talented and promising new author whose next works I will definitely check out!

ps. I have to spend at least one sentence on the amazing cover. Not only does it look beautiful, it is very atmospheric and portrays the novel and characters wonderfully. A fantastic job, bravo!

And a short quote which gives you a taste of the book:

"Here's the thing. There's magic everywhere in the world. Always has been. But in most of the world it's unknown. People stopped using it, believing in it. (...) It seems that each culture and each generation rejects magic a bit more than the one before. Some cultures more than others, but the general trend is to ignore magic and eventually to forget it."

Well Quarter Square is a magic-preserving community then!

Input: Floating Petals is a collection of 14 short stories inspired by Leela Devi Panikar's eclectic experience of Asia. There is a genuine beauty here, both in the tales themselves and in the language in which they are couched. The author's gentle, positive tone pulls you into the longer, more developed stories, and you quickly find yourself ensconced by the sights, sounds and smells of her world. Everything is vividly described with an economy of language and a light, reassuring humour that keep the narrative moving along nicely.

The author stumbles just a little in her treatment of negative emotions. Characters in frightening situations are never given enough time to convincingly develop their terror -- as if the author herself can't bear to be writing it. This isn't a problem when the main thrust of the plot lies outside of its unpleasant elements in stories like "The Couple" and "Homeless Sparrow". But in tense, gloomy thrillers like "Green" and "The Singeing Shadow" where the point is to evoke sympathetic fear, the result is shallow and abrupt prose that leaves you asking, "Is that it?" However, these stories comprise only a small part of the book, whose real strength is in such stories as "Floating Petals" and "After The Wedding". It's obvious the author is in her element in these tales, getting right to the core of her characters and -- whether intentionally or otherwise -- artfully challenging the reader to re-examine natural prejudices against pain and servitude. I also particularly enjoyed "Love Is All You Need".

With her charmingly optimistic voice, Panikar writes on themes of childhood, love and freedom with an effortless grace. Whatever your taste, I'm sure you'll find something to enjoy. Overall, a great read.

Input: Reviewed by me as a member of Rosie Amber's Review Team

4.5 stars

In this further adventure of the Assassin Without A Name, our hero is recruited by his ex love, Liz, for a special mission.

As with the other books in this series, I felt that its charm lay not so much in the plot itself as in the writing of the incidental parts.  I am not particularly interested in reading long, blow by blow accounts of fights or daring escapes, but I love the bits about the Assassin's life, his thoughts, etc.  I like to picture him in his 'working gear', climbing over his rooftop empire like a cat, unseen by the Black Guard who seek him below, and reading little snippets about his life, like his secret hideout in the deplorable Shambles area of town, where one takes one's life in one's hands simply by entering its streets...

Scott Marlowe has invented a marvellous character, and writes beautifully, with wit and a wonderful turn of phrase.  I'd like to see a novella telling about the Assassin's early life, something that makes more use of the writer's powers of observation, character portrayal and presentation of atmosphere.  Again, this reminded me very much of some of Roald Dahl's stories; the style of writing is very similar.  Good stuff!

Input: Never slow dance with a zombie. Sounds like good advice. The kind of good advice youd get from the Dear Abby of the supernatural set. Undeniably wise words to live by. Right up there with never put a campfire out with your face. (Or as a teacher once told me: never put a campfire out with your face. Again.)

Try slow dancing with a zombieparticularly a hungry one with an icky drool face and plump maggots squirming out of its noseand you might find yourself missing a body part afterwards. A face, an arm, maybe even a big toe. Please dear lord, anything but the big toe. No dance is worth an amputation. Even the Macarena.

This is becauseas everyone knowszombies are fearsome and brutal. They eat people like Cheetos, minus the obnoxious cheesy mouth. A good day for a zombie is ripping into some guys chest cavity and snacking on the entrails; the last zombie in getting the colon. It might not be pretty, but its a raison dtre that zombies can call their own.

Unless the zombies are in E. Van Lowes Never Slow Dance with a Zombie, in which case they are essentially non-threatening, non-violent and about as fearsome as a pissed off butterfly. Sure, this is a novel aimed at a young adult audience, but it doesnt mean the zombies cant have a little bite to them. Teens know that zombies snack on faces; in fact, they expect it.

Zombies are the unstoppable killing machine of the monster world, the Great White shark of bogeymen minus the killer John Williams soundtrack, so toning down their violence and eliminating their bloodletting is an odd choice. Using them for a novel in which they have to be toned down is an even odder choice. Like writing a YA book about a serial killer, who never kills anyone.

Lowe takes a different approach in Never Slow Dance with a Zombie, mining the zombies for comedic gold, turning them into a harmless joke. But in making them non-threatening, he eliminates any possibility of dramatic tension in the novel. The main characters Margot and Sybil, who must co-exist with an entire high school filled with zombie classmates, never feel in peril in the book. Never feel like the zombies are a real foil for them. The zombies are just too easily overcome, outsmarted at every turn. Sure outsmarting zombies is difficult, but their overwhelming numbers should balance this equation somewhat.

There is a nice message about the perils of wanting to be popular and its consequences, but Lowe belabors it, addressing it repetitively, repeating it over and over (get the point!) making the book seem like one of those not-very-special After School Specials. Instead of making kids think and challenging them to broaden their perspective, Lowes constant reiteration of his message most likely will eventually turn them off, causing them to feel as if they are being lectured to.

Despite these issues, the story still has its entertaining moments, and there are a few places where its goofy charm shines through. Most of the characters are clichs in the book: the popular girl, the girl who will do anything to be popular, the selfless best friend, and the science club geeks. None of these caricatures are offensive, but neither are they something you haven't seen before. And there is really no reason youd need to experience them here.

So wallflowers rejoice, Never Slow Dance with a Zombie is one slow dance you can miss.

Input: The problem that I have with Alan's writing styles is that its very stream-of-consciousness. The writer needs to learn how to write more densely. I will explain. But overall, Alan needs to start letting most of the content hit-the-cutting-floor. In other words - edit.

His normal approach is to do something like the following: Stone (his lead character) will get called to a meeting. But before Stone even heads to the meeting, Stone starts thinking about the meeting. Sort of. The the reader is accosted by 100 mostly stream-of-consciousness thoughts that run through Stones head, and 99% will not impact the  meeting or Stones response to the meeting - in any way.

So, here are two tools that Alan needs to start applying assiduously, and that includes, after the fact. If he hasn't done this, then he needs to go back and rewrite any section that doesnt have this. Yes. I am giving Alan homework.

1) Multi-Tasking
2) Footsteps

What do I mean by multi-tasking? I mean that every scene needs to accomplish 3 or more things, that 'move the story forward'. And Alan does not get to include "Character Development", "Exposition", or "Establishing" in any of those three. For example, if Stone enters the room, and Alan describes the situation, perhaps this scene will move the story forward by A) revealing a new bit of information that allows the story to move forward, B) have a character say something that reveals what that character is going to do next, and C) mention an object in the room that will serve as a Chekov's Gun component. Thats three things, and a decent reason for that scene to exist. Notice that none of those aspects have anything to do with what is happening inside Stones head.

Granted, I just came up with those three things off the top of my head, and we don't have context for which scene they apply to. But hopefully you (Alan) get the idea. Frankly, I am not in the mood right now, to rewrite one of your scenes. So, I am just making the overall suggestion.

2) Footsteps. I am inventing this term for you. I want you to insert a Footstep every 5 - 10 sentences. And by footsteps, I mean that you have to move the story forward, every 5-10 sentences. So, get out of the characters head, and have him do something, or have something happen. The footstep can be:
A) Someone says something
B) Someone does something
C) Someone decides something
And it always has to be onTopic. Meaning, that if Stone is heading towards a meeting, he is allowed to think about it, for 5 to 10 sentences, but then he actually needs to "GO" to the meeting. If he is then going to the meeting, he is allowed to think about going or about the meeting for 5 to 10 sentences, but then he needs to perhaps, discover something that is relevant to the story. He might see his crew doing something relevant, and it changes his plan for how to deal with the meeting (change). or he runs into someone that walks along with him because they were also called to the meeting. He did not know they were coming, so this is new information. And even better, if he does not want them there, or does not know why they would be a part of the meeting.

"Keep the Heroes thinking processes, focused on the meeting".

Ok. Thats enough instruction for now. Of course, I don't actually expect that Alan will read this diatribe. But  now he knows that this particular reader finds his rambles to be too often, too off-topic, and tooooooo-long.

Move the story forward faster. This does not mean that more will happen, as the story arc can be the same. It will simply mean that the story will be more packed with meaning, instead of the drivel that goes on the the day-dreaming-heroes head. For example, instead of listening to a thousand meaningless thoughts in Stones head that rarely affect the story, Alan would have more room to let us get to know some of the other characters, instead of them all being paper-secondary-characters.

Alan can still have all the insights be coming from the Hero. Just make him more observant about others, so that we can learn about them.

Ok. Thats enough.

Will I read any more Alan Black stories? Maybe, but not enthusiastically.

Spoiler Alert: When I think back on this story, very little happened. We had to put up with an inane scientist that needed to be shot in the head on the first page that she was introduced. Then we had to put up with chapters of people arguing about the legal rights of said scientist. All the while, we expected this to be a story about how the world starts to become brought into the empire. And yet we never got to that. The story gets sidetracked, and everyone goes on a camping trip. By the end of the story, they get back from the camping trip, and now, at the end, they are ready to start exploring the world. Soooo. Maybe in the next book?

As well, they land on this incredibly complex world,  but we don't get to learn more about it. Oh. And the hero now has super-powers that he doesnt use to move the story forward. Sigh.

Input: *Reviewed on BackPorchReader[dot]com*

***this review contains some mild spoilers***

Sorry, but this wasn't a win for me and I will not be advancing to the next level.

Firstly, I really liked the cover, but in no way is it representative of the character descriptions, including the dog. Thats just a statement and has no bearing on my rating.

The blurbwhen I read it a few weeks ago I was intrigued enough to pre-order the book. Reading it again, after having read the book, it kind of makes me snicker and wonder what I was thinking.

The story felt like trope after trope after trope all dumped in a crock pot. Unfortunately, the flavors didn't blend so well for me. And, spoiler: a crock pot nearly has a starring role.

Theres the snowed in tropeand it was a little bit of a twist from what we normally see, considering this was in an RV that actually moved as opposed to some remote cabin in the woods. I thought that was done relatively well.

Theres the Im stranded and have to get home to a wedding and I gotta have a date or Im a loser. So the RV was handy.

Theres the closeted guy/complete virgin. I had a hard time with the whys of these.

Theres insta-love which I have a really hard time buying into when combined with closeted virgins.

Theres the age gap that was never really addressed, not that it really matters. But it was there.

Theres confrontation with the exwhich, sorry, but was lackluster, felt forced and far too coincidental to be believable.

There's a grand gesture toward the end on Noahs part. Grand Gestures really aren't needed for believable romance.

Im not a gamerand this is a huge undercurrent of the story and the one thing these heroes have in common, along with taste in movies. I wasn't scared of the gaming element, nor did I find it overbearing. Sometimes it got big, and Ill admit I skimmed a few paragraphs to get around it. But for the most part it was fine.

I couldn't get a good bead on Adrian. His sexy tats drew me in some. But beyond thathe was kind of a flake, but really sweet and nurturing at times. I couldn't make sense of him, other than hes just the sort who dances to the beat of his own drum. Nothing wrong with that, but it made it really hard to connect. His family drama seemed to be all in his head because they adored him even when he exasperated them.

Noahand with him Ive got to try really hard not to be judgmental. Hes 35, suuuper closeted, and a complete virgin. I don't judge those thingsexcept the age part, and I REALLY don't want to judge that either. Its just, I never bought into the WHY of it all. Why at 35, and such an intellectual, hes so closeted and inexperienced. And I couldn't buy into it being because of his place of employment because he USED that as a way to hide himself and knew what he was getting into by working there. Hes way far away from familyso getting away was his first chance to be himself. Instead he hid behind religion he didn't fully buy into, what he thought his family would think, and gaining tenure at an ultra-conservative religious college whose tenets he didn't believe in. I get everyones journey is differentbut, the WHYs all piled up fell short for me.

Together, I didn't get the attraction of anything deeper than looks and common interest in video games. The chemistry was lacking and the sexual tension wasmeh.

Their dogs didn't even like each other much in the beginning, and thats usually a sign to run like hell.

Yet, within mere days of a snowy RV journey, they're in love.

Uhhhh okay.

(Not really.)

The rest is them trying to figure it out, deny it, fight against it, fight for it, etc. with lots of boring talk, talk, talk over text and Skype until the aforementioned Grand Gesture.

As the reader, by this point, I didn't care a whole lot.

The One-Year-Later epilogue

*harassed sigh*

I don't think its written in stone that at the end of a romance the people have to get engaged in order to have a believable HEA.

So nopeGame Over.

Input: Well, my impressions of this book are about 50/50 feel good, feel not so good.
The good : The writing is excellent and engaging. I only found one grammatical error on the first read. (I wasn't looking for any, it just kind of jumped out at me).
The neutral : I was kind of puzzled by the fact that Dan felt the need to immerse himself in public self-flagellation over what appeared to be simple, normal,  human regressions on the path of self-discovery. I mean, rather than just notice his perceived missteps and move on, which would be the prescribed/normal behavior for someone engaged in self-realization, meditation, mindfulness. But what is "normal", right? And who am I to assign that moniker to anything or anyone. So I pressed on and kept reading.
The bad (just my perception, of course): Then, after reading the whole "book", I suddenly realized what this really was: just another clever way to get people to buy more copies of his real book. And, I must admit, it really is a very clever way of capitalizing on human nature, combined with the ability to "give" away free books on Amazon. And I, being of the (reluctantly) human persuasion, took the bait. Hook, line, and sinker, as it were. At first, I totally missed the fact that only 17% of this "book" is new material. The rest is just chapter one of the real book: 10% Happier.

I was looking through the Amazon free Kindle books section and came upon Dan's freebie. It intrigued me, not because of the fact that Dan is a well-known newscaster, but because of the title. Dan is not known to me because I stopped following anything media-related since about six years ago. Stopped watching TV, listening to radio, and unsubscribed from all news-related and/or commercial driven feeds on the Internet. With that, slowly but surely, the names of most newscasters kind of slid into the nether regions of my memory. Life is so much more peaceful when we don't allow ourselves to be hyped up and stressed out artificially by things we can do nothing about. But I digress. I got curious because I wanted to know if the author regretted writing a book about becoming 10% happier or, if regret wasn't his issue, what was? So I plunged in and started reading.

As I mentioned before, the "book" is very well written. And engaging. But it's not a book. It starts out with a few pages of Woody-Allenish neurosis and self-flagellation about Dan's perceptions that enjoying his (real) book's success in an excessive way and obsessively watching its rise in the rankings is somehow a failing on his part.

Note to Dan: that's just being human. And while being human often has felt like a failing even to me in the past, I have learned to accept certain aspects of my own and others' humanity too as I grow older, but none the wiser. Being human, and displaying human traits like backsliding on intentions every once in a while, is no more wrong than being a tree and shedding a leaf or more here and there (and sometimes everywhere). Inconvenient, yes - mostly to humans, not so much to the trees. But a subject for blame, no. We learn in bits. And that involves backsliding. Perhaps it even enriches our experience, because we learn from it. We learn to be more aware. And that is what meditation is all about, right?

Which might have been what Dan was trying to do with this "book" - but in a public forum? And with that title? And the way it was presented with just a tiny bit of new material and a whole chapter of the "real" book included? With a Perils of Pauline type of cliffhanger ending? I think not. No. This little "freebie" is really nothing more than a new and innovative way to advertise the book.

I have to admit that I feel kinda conned. Sucked in. Suckered. I would probably be pretty pissed off if I had spent money on this item. But still, I did get pulled into spending time on it. Under false pretenses. I was given the impression that this was a real book that was available free of charge, as many other bona-fide books are available free of charge at one time or another on Amazon. This is not a bona fide book. It's a hook. An advertising hook. And it should be touted as such, just like the preview chapters are on other Amazon books. That way, the reader has a choice and does not come away with a feeling of having been taken for a ride.

Had this been handled properly, I might have bought Dan's real book. But now I no longer feel like it. Maybe later, after I have gotten over feeling victimized. For now, this non-book gets 2 stars from me: 5 stars for writing style and 0 stars for truth in advertising. And 0 stars for taking advantage of the reader.

Input: There are some good tips in here, and some useful ways about thinking about the guitar.  I realize a guitarist of any level might pick up the book, so what is obvious to a veteran might be a revelation to a beginner.  One bit of advice I enjoyed was learn how to play outside by playing only the "bad" notes.  I plan to give that a try and see where it leads.  A few other tidbits worth thinking about too.  But there was also a fair bit of fluff stuff in there.  For example, only watch beneficial Youtube videos and not bad ones.  uh, thanks.  Hack No. 22 was to essentially use brute force to solve your picking technique (brute force is not a hack).  And a few of these hacks had me scratching my head.

 One is his "hack" to avoid using a metronome.  That's just flat bad advice.  Virtually all top players have practiced extensively with a metronome.  Steve Vai used to practice a metronome 10 hours a day.  Petrucci writes all of his solos with a metronome.  On and on.  Bad advice.

Another problem was his misunderstanding of the 10,000 hour rule.  Tippet kind of says it takes 10,000 hours of practice to get "good" and you want to achieve a state of flow in practice.  However, that's NOT what Anders Erickson who created the 10,000 rule says.  Erickson says it takes 10,000 hours of deliberate practice.  He elaborates saying the amount of time spent doesn't really matter much, it is how you spend it.  To put it another way 10,000 hours of flow doesn't do much for you.  You have to spend the time working.

Finally, a couple of his hacks were just plugs for another book.  A plug for a book isn't a hack, it is a plug.
