Input: I played my first round with the Garmin Approach G5 today. I was very satisfied.

Strong points:
--finds satellites quickly
--lists golf courses by order of how far you are from them...closest first...makes finding local courses easy (you can also type in names, but I don't see why you'd do it this way)
--automatic hole advance worked flawlessly
--tap-screen feature to zero in on the green and the area around the green (incluing traps and stuff) was very helpful...I used it on most holes
--distances to hazards like traps was very helpful...it's good knowing that you can aim at a trap (because you know you can't reach it)
--tap-screen feature to "place" the flag on the green is very useful...greens can be quite large, and there can be a 1-club difference between hitting to a front flag rather than a rear flag...I credit it with getting me a par on a long par-3 by indicating to use an extra club for a rear pin position
--with July's update, there are 4400 courses mapped out
--all courses are stored in the device, not on your PC
--monthly course updates are free, never(?) a subscription fee nor disabling of courses you've already received...this makes up for the initial high price of the unit, in my opinion
--course downloads are handled by Garmin as a "purchase" of an item that costs $0.00, very straightforward once you understand that's what's happening
--once the unit is registered and you "purchase" this month's course updates, the downloading process itself took only about 5 minutes, which seems remarkable for 4400 courses
--color screen easily visible in bright outdoor light
--very sturdy and waterproof
--only one physical buttton (on-off switch)
--all other functions are handled by the touchscreen, and everything was pretty intuitive
--measuring a shot was easy and fun (I do hit my 3-wood as far as I thought)

A couple of drawbacks:
--I walk and carry my clubs, and was not satisfied with using the belt clip to attach to my bag; I was afraid it would snap off
--Clipping the belt clip to your belt makes the unit hang in an unuseable position...you'd have to keep unclipping it
--It seems a little too big to put in your pocket without noticing it
--So I've ordered the separate slipcase with caribiner clip to hold it to my bag...I think I'll feel more confident with that setup
--Got just one round out of pair of batteries...you'll definitely want to order a couple sets of rechargeable batteries and a recharging device
--Quick-start booklet contains little information...it tells nothing about the initial steps of registering your unit online, how to find the serial number, or how to order course updates
--That said, the website has all the clues you need, although a few were hard to find and not entriely intuitive

Overall, my first impression is very positive. I formerly used a first-generation unit from iGolf, which just gave distances to the green. On this unit, the course map showing the shape of the hole, distances to hazards, closeup of the green, and ability to place the pin anywhere on the green were big improvements.

Input: The T612 is a great dock/speaker system for the iPhone 3G, though there are a few minor issues that prevent me from giving it a five star review.

As advertised, the device is properly shielded, so there is no signal interference from the phone when it's connected.  The sound quality is quite good for my purposes whether I'm listening to mp3 tracks using the iPhone's iPod functionality or using another audio producing application like Last. FM or Minnesota Public Radio's audio stream application.  The unit itself is quite easy to setup, just open the box, plug it in and away you go.  It also includes support for connecting non-iPod mp3 players via an auxilary jack on the back of the unit.  It even includes the cable for the aux connection which was really nice, I had assumed I'd have to buy one separately.

I only have two complaints about this unit.  First, despite being advertised as iPhone 3G compatible, for optimal functionality with the iPhone 3G, you need the iPhone 3G adapter base which is not included with the unit.  It is however available for free from Altec Lansing.  Another reviewer mentioned that they had to pay shipping when they ordered their 3G adapter, I did not, so I'm not sure if ALS has changed their policies or what.  Unfortunately I received notice that the adapter is currently on back order, so I don't know when I'll receive it.  To be clear though, the unit will work with the 3G iPhone without the specific 3G adapter, you'll just have to fiddle with it to get it properly seated on the connector.

The other minor gripe I have about this unit is that when you plug in the iPhone 3G, the phone displays a message stating that the accessory isn't compatible and asks if you'd like to turn on "airplane mode".  Since the speakers are properly shielded, this isn't necessary, you can just choose "No".  Not a big deal but a bit of a nuisance.

Overall I'm very happy with this unit and from what I can tell, there isn't a better alternative on the market at this time.

Input: This review is not so much about the SI-2150 as it is about adding another set of front speakers. I added this amplifier (SI-2150) to an Onkyo TX-NR709 to drive the additional pair of front channels.

My Home Theater (HT) system is a Klipsch Reference 7 series:  RF-7 fronts.  RC-7 center.  RS-7 surrounds.  RS-7 back. RSW-15 and an RSW-10 subs.  I had a Sony STR-DA1000ES receiver, or something like that, driving this system, minus the back channels, and it was pretty good.  I upgraded to the Onkyo strictly for the HDMI interface and it didn't seem to have what the Sony had, although they were very close in the wattage output, the Sony being 100 watts per channel (WPC) and the Onkyo 110 WPC, so, I decided to add another set of front speakers to the existing setup.

I had a nice pair of Infinity speakers that weren't being used, so I decided to add them to the mix.  They have a nice warm sound to them in contrast to the Klipschs, which I liked since the Klipschs are a little bright for my taste.  Don't get me wrong.  For movie watching, the Kilpschs are great.  But, they could still use a little warmth.  I used the Onkyo to drive the Infinitys and I used the SI-2150 to drive the Klipschs.  The sound stage, with four front speakers, was totally transformed.  Adding another set of fronts should be a must do on everyone's HT list.  It is very highly recommended.  I haven't watched many movies with the new setup, but the one movie I did use to test it (King Kong, with Jack Black, Academy nominated or winner for best sound effects) was excellent.  I alternated between the two speaker and the four speaker setup and the difference was amazing.

To be totally objective, I did not see much difference in sound quality or quantity between the SI-2150 and the Onkyo.  I was actually expecting to see some difference since the Onkyo is rated at 110 WPC and the SI-2150 at 150 WPC.  That was a bit disappointing.  I was hoping to see a noticable improvement having the Klipschs being driven by a dedicated, more powerful amp.  I am always reading about how a good amplifier is needed to get the Klipschs to perform, so I was expecting to experience some improvement.  Result: Same sound.  Same level of loudness.  And for reference, the gain on the amplifier was set at the midway point.

The physical quality of the unit is good.  Seems to be well made.  Everything seems to be intact and in place.  It came with no defects, although the box had slight damage.  It was double boxed, though.

I am not saying that this amp is no good.  What I'm saying is, don't expect too much.  It's just a means for adding channels.  Maybe that's its intended purpose.  If that's the case, then it has achieved its goal with flying colors.

This amp was not purchased from Amazon but directly from one of Amazon's retailers.

P.S.  I ended up purchasing another one of these amps, this time directly from Amazon, although, it came from the same company from which I ordered the first one.  They both arrived in perfect condition and on time.  Good amplifiers.  The second one was purchased so that I can further expand my home theater surround sound.

One note, though, I noticed that those amps emit a quite a bit of hum while running.  Although, not noticeable while there is sound being played, but when you pause, or mute the sound, you can hear it.  It is rather noticeable, but as I said, doesn't interfere with the sound quality while producing sound.

I really gotta stop buying these things.  They're addictive since they allow you to expand your home theater almost endlessly.

Input: I've been using the ASUS Transformer Infinity for about a month now, and I have to say I really like it. I haven't had a chance to thoroughly use all the features - such as camera and video recording but I have a pretty good sense of the device. The reason I did not give it a five star review is because sometimes there is lag - for example after unlocking - but other than that it is indeed very, very fast, has good hardware materials, and excellent battery life.

Pros:
- Excellent screen resolution - text is very sharp
- Durable hardware materials - aluminum chassis is great, and the champagne color looks awesome
- Upgradeable to Jelly Bean out of the box
- Great amount of storage, and expandable by 32gb micro sd card
- Good price point considering all its features
- Excellent battery life - I tend to lower the brightness significantly due to personal preference
- Watching HD netflix movies on the 10" screen is great - the size is just right
- This depends on personal preference, but I find reading ebooks on it very comfortable. I thought it would be too big and heavy compared to a kindle, but it really works just fine for this function

Cons:
- Sometimes lags after unlocking - probably because it's updating widgets (certainly not a deal breaker)
- On mine the top two corners of glass must not be set completely or completely adhered to the unibody chassis because when I push on them I can feel the glass move a little and here a noise - probably a quality issue. Annoying, but not so much for me to return it (my hands aren't in those areas enough for me to care too much)

Overall - very much worth the money and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a top of the line general purpose Android tablet

Input: A lot have already been written about the Sabbath but the need far outstrips the supply. What is the Sabbath? What makes this book unique compared to the other books? For author Shelly Miller, the first thing with regard to taking a rest is her mantra: "I Don't Do Guilt." There is no need to be guilty about taking a day off per week, or to rest where needed. Sabbath rest is about receiving a gift and not an excuse for guilt. While the world teaches us to rely on ourselves and our own abilities, taking a rest is in effect an acknowledgement that things will take care of themselves even as we rest. It requires surrender and deep trust. The way forward is not simply an obligation to force a weekly sabbath but to joyfully discover rhythms in which we can rest well. Sabbath is a gift. It is a reflection of God's creativity. It is an opportunity for us to demonstrate to others that rest is not only possible, it is beneficial. Miller goes beyond simply taking a break. Sabbath is a time in which we commune with God in an intentional space. It is an invitation to intimate conversation, unhurried by the hustle and bustle of the world. It is a way in which we say to the world: "You shall have no hold on me."

While the benefits are many, there are also myths and deceptions that threaten to derail our pursuit of Sabbath rest. That is why Miller spends time dispelling myths like doing Church as a form of Sabbath. She writes:

"I tell her that I don't do church anymore. I try to be the church to people. For me, doing church is an illustration in slothful living - not laziness, but mindless busyness, something you check off on a list for your week. The heart can become detached, the ritual commonplace, like a child's piece of art hanging on your refrigerator for month. Initially, it takes the centerpiece of daily activity, but over time the beauty is overlooked, lost in the mundane. Celebrating faith can become a callous responsibility." (69)

Right on.

Just because we do religion or church does not make our doing a restful act. In fact, Sundays can be particularly busy time for believers. Miller believes that belonging precedes believing. She dispels myths:

Needing long periods of quiet and stillness before one can rest well
Needing everything to be done before one can rest well
Becoming mature before one can rest well
Can only be done on Sundays
Using rest as a way of improving productivity
...
The key to true Sabbath is not in the what but in the who. It is not in terms of the activities but in terms of relationships. It is the discipline to stop and to pause without guilt, lest we be forced to stop through physical ailment or other unfortunate circumstances. Rest is a need. We are not created to run 24x7. Muller shows us the need to watch for the arrows of the Lord that direct us toward trust. Signs are there for us to see. From signs of rainbows and weather changes to sipping a cup of coffee leisurely, we avoid the temptation of non-stop action define us. Our identity is not based on what we do but who we are. Sabbath restores this truth. When this happens, we do not feel guilty about "wasting time." When we experience true rest, we see the miraculous among the monotonous; the quest in the question; delighting in playfulness instead of detesting endless chores. In true rest, we find love.

Miller knows that a lot has been written on the Sabbath, and she creatively includes the many poignant observations on the Sabbath from many spiritual writers. From Mark Buchanan, we learn that 'rhythm' is better than 'balance.' From Abraham Heschel, we learn of the Sabbath being the purpose of the other six days and how marriage can be a metaphor for the meaning of the Sabbath. From Matthew Sleeth, we learn of how Sabbath means less doing and more being. From Wayne Muller, we are warned that if we do not make time for Sabbath, something else would, even unpleasant things. From Eugene Peterson, we are reminded of another perspective besides mere progress and constant busyness. Sabbath restores us back to our creativity, instead of perpetual repetitive production activities. There are lots more from individual interviews and sharing. Comprising twelve chapters of fresh observations about the Sabbath and the practical ways to rest, I find myself hard to put this book down. Perhaps, for anyone who do not know where to start with regard to the Sabbath, why not begin with this book?

The single biggest reason to read this book is that it enables us to read not just for information but for inner formation. I like the way Miller flows in and out with stories, illustrations, observations, and Scripture references to show us the fluidity of swimming with the waves, dancing with the wind, and embracing the elements that often come across as problems for the restless world. The reason why there are many who hurry and let stress get to them is because they have failed to understand the benefits of Sabbath rest. That is why the dispelling of myths chapter is so important. Before we can learn the new, the old has to be put aside. We need a paradigm shift. We do not need to do more in order to feel fulfilled. We simply need to establish a gradual rhythm of rest. Miller shows us how and much more. If you are in need of a rest, this book is highly recommended to dispel the myths that often surround us. Do not let the gift of the Sabbath come to us and we leave it unwrapped. Open it and enjoy it.

Shelly Miller leads the Sabbath Society, an online community of people seeking to make rest a priority in this busy world. She lives in London, England with her husband where they work on church planting efforts. Her website is ShellyMillerWriter.com

Rating: 5 stars of 5.

Input: Jon Meacham has tried to go where others have really not gone before - to explore the friendship between President Franklin Roosevelt and his counterpart, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill in his new book Franklin and Winston.
Meacham has done a great job of describing, in intimate detail, the relationship between these two men.  I consider the book to be a true hybrid between a biography and a history because of the style of writing - intermixing details about the individual (the biography part) with situations in which the person played a role (the historical part).  Meacham intertwines these two in remarkable fashion.
This is an important book that truly displays how Roosevelt and Churchill were not only political compadres, but were indeed friends.  I greatly enjoyed how Meacham discussed, with such attention to details, those situations in which both men were involved and played a critical role.  I also appreciated the way in which Meacham explained how those encounters bolstered the friendship between the men - and why.
Although the friendship was rocky at times, with Roosevelt bowing to political necessity in lieu of being true friends, there is no doubt in my mind, based on Meacham's book, that these two men were so much more than just political heavyweights - they were indeed friends.

Input: Wow.  What a fab deck.  I just knew it was going to be beautiful and ordered without even doing my usual hunt on the net to get sneak advance peaks!  (Silly of me really, as there is a site called fairytaletarot.com where you can see loads of cards and read the foreword by Rachel Pollack too!)

Anyway, the artwork is gorgeous, detailed and beautifully coloured.  The colours are perfect - it's not bright, like the inner child cards - nor pastelly - but neither is it dark.  The book gives the tale behind each card - there are some I knew, and many I didn't.  I recommend buying the kit, as the tales give more to the meanings of the cards.

Is this a Rider-Waite clone?  I have no idea.  You'd need to visit one of the many tarot review websites to get their more professional opinion - I'm just a collector of cards with beautiful artwork - not an expert.

The cards are made nicely too - reversible backs, nice stock which should stand up to use.  And the book has an illustration of each card at the beginning of the relevant story, which is a plus for me.

Note:  This is definitely not for use with children, like Inner Child and the other fairytale deck by I can't quite remember who.  It is a deck for adults, as the fairytales here are the real versions, not the expurgated ones normally found in kids's books - and thus much more interesting!

Highly recommended.

Input: This is so beautifully crafted, reading it makes my heart break that the author is not earning royalties.  a LOT of work went into this...I know, because I'm a writer too... A LOT OF WORK went into this gorgeous, layered, rich story.

Why on earth is this free?  I'm not meaning to complain, here. I think it's great that it's free, because if it hadn't been, I most likely would not have found this author.

But ... this is so beautifully done, I stopped several times while I was reading it, just to mourn the fact that it's free.  That's a first for me.

The only thing unfortunate about it is the title, which isn't compelling enough to  adequately represent the haunting, beautiful writing contained in this piece of work.

Who will like this:  readers who liked The Hunger Games, the Pendragon series by D.J. Machale, books by Garth Nix or Terry Brooks; readers who like fantasy with danger and more sophisticated themes will enjoy this.  It's an exploration of the effects of war on society and an individual coming of age story; it's also an examination of the effects of isolation on a person, and what it means to be "outcast," whether by choice or force.

the author is comfortable in the world he's created, so the reader can slip right into it--there aren't so many made-up words and names that you become aware of the writing and are constantly jolted out of immersion in the story.

Snap it up while it's free!

**edited:  it looks like there is an update to this book, I'm assuming it's been edited.  I love authors who do this - they're showing that they care about the quality of their product, and showing respect to the readers as well...another reason to appreciate this author.

This is a heart warming story, which touched me deeply. This book is not my usual reading material, but I can say with hand on heart that I absolutely LOVED it!

Marissa Lyons is a divorced mother of two, who lives in the suburb of Vista Heights, San Martino near San Francisco. She is a wonderful mother, but when she finds out her high school nemesis, Beatrice Munson is moving in across the street, she's a nervous wreck! However, she takes the bull by the horns and goes to welcome her.
Beatrice Munson is a force to be reckoned with! She is like a whirlwind, bringing new life to the staid suburb. She has a very Zen outlook, and is very colourful in her personality and her dress.
I don't want to say too much and put in spoilers, but it is a fantastic book about friendship, following one's dreams, love, loss, new beginnings and family. The residents of Vista Heights are challenged and changed in ways they never thought possible.
There are some wonderful characters in this book, and my favourite has to be Jeffrey. He is the sweetest, funniest, most glamorous and generous person I have ever come across. His parties are to die for!

Lorena Bathey has written a witty, fast paced story that made me laugh and cry. As I have stated previously, I don't usually read this genre, but I am glad I gave this book a chance. It does have one scene of an attempted rape, so I do not recommend it for younger readers (under 16). I am now a fan of Lorena Bathey's, and I will be on the lookout for more of her books in the future.

Input: 4.5 stars. I confess that I am a New Adult junkie. In the few weeks since The Deal was released, I have lost count of the number of times someone recommended that I read it. I have to admit that I become nervous about well-hyped books because I worry that they won't live up to my expectations. Fortunately, that was not the case here. The Deal was fantastic read with everything I love wrapped up into one entertaining storyline. The writing was solid and the characters were fun, but more importantly was the fact that I felt everything  the steam, the romance, and the heartbreak.

When I first read the synopsis of this book I remember rubbing my hands together and thinking Here we go! I love the idea of two people who don't particularly like one another having to help each other out in order to get what they want. Hannah was a wonderful heroine. She was intelligent, hardworking, and spunky. There were many times that I wanted to high five her for standing up for herself and being honest with Garrett. I felt horrible for what she had been through and how it had affected her parents, but she was nothing if not strong and resilient.

Garrett was amazing. While he was a bit of a playboy, at least he was clear about the fact that he wasn't interested in a relationship. When Garrett realized that he could have something more with Hannah, I admired how he was willing to go all in. I enjoyed his protective side, but I especially adored how tender and supportive he was of Hannah. Garretts commitment to his teammates was commendable, and I just loved his interactions with them. Those boys were so real and funny. As the book progressed I couldn't decided what I want to do more, hug Garrett or punch his father in the face.

Elle Kennedys writing style was fresh and engaging. There were plenty of romantic moments that made my heart happy and steamy parts that had me fanning myself. However, my absolute favorite aspect of this book was the banter between Hannah and Garrett. This book was genuinely laugh out loud funny. Kennedy did a wonderful job of making The Deal one of the most entertaining stories I have read in a long time. I believe I highlighted a good half of the book and not just the humorous scenes. Bring on Logans story!

Input: This is a novel about relationship, relationship between an older and a younger woman, between civilized and wild, the wounded and the healer, the self and all beings. Deena Metzger takes the reader on a journey into a world where these distinctions blur. New meaning, in-sight, emerges in the gap between what the narrator thinks she knows and what she comes to know when sees how porous reality is and learns in the deepest of ways how our wanton killing is not the burden of others but each one of us.

Metzger doesn't write about this abstractly. She takes us on a visceral journey. Just one example:
"Learning from Azul, (the woman) began searching out her own images and her own nightmare geography. The third rail of the subway. Sparks flying. Vast dump sites smoldering. Endless landscapes of twisted fenders, greasy, bent, rusted, unserviceable automobile parts. Miles of cracked plastic tubing. Storm clouds of plastic bags wafted by fierce winds. Mangled rubber hoses. Cities collapsed into endless miles of sewers. The woman was always lost in deserted subway stations, stairs going down and then down again and then down again...."

Only a poet of great power could make a reader see with new eyes. Only a fine storyteller could make us care about the relationship between these two women as they teach each other new ways of being in the world.

I highly recommend this novel.

Input: Mark Bittman is not vegan, but he spends a good portion of every day eating that way. Bittman refers to his dietary choices as VB6, which is also the title of his new book. VB6: Eat Vegan Before 6:00 outlines what he believes is an ideal balance of healthfor you and for the planetand satisfaction. He outlines the six principles of VB6: eat fruits and vegetables in abundance, eat fewer animal products, eat (almost) no junk food, cook at home as much as possible, consider quality over quantity, and see your weight as just one component of good health. He outlines food that you should eat (and food that should be eating sparingly or not at all), gives ideas for how to make his plan work for you, and even offers a 28-day meal plan to get started, using the recipes considerately provided at the end. But Bittman makes sure to point out that VB6 is not a diet, per say; there are no calories to be counted, no guilt to be felt if you stray for a meal or a day or a week, no temporary rules to follow before returning to the way you eat normally. VB6 is a lifestyle, a long-term change that will make you healthier (Bittman has been eating this way for six years and has lost weight and seen his numbers improve) without making you feel deprived. If you're looking for new ideas for a healthier life, check this out.

This review originally written for Sacramento/San Francisco Book Review.

Input: The scope of this book is wider than the story of how people populated Scotland over thousands of years. It's also about all of the British Isles and Europe and Africa, and how various groups, mostly farmers, moved incrementally westward toward Britain. It's full of stories about archaeological evidence of ancient settlers, and place names that have survived from ancient times. DNA sampling reveals areas where Norse, German, French and other settlers dwelt.

One of the most interesting stories to me was about the last Ice Age, when ice was piled high in Scotland and around the northern hemisphere. The water that formed all that ice came from the world's oceans, to the extent that the sea level was low enough that people and animals could walk from Africa and Europe to what is now Britain. Skeletal remains of animals native to Africa have been found in Britain. There was a settlement in what is now the English Channel. The ice melted, and the oceans rose, forming the English Channel. Later migrations to Britain were by boat.

The book has no pretensions of a page-turning plot, but I remained fascinated throughout. I am very happy to know so much more about my ancient ancestors.

Input: Nothing could have prepared me for the astonishment when this book came out of an ordinary brown box.

It's huge. It's heavy. Yet each page immaculately and intimately portrays a superb piece of jewelry with a scholarship that can only come from a life's work, in fact two lives' work. Ethnic Jewellery and Adornment comes from the shared passion of Truus and Joost Daalder for jewelry, history, world cultures, and each other.

This book is like the Sistine Chapel. You can't understand it in pieces. Internet researchers might see an online photograph of a Mongolian headdress with an excellent description and say, "Oh, isn't that interesting," satisfied that they have learned something.

Yes... they have, but the totality of the passion that comes from this book is not there. You have to start at the beginning. Fill yourself with wonder at a collection that darts from antiquity to the present day as easily as it travels the world.

Ethnic Jewellery and Adornment is an extraordinary journey. Take it. When you quote from it, you can be secure the information is correct. That is rare -- anywhere.

I now have to put on my hair ornament in the shape of a round hat from the Tai Lue (Dai) people of Laos and go for a walk. Oh, and I must make sure the characters and flowers that symbolize winter are seen in front, because it is February in Idlewild Park, Reno, Nevada, and the geese will expect me to be correctly attired.

Thank you for writing this book. Thank you for living the lives you did.

BarbaraAnne
BarbaraAnne's Hair Comb Blog

Input: This book was written in 1994 but the questions it asks and answers it gives still apply.  Depending on how the question is viewed it can be seen as trite or provocative. Trite because the answer is obviously yes:  there are Catholic universities and hospitals; there are buildings that house Catholic churches; there are people who call themselves Catholic; and provocative because if the answer is so obviously "yes", then why ask the question?  Because if the answer is "yes" than the further question is What exactly is Catholicism?  There is the Joe Biden brand of Catholicism, which pays lip service to the teachings of the Church but is really seeking something else - popularity, wealth, etc.  And then there is the Catholicism that Fr. Schall espouses - a faith that seeks to follow the teachings of the Church as the institution that was founded by Jesus Christ himself.  The goal is personal sanctity, achieved by self-giving.  Many of the problems that Fr. Schall lists still exist today although some have begun to improve; e.g. there are more bishops and cardinals who are forcefully standing for what the Church teaches; this is no longer left to the Pope only.  This book is not an easy read.  It is written at times in a way that makes it hard to grasp the concepts.  I feel sometimes that this is because the author is trying to teach profound insights that are not easily translatable into accessible language.  For example, one of the recurring themes is that the Church's teachings reflects how things are, that is the nature of things, so that its teaching aligns with reality as it actually is and not as we would want it to be.  Perhaps, the clearest example is on marriage, where natural law (the law of nature) is embedded in the teaching of the Church.  But there are other areas where this is so but that teaching is harder to grasp.  For example, that each and everyone of us has a purpose, guided by Providence.

Fr. Schall is honest and forthright, even taking on John Paul II's encyclical that could be interpreted as demonizing capitalism.  This stance was modified by a later document, but it was a bit jarring to see Fr. Schall so directly criticize the teaching of a pope who he thinks was perhaps the most brilliant man to ever sit on the Chair of Peter.

But instead of killing him and harvesting his organs for the black market, she accepts his deal: a wish in exchange for her getting him to the Alchemists of Loom.

I think the biggest selling point--for me--with this book were the characters. The book is split into four points of view--Arianna, Cvareh, Florence (Ari's partner), and Leona. I loved how Kova wrote her main protagonists; they were fleshed out and underwent amazing development. While my favourite POVs were Ari and Cvareh, Leona's and Florence's were by no means boring. They definitely moved the book along and added their own action to the story, but I was just way more involved with Ari and Cvareh.

This book is wild. The author starts just as Ari is about to start her mission and it certainly gave the book an edge. I was hooked from that moment and it didn't hurt that Ari was a pretty great and sassy character. She takes a lot of risks and has a smart mouth, but she's loyal and caring and she shows this countless times with Florence, someone Ari would die protecting. Although it took some time to find out her full story, Kova wrote it at a steady pace, dropping hints but never dumping too much on the reader. But we are told early on that she's bisexual so that was great! Finding out her story was totally worth it in the end.

I also ADORED Cvareh. I don't even know what it was about him, but I ended up loving him so much, all I want is for him to be safe and happy, two things which probably won't happen any time soon because when do they ever? But anyway, he was both sweet and loyal and despite how Ari treated him in the beginning, he still stood by her and helped her. He also took care of Florence countless times, and I liked that they had a good friendship blossoming.

Ari and Cvareh are complicated. I wasn't sure at first if Kova would pair them up, because it sure as hell wasn't looking like it, but I definitely love how she wrote their partnership. Ari absolutely hates dragons and Cvareh has no reason why. But slow, but surely, they come to slightly be friends, even through their ups and downs. Their back-and-forth turned into thoughtful conversations and at some point, Ari begins to trust him and see Cvareh in a new light, while Cvareh begins to see her as something more.

That isn't to say there's really a romance here. It's totally not the point of the story and it definitely does not take over the plot, but I loved the groundwork of a possible romance. I'm really hoping to see more because these two are my favourite tropes: enemies-to-(possibly)-lovers and sloooooow burn.

Also, I loved the friendship between Florence and Ari. It was clear that they loved each other dearly and Florence would do anything for Ari, while Ari would protect her no matter the cost.

The world Kova wrote is super intricate and intriguing. I loved how she created the guilds that focused on different talents and how she created her dragon race. They lived in the sky and it was super cool how their organs gave them different powers. It's probably one of the most unique magic systems I've ever read about and I'm excited to explore more of the guilds and dragons!

Although there wasn't much of Leona in the book, I liked her as an antagonist! She has an interesting relationship with her dragon king, sometimes which seems obsessive, but she always had her priorities straight and she was straight-up ruthless.

Overall, this was a great book. While I'm sad that book two, The Dragons of Nova, has been pushed back from April to July, I'm still eagerly awaiting it. 4 solid stars for this one!

Input: Ruby is a writer, but when her long term relationship ends she takes a job house sitting with the help of her best friend. However, this job becomes life threatening when people start dying.

It took several pages for me to really get into the plot and grasp what was going on because it was a little confusing, but then it got good. Really good!

The owner of a house contacts a company that deals with the house sitting. The owner, whom Nate and Ruby never meet face to face, becomes a very important part of the story. Though they never meet the elusive man, they discover a lot about the kind of man he is and what it means for Ruby because she is house sitting. Ruby comes to work for Nate, who owns the house sitting company, through a mutual connection. What starts as a convenient working relationship evolves into so much more when Ruby begins to uncover the secrets of the house.

As a writer, Ruby is naturally curious and theres plenty to discover on this assignment. First and foremost is the absentee owner who likes to play with women. And then there are the mysterious deaths.

The characters were for me what made this book special. Nate and Ruby had an instant attraction from the beginning. Though this book is more mystery than romance, I was able to watch their relationship develop and witness them learning to trust each other through the incidents and deaths that occur in the book. Through everything they learn a lot about each other.

The mystery and attraction turned romance is a perfect beach read. The mystery took some time to develop but that time was insightful towards knowing more about Nate and Ruby and their relationship. The climax was the highlight because all of the clues and bits and pieces that Ruby unraveled. It all came together for a realistic and satisfying conclusion.

Input: I love Sharon Sala's books, in fact I really enjoyed A Field of Poppies.  I found the characters and plot intriguing and well-developed.  I liked that it was a departure from her usual style and genre, but I still felt it was romance-y enough...exactly what I expect from a Sala novel.

This book only earns 4 stars (well, 3.5 if I could offer half-stars) due to the confusion of dates being bandied about in relation to age and birthdays.

You learn early on that Poppy is 20 and a little later that Poppy's mom (Helen) was born July 4, 1962 and died September 12, 2011 (aged 49).

Fast-forward a few chapters, all of a sudden, Helen graduated from high school in 1973 and Poppy was born December 9, 1973, when Helen was 18 (so now she should have been born in 1955).  And should have died at age 38 (1993).

Fast-forward a few more chapters and Poppy is aghast that she forgot her mom's birthday...in OCTOBER!

Sharon, honey, I love your books and look forward to reading them as quickly as they're published, but these types of errors drive me crazy and totally take me out of the moment in the story.  Self-publishing a book does not excuse the lack of copy editing.  However, if a person can look beyond these errors, the book is totally worth it.  Poppy is strong and resilient and everything I wished I'd been at the age of 20.

Grade: B-

Input: Think of megachurch pastors and names like Bill Hybels, Mike Breaux, Rick Warren, and Joel Osteen come to mind. Rarely does one think of Bob Russell. Now that I have had the chance to get to know Bob Russell personally, I bet that doesn't bother him a bit.

Russell was at the helm of Southeast Christian Church in Louisville, KY, one of the largest churches in the nation for more than 40 years. His book, When God Builds a Church: 10 Principles for Growing a Dynamic Church tells the story of Southeast Christian, while distilling principles from Scripture for implementation in other churches.

When God Builds a Church unveils Russell's philosophy about church growth, as much by what it says as by what it doesn't say. It is rare that a pastor can give so much practical, godly counsel without his advice devolving into formulas to be replicated everywhere else.

Russell's principles for a dynamic church begin with Truth (he argues strongly for biblical authority, conservative theology, and a Bible-centured focus) and Worship (he avoids the "worship wars" by calling for selflessness). In the chapter on Leadership, he lays out the biblical case and practical rationale for a plurality of elders.

As one who has frequented Southeast on occasion (and even taught there several times), I appreciated the chapter on Excellence. Say what you may about the mega-church movement. No one can deny that everything at Southeast is done with a spirit of excellence. Would that more churches seek to honor the Lord by offering excellence in every part of church life!

Interspersed throughout the book are Russell's recollections from his forty years of ministry. In the chapter on Faith, he recalls the sacrificial giving of the congregation. In the chapter on Harmony, he tells of tough moments when the church exercised discipline (highly unusual for a megachurch). Two other chapters (Participation and Fellowship) outline practical ways to get members involved.

Perhaps the most unique part of Russell's contribution to church growth is his insistence on preaching the truth, even when it makes people uncomfortable. In the chapter on Stewardship, he argues for more preaching on money, even if people do not want to hear it. Russell constantly cuts against the prevalent megachurch mentality that avoids confrontation at all costs.

In the final chapter, Evangelism, Russell explains that being seeker-sensitive does not mean crafting a worship service with the seeker in mind. Instead, it means we should genuinely worship God and grow in our walk, while welcoming seekers into our midst. Southeast does this by having sermons crafted with Christians in mind, and also by serving Communion and baptizing new converts every Sunday.

All in all, When God Builds a Church is the best book I've read from anyone associated with the megachurch movement. It is practical and full of sound wisdom and its author is one of the godliest men I know.

Input: The Second Edition of Way Beyond Monochrome goes way beyond just the basics... this dense, 500 plus page book covers every technical aspect of traditional black and white photography including such arcane information as to how to mix your own darkroom chemicals (this might turn out to be quite useful as traditional photography continues become a niche market and the supplies necessary to practice it becomes harder to casually come by).

The first 100 pages of Way Beyond Monochrome focuses on the basics: Visualization, Print Control, and Presentation. The print control and presentations chapters are very strong useful, especially the nearly 50 pages dedicated to the presentation of the end print... an area just as important as getting the print right. As great as this book is, it lost half of the fifth star in this section... only a measly 20 pages or so dedicated to visualization, composition, etc. Yes, there are plenty of books dedicated to this topic, but this book is so committed to every other aspect of black and white photography that another 50 pages on just the process of visualizing the image long before the print.

The next 300 pages are dedicated to the science of black and white photography... Tone Reproduction, Image Capture, Negative Control, and case studies. This is where this book really shines! Every technical aspect of black and white photography and the science behind is covered here, including numerous graphs and charts that will make your head spin. From the Zone System to critical focusing to fine exposure control to creating and maintaining a personal standard... these 300 or so pages will deliver.

The last 100 or so pages cover what you will need in equipment and facilities, and it will provide some invaluable tips, tricks, and tools such as building your tools like a zone ruler, test strip printers.

And, all of this material is supported by some very nice photography as well... a plus for a book like this.

Where else did it loose the half a star? Well, this is 2010 after all and though this second edition does include new material on the digital aspect of black and white photography, it mostly focuses on it as either a bastard step child or as just a tool to be utilized sparingly. And, this is unfortunate. As awesome as traditional photography is, digital cannot be ignored. And, for this book to have been truly great, it would have been more forward looking... It should have taken digital as a standalone technology more seriously; but, it really missed an opportunity to teach the digital photography much more about the photographic science of old and how it correlates to the photographic science of new. Rightly, it points out how much manipulation Ansel Adams did with his photograph, but it missed an opportunity to correlate that to the digital darkroom that so many photographers are now utilizing exclusively.

>>>>>>><<<<<<<

A Guide to my Book Rating System:

5 stars = This book changed my world in at least some small way.
4 stars = Good book, but not life altering.
3 stars = Wasn't a waste of time, but it was time wasted.
2 stars = Don't bother, clean your bathroom instead.
1 star = The wood pulp would have been better utilized as toilet paper.

Input: The Bering Sea Pollock fishery is currently the largest single fishery, by volume, for the U.S. and Russia, which share the Bering Sea.  Kevin Bailey's "Billion-Dollar Fish" tells the history of that fishery and in the process explores the challenges of modern fisheries management.

Bailey takes a meandering path through his topic, mixing personal anecdotes about time at sea in the Bering with almost breathless accounts of the intense commercial competition to exploit the Pollock fishery, and with some careful commentary on the shifting and evolving state of the marine science which has influenced the management of the fishery over the years.  There are well-developed vignettes about some of the colorful and strong characters one can encounter in Alaskan fisheries.  Bailey devotes time and effort to describing the controversial politics of managing the Bering Sea fishery, especially as it has played out in the State of Alaska and in the U.S. Congress.  The processes Bailey describes have led on the one hand to the undoubted disaster of the doughnut hole, still barren of Pollock twenty years after a moratorium ending fishing there, and on the other hand, to the current thriving Bering Sea Pollock fishery, albeit with a challenging future.

This book would likely have benefited from additional editing; those readers not already familiar with the fisheries business may find it hard to follow.  Readers wedded to a particular point of view on the subject of fisheries may be frustrated by Bailey's evenhanded approach.  However, this fisheries analyst and former Alaska resident found much of interest in the book, and appreciated Bailey's willingness to admit the limits of the current science and to explore all sides of a complicated topic.  Recommended.

Input: For starters: I've never read any McEwan before, and generally do not care for modern writers, but I was absolutely floored by his prose.  The writing is amazing.

His portrayal of naive, pre-teen Briony is dead-on and eerie, and, even though she is far less developed, I could identify some with Cecelia's feelings of being a bit lost and out-of-place at home after the relative independence of college.

I've read a lot of reviews that are impatient with the slow pace, especially of the first part of the novel.  While I agree that it is a novel that immerses the reader fully in descriptions, I think such criticism is a little unfair.  It is not a novel that should be read in anticipation of getting to a juicy ending; it's a novel that should be read with the mindset that getting there is half (most of) the enjoyment.

While I didn't especially *like*, or closely identify with, any of the characters, I thought they were reasonable (I don't like most real, live, people that much, either).  I didn't think Briony was horrible so much as she was ignorant, confused, and self-centered, as are most 13-year-olds; I include myself in that, as embarrassing as it is to remember it.  I thought she was an excellent characterization of an adolescent at an awkward place in life, with an incomplete view and as-yet poor understanding of the world.

The ending was complicated.  No, I don't think anything she did later could actually atone for the mess Briony made.  On the other hand, she was 13 and acting out of ignorance more than viciousness.  And, frankly, I thought the title referred more at her attempt to atone to herself, to lay her conscience to rest, than to actually achieving any sort of atonement in the eyes of the rest of the world.  I think it should not be taken too literally.

Input: There is a lot to like in this book. Douglas Harris does a nice job of describing all of the statisitical cautions associated with using student achievement data for the purposes of evaluating schools and teachers. Great information in and of itself. However, professor Harris' analysis is incomplete. Though he rightfully argues for "advanced value-added" methods of accountability which adjust achievement scores for uncontrollable variables, he neglects the one uncontrollable variable that produces the most variation in student achievement - cognitive ability. For large groups of students of about the same age, say all fifth graders in a state, more than half of the variation observed in achievement test scores is due to differences in cognitive ability. While other variables, such as quality of classroom instruction and home support play important roles in achievement variation, fair comparisons among schools and teachers require that differences in cognitive ability be accounted for and systematically factored out of value-added calculations.

To date, none of the value-added accountbility schemes employed in the United States, including all of the examples described by Professor Harris in his book, have applied controls for cognitive ability thus rendering all of them problematic for high stakes decision-making - such as school sanctions or teacher tenure, compensation, or continued employment decisions.

Value-added measures of schools and teachers are potentially very valuble accountability tools. But basic designs must capture and control all of the most relevent factors affecting student achievement. This book does a good job of informing the design of robust value-added measures. With specific guidance related to controlling for cognitive ability, it could be great.

Input: So I just finished this novel last night by an author I've never heard of before and the experience has left me with more questions then answers. That's the only reason this novel falls short. Let me explain:

 Chris Neilson is a successful writer and father of three married to his wife Ann for over 20 years. One fateful night, Chris gets into a fatal car crash and finds himself dead in a purgatory-like state. When he finally accepts the fact that he is dead, he is transported to Summerland, (a fanciful way of saying "heaven") where he meets a long dead friend named Albert who teaches him lessons about his life and his purpose. Chris is deadlocked with indecision and dread however because he loves and misses his wife and can't bare eternity without her. To make a long story short, he finds out she killed herself because of her grief and is now residing in hell for an ungodly (no pun intended) length of time. Chris leaves the comforts of Summerland and travels with Albert into hell where he braves demons, mental torture, and physical pain all in the name of love.  I won't go on further as I believe it will spoil the rest of the story, but suffice it to say the author goes on and on about death, indefinite immortality, reincarnation, good and evil, e.t.c. And what makes me give this only four stars is the way all this information contradicts each other multiple times throughout the story. I won't go into exactly where it can be found since it, again, will spoil the story, but the instances are there, and yeah- a lot of unanswered questions there. I guess if you're not as analytical a person as me, you won't even care and will consider this a well-written, carefully-reserached novel offering both adventure and philosophy.

It is a good first contact novel, with a space opera setting, an untested captain too young for his post, a human empire spanning most of known space complete with aristocracy. The details of the first contact are what really drive the book. The cultural nuances humans and the aliens must come to terms with. This is what makes good sci-fi, the human element, not other details like the science and future science.

Modern readers often comment that comparisons between this book and a certain famous scifi television series are annoying or too perceptible. I on the other hand don't mind the comparisons since these authors actually wrote some of the episodes and later movies. I actually kind of like the parallels. I loved that show, and this book has the same tone. Not surprising that I love this book too.

Some books I tear through. And some just lag. For me, this book was engaging and entertaining enough that I was not quite tearing through it, but, had problems putting it down.

Input: 3.5 stars

This book took me so long to get into, and quite frankly, Im not sure why I stuck with it. But I am really glad I did, as I ended up enjoying it. I adored Vaughn and his easygoing, and at times, boyish nature. He was so honest and kind, just the sort of guy youd want in your circle of friends. I love that he was so willing to just go with the flow. He wasn't one to question why life was the way it was. It just was, and he was going with it. Jonah, on the other hand, was Vaughns complete opposite. I felt like he went with the flow, but it was a deliberate choice instead of being part of his nature. Jonah spent his life trying to appear normal, but I get the feeling that he was really looking for lovein all the wrong places, as they say. This book gives a new meaning to slow build, and Im sure that was intentional and directly related to Vaughns indifference (or possibly aversion) to sex.

Now, I loved the friendship portion of this story. I like that Jonah found Vaughn intriguing enough that he was willing to stop bringing sex into their relationship and try to be buddies. But the part where they actually do decide to delve into relationship territory and make the choices that would work best for them was a bit dicey for me. I didn't understand the haste behind their decisions, and why there weren't different things they could try. But Im going to be honest  after this book, I don't think I have a grasp on what asexuality is at all, and while I don't understand their choices, I don't think the credibility of them depends on me getting it. So while Im not totally sold on the way things ended up, I did appreciate this story.

The mystery behind the missing paintings was predictable, but that was fine with me, because that was just the catalyst for what brought Jonah and Vaughn together. I don't think it was really meant to be suspenseful or a whodunnit. I think the pacing of this one was OK; if it had been a bit tighter, maybe the story would have gripped me from the beginning. The highlight of this book for me was the drunk scene. It was quite possibly the best drunk scene I have ever read, and it left me in stitches. Just when I thought Vaughn couldn't get any more adorable, he goes and turns into the giddiest drunk ever and proved me wrong!

When Blank Spaces finally pulled me in, it pulled me all the way in, and I ended up loving this story. If you're a fan of quirky characters and hard won relationships, this book is right up your alley.

ARC from Netgalley.

This review was originally posted on Books & Beauty Are My Bag.

Input: I was excited to receive Buried Secrets, the first in the Men of Valor series, by Irene Hannon. I loved the cover and the title begged me to stop everything and read the book.

The prologue begins with a bang. It was meant to be a joyride. No one was supposed to die. As soon as I read these words, I knew I was in for a great read.

Years after the event described in the prologue, police chief Lisa Grant and detective and former Navy-Seal Mac McGregor join forces to investigate the discovery of a buried skeleton in an unmarked grave. The plot is well thought out, and the story is well told. As a result of the prologue, it is pretty obvious who the culprits are, and it's only a matter of the detectives solving their case.

I admit to being a bit disappointed with this book. The suspense was there, the story gripping, but I found the romance angle overplayed. Instead of being a thriller with a touch of romance, I felt it was more a romance story with a touch of suspense.

It is great to have strong Christians as characters, but the attraction between the two main character was too "in your face" for my liking. Despite a promising "bad start" when they first meet, they almost immediately find the other to be irresistable. I would have preferred this to be less obvious, especially in the beginning, and their relationship to have faced more of a challenge.

Despite these short-comings (which are my own opinion) the book is a good read and I would recommend it to others who enjoy Christian romance in a suspenseful setting. I've given it four stars.

** I received a free advanced digital copy of this novel from the publisher through the "Revell Reads" program in exchange for my unbiased opinion. Thank you to them and to Net-Galley for making it available.

Input: 4.5 STARS!

Stuart and Mariska. I love that the author decided to give us readers a glimpse into their ever after. Now engaged, Stuart and Mariska are now looking forward to the rest of their lives. Stuart wants nothing more than to make a home with Mariska, but he faces some choices when it comes to his uncles ranch. His home is with Mariska and he knows it. But what if home is also at the ranch? Can he live his dream while making Mariska happy? We witness his internal struggle as he tries to balance both. When an unfortunate event occurs, Stuart is left in despair and full of guilt. He spirals down and old habits come to the surface. Can Stuart and Mariska survive this?

I don't want to give too much away, but my heart hurt so much for these two. The situation they are left to deal with is such a sensitive, relevant, and important issue. I think the author gracefully deals with everything that Stuart and Mariska go through. It was dealt with in such a realistic manner. Whether you have been in their situation or not, you WILL feel for them. Understand their pain and grief. Why they react the way they did. But one thing that never faltered was their love. Their love remained constant.
Unwavering. Stuart and Mariska truly demonstrate such growth in their relationship and as individuals. No matter what happens, they always believe in their love.

I found myself lost in this story from beginning to the end. Oh Stuart, my sexy cowboy how I've missed you so! Stuart is his usual alpha self, always ready to protect his love, Mariska. He loves so deeply. Fiercely. It felt in not only his words, but how he looks at her as if she is his whole life.

One To Take adds another amazing layer to this series. I am once again reminded on why each couple is such a vital part to this entire series. And these two are no different. Stuart and Mariska found each other through darkness and despair. And once again, darkness threatens them. But their love? Even in the face of tragedy, their love shines. No matter what shakes them to their core, their love is always felt. Their love is powerful. Their love overcomes. Their story isn't an easy one, but its theirs. While this can be read as a standalone, I highly recommend the entire series as it remains as one of my favorites. The author is a brilliant storyteller in that with each addition to the series, the characters easily embed themselves into your heart. Its like a family that you never want to part with.

Input: How very sad. I've been an admirer of Kate's work since I discovered it in about 1985, and I was hoping this book would offer some fresh insights to her life, work, thoughts, and creative methods. Instead, I found a grotty little mishmash. "Waiting for Kate Bush"  doesn't know what it wants to be -- music bio or fan fiction? It veers annoyingly between the two instead, doing neither very well, leaving me very irritated that I spent so much to get this, and all the way from the UK to boot (before it was available in the US). I found the brief overview of Kate's career the more interesting part, but this seems to be mainly a by-the-numbers clip job that anyone could have put together from UK press archives, previous Bush bios, videos of TV shows, or fan magazines. I learned very little I didn't already know about Kate -- a real shame, since the author is in a position to give us so much more, or so I would have thought. This reporting is delivered in the patented snarky snarl that  exemplifies the worst sort of music journalism practiced the UK: breezy, opinionated, terminally cynical, openly contemptuous at whim, and insufferably self-absorbed. As for the framing "story", which really is the dominant part of the book, I couldn't even get through it all. I found it more or less loathsome and unpleasant, full of repellent characters and oppressive surroundings and situations.  No wonder Kate prefers to stay apart from all of this and all these "fans"! This book made made me feel depressed and unclean -- I suppose it may hold a certain fascination for some disturbed souls, and I guess I'll keep it on my shelves as another curio/collectible, but I truly disliked it and wouldn't recommend it to anyone but those who enjoy wallowing in sordid and unappetizing realities.

Input: For the life of me, I will never understand why Americans who try their hand at "Troubles fiction" don't have their scripts proofread by someone who's actually from Ireland.  These books are always full of authenticity-shredding mistakes and this one is no exception!  In fact, just about every category of mistake can be found here, for example:

HISTORICAL/CHRONOLOGICAL ERRORS: One character's parents are killed in a car bomb years before car bombs came into use.  Another's parents both die in a prison riot - at a male-only prison.  Children are made into "Troubles orphans" well before the "Troubles" even began.

TERMINOLOGY: IRA members use terms ("Londonderry", "Northern Ireland") which no Irish republican would EVER use.  Irish and English characters use American terms ("brogue", "subway", "blocks") which Irish and English people do not actually use, at least not in these ways.  "Sinn Fein" is twice misspelled as "Sein Fein" and on one occasion preceded by a completely inappropriate "the".

NAMES: Several of the characters have names which sound like an American's idea of an Irish name (Erin, Meaghan, McGlaughlin)

REDUCTION OF CONFLICT TO NARROW SECTARIANISM: IRA members set off bombs in the shape of a cross, never refer to their opposite paramilitaries as "loyalists" or "unionists" but only as "the Prods"

"OIRISH" SPEECH: When the characters aren't talking like Americans, they're talking the way that Americans think Irish people talk ("Be you Provo?")

AND OF COURSE: a woman at the centre of the story with red hair and brilliant green eyes (actually very uncommon in Ireland, but Americans can't seem to write an "Irish" book without this woman!).

I could go on, but in truth, the book doesn't seem to have been proofread by anyone. It's full of clumsy sentences, misused words, typos, sometimes hilarious misspellings ("Rory was a lost sole") - it's just bad writing, apart from its other shortcomings.

The story itself is not gripping, and is so thoroughly unbelievable I just found it impossible to get interested in.  If I had known nothing about the conflict in Ireland I still do not think I would have enjoyed this book, but as someone who reads a lot on the subject I can honestly say that this ranks down there with the WORST Irish-themed books I have ever read.

Input: First let me say: I detest survival novels where the characters just "magically" happen to have every single thing they're ever going to need to survive the breakdown of society/technology. There's little to no drama, bravery or gallantry involved if you just happen to have enough preserved food, gallons of gasoline, medicines and all the warm clothing/boots/gloves and camping gear you'll need to get you through.

The beginning of this book reads like an inventory. The man and his family have just been through a [literally] earth-shattering experience and he's taking inventory. And smug. This character is so very, very smug in his absolute certainty that his Christian values and hard work have led him to purchase all the things that he and his family will need to survive. Within a couple chapters I didn't like him. After five or six, I actively detested him.

The main character, Rick Drummond, is overbearing, obnoxious and condescending. The wife is a cipher. The daughter is there only for Rick to have his "heh heh, teen girls are so self-centered" moments and apparently his son is only there so Rick can demonstrate "manly men doing manly things"...oh, and the son is apparently there to tote and carry on order. Rick Drummond makes a point of telling us that only a fool lives "paycheck to paycheck" when he magnanimously goes over to help his neighbors, a young couple with small children...despite the fact that most young couples live "paycheck to paycheck" when they're starting out. The author never explains how this family -- who appear to be an average middle class family -- has managed to accumulate several hundred grand worth of tools, equipment, food, gasoline, vehicles for every purpose, camping gear and trailers, etc.

This is pure male fantasy -- he saves the day over and over because of his ultra-preparedness and his planning...this reads like a survivalist's manual in parts. I quit about halfway into the book. Save your brain cells and don't start. I'd have given it 0 stars if Amazon would let me.

Input: I must admit I enjoyed reading Brain Rules, but the book has at least two serious problems. First, Dr. Medina claims that he is a stickler for insisting all his "rules" are backed by solid research. However, at least one chapter about the 10 minute attention span, is based on almost no research whatsoever. Quite simply, there appears to be no empirical published data that supports this rule. It's almost as if Dr. Medina made it up. So then I wonder, how much rigor has been put into the remaining chapters. The other issue I have is that the teaching advice given at the end of each chapter is very superficial. It is clear that Dr. Medina has never taught in a K-12 environment. I think the premise of the book is excellent - combining neuroscience and education. Perhaps in edition number 2, Dr. Medina could team up with an experienced educator. Bottom line: it is critical to make sure the facts are accurate and making statements like "we know our attention span is 10 minutes" is misleading and almost unethical, simply because Dr. Medina presents himself as an authority.

Input: I purchased this book as a text for a Java class.  It is one of the all-time worst textbooks I have ever read.  I stopped using this book half-way through the course as I found it made simple concepts grossly complicated.  I used two other texts to clear the cobwebs: Holzner's Java Black Book combined with the exceptional OO book Java Objects by Barker. There are many problems with the book.  The typeface makes the book visually unreadable: the authors insist on bolding all keywords, datatypes, methods, classnames, and code examples such that half the text on each page is bold.  At least for the first half of the book, almost all of the coding takes place in the class constructors and main (with absolutely no discussion of why this is good programming practice).  There is no sense of creating any type of OO programming hierarchy.  Each chapter has redundant confusing explanations that don't reinforce the topic at hand.  The chapters appear to have been written like a bill passing through Congress; everyone insists on adding their two cents worth, and at the end some completely unrelated topic is tacked on with no explanation of how this relates to the primary intent of the chapter.  The sphagetti-code nature of the text makes it difficult to understand what exactly is going on and makes the book useless as a reference. Save your receipt and don't write your name in this one - you'll want a full refund.

Input: This book was so bad I got rid of it the next day.  I was able to get through the first 75 pages but then the book lost me, totally lost me, when court transcripts were used instead of "real" writing.  These court documents were all in capitals, making reading so hard, As someone who's been a lifelong reader and a computer user, using ALLCAPS is like screaming. It's also incredibly hard to follow. The book showed the Q & A from the witnesses court statements.  This made for really jerky writing, making the reader so lost so quickly.  Trying to follow the train of thought just continuously showed that the train crashed pages ago.  About 5-10 pages into this impossible to read, literally, that I no longer had empathy from the writer.

I am from Utah and have lived in South west Salt Lake Valley where many polygamists lived. In fact I live around the corner from the employment where the author worked. I used to work next to the Allread (AUB) temple, had former polygamists as part of my daily life whether at work or my outside family activities. Being around and seeing polygamists were a part of my everything life here in Utah.  I'm not Latter Day Saints (LDS) but as a non-LDS in a highly concentrated LDS town, I know what it's like to be an outsider as I watched the "normal" LDS mothers stare scornfully at the two polygamist mothers (non-FLDS and non-AUB) mothers who were at our school as part of a family supporting our kids in their school activities. The local LDS culture is to ignore the polygamists  (if you don't see it, it doesn't exist) but to not tolerate in any way.

The book started out trying to lay things out from a LDS point of view with the Doctrine and Covenants 132 (D&C) section that was created supporting polygamy or celestial marriage as they call it.  I had to skip that part of the book just to get the background story.  The Book of Mormon (BOM) is a dry read any way  Back to this book after trying to read more, the court case seems to be focused on the legal right of who owned the land in West Jordan and who had life residency on them. The court case tried to show the "slave-like" conditions the author had under her polygamist husband but failed miserably.  By this time, I had well given up on the book and with some 30 pages left, I closed the book and said, "that's it."

If you are interested in a well written book about life in the FLDS, I refer you to read "Under the Banner of Heaven" by Jon Krakauer, then Carol Jessop book, "Escape." These both will give you a good idea of what life was and is like for polygamy families living in groups splintered off from the main LDS religion.

Input: Let's start this one off with a quiz for married women: Think back to the last time you corrected or criticized your husband. Why did you do this? A. He was wrong B. I'm smarter than him so I always tell him how to do things C. Both or D. Other

Laura Doyle writes this book from the fatally flawed position that, because as a "strong and controlling feminist woman" she would have been likely to answer "B", that means that all the rest of us would too. She seems to think that because her husband was finally able to catch HIS breath when she quit her nagging, that simply means you can apply a blanket salve that will solve all marital problems with one simple action: shut the hell up, and stay shut the hell up. In one rather extreme example, Doyle advises us:

"Respect means when he takes the wrong freeway exit you don't correct him by telling him where to turn. It means that if he keeps going in the wrong direction you will go past the state line and still not correct what he is doing. In fact, no matter what your husband does, you will not try to teach, improve, or correct him."

Imagine applying this to your household finances or parenting. What if a man is spending all of a family's money before the bills can be paid? What if your husband says it's okay for your teenage daughter to have sex with her boyfriend, and you deeply believe that she isn't ready? A family outing ruined by getting lost is a pain, but it's the least of the problems you're going to have to worry about if you take a consistent policy of never pointing out when your husband is about to make a really big mistake. She also leaves out the part about the ugly fight that will result when the husband realizes that his passive-aggressive, Laura-Doyle-game-playing wife has allowed him to drive 200 miles past their putative destination because she "respects" him too much to tell him, "It's this exit right here."

This is just one example of how this book is a self-contradicting mess - Doyle chides women for treating their husbands "like another one of your children" but apparently doesn't consider allowing someone to go on being disastrously wrong about something because the truth would hurt their pride too much to be treating them like a child. How is allowing a man his illusions and clamming the hell up when he's about to screw up royally "respecting" that man by any definition? Doyle seems to have confused respect with fear.

Put yourself in the husband's shoes while reading this book. You'll probably be insulted by Doyle's insistence on making a blanket characterization of all men as so at the mercy of their tender egos, so fragile in their self-esteem, that they need a wife to handle them with constant emotional kid gloves and never provide them with any kind of advice or counsel!

Laura Doyle seems to think marriage as an institution can never be a union of two equals; one spouse has to be the parent and the other has to willingly assume the role of a child. Since she's already established that it's bad for the husband's psyche to be that child...guess what option that leaves you, the wife, with?

I might be a little prejudiced here; Helen Smith's book that essentially says the same crap as this one does was still leaving a bad taste in my mouth when I read this, and quite frankly I nearly destroyed my own marriage and health by acting as Doyle advises us is the correct way in this book. Speaking up when your husband is wrong is not disrespect. It's part of loving someone to foster, nurture, and teach them. Not all of us are inclined to be screeching harpies like Laura Doyle apparently was; advice, counsel and correction can all be conveyed without disrespect.

If you really love someone and want to spend the rest of your life with them, following the advice in this book will indeed transform you. It will transform you into someone who will likely at some point grow to hate your spouse and quietly start crossing your fingers that they die first so you can have some peace.

Input: The Bible has been my favorite book since childhood. I find the more I read it, the more it explains itself quite well. While there is much to learn and room for growth, I am open to books about the Bible that add to understanding.

That's why I got this book. Sad to say, it didn't measure up. All the quotations and footnotes seemed to indicate a lopsided unbalanced reliance on modern professionals to tell me what to believe and how the Bible should be properly interpreted. Why should any inquiring person need Mr. Wink or Mr. Willard or Mr. McLaren or Mr. Wright to show us the correct way to understand Jesus and his message? Can't Jesus and his disciples in the new testament get their point across just fine without all the "latest research" and scholarly theories?

To me, the Bible is like a download from the mind and heart of God Himself put in language we can relate to by hand-picked writers who used their own style, personality and eyewitness factfinding to reveal heavenly truth in earthly terminology.

This has been quite sufficient for over 2000 years to get God's point across and what the kingdom-gospel is all about. Now along comes this author and others like him who claim to have more figured out than the rest of us. It's his calling to enlighten us and point us in the right direction after we got it wrong. That sort of prideful know-it-all-ism really bugs me.

The Bible has its own built-in assumptions about how it was written and intended to be understood. I have my own assumptions as does Mr. McLaren. My feeling after having read Secret Message is that his assumptions and the Bible's originally intended ones are poles apart. Because he relies so heavily on Mr. Wink and catholic theologians/missionaries as well as Buddhist philosopher Ken Wilber (per the notes in Generous Orthodoxy) and anti-conservative thinkers almost exclusively, Mr. McLaren's preconceptions and mindset he brings to the Bible skews things to his personal cultural worldview and educational background. He is the religious product of his reading outside the Bible which colors and distorts Jesus' Main Message of who he is and why he came.

Every book that claims to tell you what the Bible REALLY means is nothing but a human lens or filter. It is no better than the quality of what the lens or filter is made of and the degree of scratching, smudging, fogging, clouding, imperfections and flaws in the material and design, or pre-etched patterning that overlays between the viewer and the Bible itself. For me, anyway, I want as clear and uncorrected a view of what God wants to show me in his Book. This Secret Messaging tends to overcorrect and gives me only the writer's personal slant based on the prescription in his lenses and frames and what fits his vision deficiences. I'll use my own two eyes rather than someone who professes to see Jesus and his uncovered truth way better than the rest of us can.  -Larra

The mediastinum is the central area of the chest where the heart, trachea and great vessels lie. The parathyroids are in the neck on the thyroid. I can't abide laziness.

Having the FBI villain casually murder a muckraking New York Times journalist and then drive away listening to Rush Limbaugh might have made a funny Saturday Night Live sketch, but here it comes off as just plain dumb. The descriptions of the military are simply inept - the Black Hawk helicopters that ferry around Delta carry multi-barrel miniguns, not M240 machine guns, and anyway the M240 doesn't fire an "8 mm round". Obviously Alpert didn't care enough about the subject to get those details right. The description of hardware and procedures at the Fermilab particle accelerator, on the other hand, has the ring of authenticity. But Alpert's real problem is that he doesn't like people very much (a problem for a novelist). Nearly every character in the book who is not an academic turns out to be an evil moron of one sort or another. I'm torn between hoping he returns to science journalism and wishing that he would try his hand at a physics thriller one more time, but take things a little more seriously.
