Dodger Stadium, Los Angeles CA 1998 Psycho Circus tour)- Great video & sound quality. It's probably one of the better concerts from this tour. Overall: 10/10

Disk 3:

Dodger Stadium Part 2: Same review as above

Detroit Rock City premiere party, Los Angeles CA 1999: great little gig hyped for the movie. Overall: 9.5/10

"The Last Kiss" Continental Arena, East Rutherford NJ 2000 (Farewell tour): Outstanding, outstanding video & sound quality, and one of the better concerts from this tour. Overall: 10/10

Disk 4:

Coventry, Queens NYC 1973: not the best quality, but a great & historical gig that had to be on here. It sounds terrible on Surround Sound though, but I love this concert. Overall: 10/10

Madison Square Garden, NYC 1996 (Reunion Tour): My absolute favorite out of this whole volume. Great performances, and the band sounds tight. This should have been included on the main set instead of TS. Overall: 100/10

Input: really liked plans, but wether or not i like it better than transatlanticism is a question to which i will never have an answer. I love them both for the differences they pocess. One thing that i've always like about trans is that you listen to the lyrics and you're still like wtf was that. Cause it's more like poetry than anything else. It's very plain to see the meaning of the songs at points and then other points you have no idea what gibbard is trying to get across so all that's left is for you to interpret it. With that interpretation comes the freedom to have it mean anything which is very priceless and limitless in possibilities.

I also loved the lo fi sound that all of the dcfc cd's poscess i guess excepting plans. It's really a double edged sword because chris walla is amazing in production and with that very nice major label studio he can work wonders so i'm not sure what to make of this over produced discussion i keep hearing.

I think that it's true that plans seems a lot more contained than trans. Trans was way out there and very beautiful and epic while plans is quite a bit more subdued, comfortable and decievingly simple. I think probably one of the biggest things that made me just fall in love with plans was the simple beauty it's lyrics poscess. You don't have to interpret them as much as the transatlanticism lyrics because they are very plain spoken and more of a narration.  You can appreciate ben gibbard for his thoughts and how he puts them into song. This album more than the last i thought was much more focased on human relationships, loss and loving, death and moving on. It's something we can all understand and relate to. It's comforting.

Now for my last bit off spuaff about this album My favorite two songs are probably I will follow you into the dark and what sarah said. i love the idea that even if there is a "no on the vacancy signs of heaven and hell" someone would follow me into the dark. The eternal romanticism is embarrassing is it not. Ooo well sqeeg i don't care. What sarah said just gets me everytime. Even though i've listened to the album more times than i count if i just really listen to that song and take in it's meaning the lyrics the music everything... it can bring you to tears. It's so driven by the piano and you wait for it to build up and you want this explosion of feeling... yet it dosn't quite happen that way. It builds up and then... just mutes. And you t hink about everything he's been singing and you have the time to just go... no what wait. I'm not ready for it to end. I love that.

Brothers on a hotel bed didn't necessarily shout out my name the first time i listened to this cd, but after awhile i just came to be quite fond of it. How two people can be so physically close yet emotionally at oppisite ends of the earth and this " Cause now we say goodnight from our own seperate sides like brothers on a hotel bed." I think you can link that to any straight guys sharing a bed. It's not like girls where they just hop in together any odd feelings aside. Guys are so careful to stay on very polar oppisites and not get near each other at all costs. Just enjoyed that.

Input: I must agree with the previous reviewer.  I'm accustomed to the adult-contemporary, "gentle" sounding Randy Crawford, so when I first heard "Raw Silk" I was astounded.  I never knew Randy Crawford could sing like this!  I knew she grew up singing in church...this album confirms that fact.
Song for song, lyric for lyric, and note for note -- this album belongs in everyone's collection, no matter WHAT type of music is your favorite.  You may be in for a shock if you're used to the laid-back Randy, just as I was...but what a pleasant shock it will be!  If you remember when she covered Stevie Wonder's "Joy Inside My Tears" in 1995, and it sounded like she was about to let it loose then, you'll have an idea what this entire album is about...except she chooses to actually LET it loose here.
I disagree that Randy's own composition is a dud, because all of the songs are gems.  There is enough variety and depth here to keep the listener from ever getting bored, and not one of the songs is over-produced (something that occasionally happens on her recent recordings).
I am confident that you will enjoy this album, and it will probably leave you wishing that Ms. Crawford recorded more music of this nature!

Fun Fact: Young Pilgrim's physical release was put under strain after all 30,000 copies of the album were destroyed in an arson fire at the warehouse and distribution centre for PIAS Entertainment Group during the 2011 London Riots on 8 August 2011. Input: What made me get this CD of Julia Wolfe's String Quartets was her citing of influences from Beethoven to Led Zeppelin.  Specifically these string quartets were said to be inspired by Led Zeppelin and other American 'pop' music.  I had to hear it.

Know what you're getting into before you buy this CD.  All the pieces brush close to minimalism but with more intensity, less pure harmonies, and much better rhythm.  You won't find shimmering, sweet harmonies but rather harsh and blunt harmonies.  Her influences for these works seem to come from rock and metal less than from Beethoven, Schubert, or the like.

The first quartet, 'Big Deep', plays true to its name.  It's an almost non-stop rhythmic work on some harsh, low chords.  It almost reminds me of a metal band like Meshuggah being transcribed to String Quartet.  It sounds like the soundtrack to an aggressive underwater expedition by the Discovery Channel.  Different short, adventurous melodies try to break through on the violins occasionally but are always beaten down back into the 'big deep' of the rhythmic chords.  It gets progressively more dissonant and harsher towards the end, building up a violent undercurrent that crashes against the end as suddenly as it began.

'Four Marys' is definately the most abstract sounding of the pieces.  It is less repetitive than Big Deep.  It begins with all parts doing glissandos, sliding around the middle registers.  This eventually turns into some webs of soft harmonies sustained, and occasionally reverts back to its searching, sliding beginnings.

'Last Summer' is more remeniscent of the first piece, back to the grinding chords, but not as deep and to me not as memorable.  It has more moments of melody, which is to say a few brief snatches of melody over 10 minutes.  It's the least impressive work on the album to me.

If you're looking for music with brilliant progression, challenging harmonies and deeply emotional melody, this CD is not for you.  If you want to hear some excellent rhythm work and see what happens when you take a classical medium into more modern rhythm and chord methods of rock and metal music (though i'm sure Wolfe wouldn't characterize it quite like that), then definately give this CD a shot.

Input: `Every Picture Tells A Story' is as perfect an album as you could come by.  But in his senior citizen years, Stewart has prostituted himself with bastardized versions of standards via those mega-selling, artistically execrable `Songbook' series - musical abominations for sure.  He's long lost his classic-era voice, but I had hoped that this new collection would rouse his long-lost aesthetic.  His Muse, once upon a time, was about the Music - he's long sold his soul for gold [and platinum].  But the biggest fallacy is the title of the collection:  'Great Rock Classics'?!  Is he fooling himself, or just his hardcore, hausfrau demographic?  Bland Eagles, Cat Stevens, Bonnie Tyler, Elvin friggin' Bishop?  The Pretenders' most UN-rock single ever?  BREAD?!?!?!  He should have dubbed the CD 'The Great Lite-Radio Classics'.  And the true identifiable traditionals on the CD are rendered as mushy karaoke retreads, as the first single - the useless, uneventful remake of `Have You Ever Seen The Rain' - demonstrates.  If it sells well [and why should we surmise it won't?], methinks me smells a `Still The Same, Part II' that will be, rest-assuredly, dropped right around next Christmas.  Ah, Rod - Pop as Commerce.  My grade:  C-

So instead of working with someone like Timbaland, Britney had to settle for a Timbaland lackey Nate Hills to help write and produce half of the songs on Blackout which come out sounding just a step above the Paris Hilton album. Then Get Naked (I Got a Plan) and Freakshow, where Britney inexplicably raps, will most likely be Exhibit U and V in Kevin Federline's plan to get full custody.

The songs basically are just one bad techno track bleeding into each other which may work at a rave while on mind altering drugs, but for those of you that are sober, the album is as bad as you could expect. But at least Britney can in solace that it is better than her ex-husband's. But not by much. Here is usually where I suggest a song to download but you are better off saving your money. Input: Ah, Linkin Park. After their long and respected career that has so far consisted of an album and their remix album, Linkin Park returns to us with Meteora, a majestic opus that lasts a breathtaking 36 minutes, leaving the listener in awe at how this incredible group could have packed so much music on just one cd.
The album starts out strongly with Foreword, which consists of some random noises that only add to the staggering length of
this album. Foreword smoothly transforms into the first "real song," Don't Stay. After the incredible talents of "Phoenix" and the guy who always wears earmuffs in his videos, Chester mourns soulfully. A few seconds  later... uh oh, what happened here? Chester is ANGRY. Open about his teen angst, Chester screams about his broken relationship with his mother, presumably about how she forgot his birthday party.
The next track, Somewhere I Belong, turns up the angst full volume. It starts with some sound effects courtesy of the DJ and
some beautiful piano a la "In The End." There's the standard nu metal riffage for a few seconds, and the rapper comes in, with
Chester wailing ocasionally, like a girl, about how confused he is.
Somewhere I Belong is a track that illustrates one of the things I love most about Linkin Park: BEAUTIFUL PIANO. The beautiful piano piece found here is incredible, the work of someone who has played countless years. However, I can't help but wonder : who is this pianist, this genius, this modern-day Chopin? My money is on Chester. It seems fit that Chester, who aside from being a vocalist extraordinaire, is also a gifted musician.
While the rest of the album is equally a tour de force, the last two tracks deserve special mention. On track 12, the mystery
pianist we met on Somewhere I Belong is back to blow minds as he resumes his position on this two minute epic, easily one of
the most complex instrumentals of all time. Thankfully, he sticks around for the last track, Numb. Numb ends Meteora in all
Linkin Park's splendor. Chester doing his best Justin Timberlake imitation. The expert pianist at his finest, playing a piano piece with such depth and complexity that it only rivals a one-handed Mary Had A Little Lamb. The drummer pounding his drum kit so fast it has to be heard to be believed. The guitarist showing us that he is truly the Jimi Hendrix of our generation.
Beautiful.

Input: If your favorite Lita Ford songs are among the following; "Gotta Let Go", "Back To The Cave", "Shot Of Poison", "Falling In & Out Of Love", "Hungry", "Close My Eyes Forever", "Kiss Me Deadly", "Only Women Bleed", Don't Let Me Down Tonight", "Under The Gun", and "Lisa" then you might as well set fire to your hard earned cash rather than spend it on this abomination. I understand that Lita has a family now, but that doesn't excuse her husband Jim Gillette's (formerly of speed/shred metal band Nitro) vocals being arguably more prominent than hers on HER album. He may have been able to shatter glass with his huge vocal range back in the late 80's, but his former band was a musical circus act that featured great technical ability on top of songs that displayed the sense of melody and lyrical sophistication one would expect to hear if a middle school kid had written them. This CD takes that sort of "musical" sense and combines it with a Nine Inch Nails sort of techno experimental vibe with only a little bit of the Lita of old to tease the fans hoping for something that could stand beside her late 80's/early 90's heyday. The lyrical content is overtly sexual banality of the sort one would expect to spring from the mind of a 12 year old boy who has spent entirely too much unsupervised time watching the likes of Vivid video or Girls Gone Wild and surfing endless internet porn. Now, I know Lita's lyrics often had a sexual tinge in the past, but were often witty, coy, and playful. The difference between then and now is like comparing Gypsy Rose Lee with her big feather arrays showing glimpses of skin to titillate as opposed to breaking out a speculum and performing a full pelvic exam on a typical streetwalking prostitute. Lita's previous CD "Black" was a bit of a disappointment as well with it's grungey sound, but at least it had a couple songs worthy of making my 80 minute CDR compilation of her best work. This CD has NOTHING that comes close to being her best work and really sounds like an experimental Jim Gillette project with Lita as a guest rather than her own solo CD. The record company should have refused to release this debauched mess of a CD and told her to try again by bringing in some outside writers to work with Lita and locking her husband out of the studio......

Input: In reading the reviews of this album I, also a classically trained musician interested in ensuring that younger audiences find this particular type of music (speaking of the composers Bond has covered, not the absolute crap that resulted) more accessible, was hopeful.  However.  After having heard the nonsense that Bond has tried to pass off as some kind of art or "cool new thing to do", I am mortified.  Does destroying Barber by adding cheesy studio backbeats make you innovative?  No.  Does butchering Bizet put you on ANYONE's "it" list?  No.  There is a reason no one knows who they are.  Aside from the additions to the original pieces they drew on, (which by the way, are not properly credited in the first place), Bond's album is so over-mixed by the studio that you can hardly tell it's them performing on real instruments.  Perhaps they're not.  We may never know...technology is sometimes an ugly thing in the world of music.  Giving them the benefit of the doubt, let's say they ARE actually playing their instruments.  The delivery of every track is mundane and in no way reflects a unique or carefully considered mood.  Bond has taken the stereotypical "second choice career" of the failed classical musician to a level lower than waitressing.  I would sooner support the arts by ordering a burger with fries and tipping my waitress well than by purchasing this album.

Input: Jose Serebrier is best known as a conductor, although he has been active as a composer since age nine when he penned a remarkable solo violin sonata (on Naxos 8.559303). His First Symphony dates from 1956, when he was a relatively mature 18 years old. It is, undoubtedly, the most satisfying work on this well-filled program.

The symphony was hardly Serebrier's first orchestral score. Nonetheless, he clearly took full advantage of this opportunity to explore the rich timbres of the modern symphony orchestra. In the booklet, Serebrier claims not to have been familiar with the work of other classical composers of that era. Even so, I hear echoes of Hindemith, Shostakovich, Sibelius, and Roy Harris. Like the last two men on that list, Serebrier casts his symphony in a single, continuous movement that incorporates all the elements of the traditional four movement symphonic form. The result is compelling and often quite lovely--especially the haunting final bars.

The Double Bass Concerto is a goofy relic of the 1970s that is notable for its use of aleatoric techniques, lack of bar lines, clarinets cleverly concealed in the audience, and a narrator earnestly reciting lines from "Prometheus Unbound". At one point he intones an ironically appropriate question: "What was that awful sound?" In truth the piece isn't quite that bad, though it's hardly a masterwork. Bassist Gary Karr sounds glorious, as always. The Violin Concerto (1991) is more "conventional", but perhaps even less appealing. By this point in the program, Serebrier's standard formula of alternating soft, flowing lines with ferocious, percussive outbursts has worn rather thin.

The tangos are a pair of charming miniatures--especially "Casi un Tango" with its sweetly lyrical English horn solo. Lastly, the "Imaginary" film score was, in truth, composed for a real film that was never produced. Despite a hopelessly corny ending, the work is at least easier on the ears than most of Serebrier's recent music. Sound and playing are ideal. The composer could hardly hope for more satisfying realizations of his quirky, yet generally accessible orchestral music.

Input: Jagged Edge is a pretty talented male R&B group (and probably one of the only ones around right now) that is still capable of making good stuff. I liked "Walked Outta Heaven" as soon as I heard it, and their new song, "What's It Like", is pretty good too. But as far as the remainder of this album called Hard, well, they didn't really hit very hard.
The thing is, I think Jagged Edge are far more impressive when they do slow songs. Because as far as uptempo tracks go, the only one they ever did that really stood out was, of course, "Where the Party At". The fast songs on here aren't bad, but they're not that memorable either. Songs like "Tryna Be Your Man" and the Neptunes-inspired "Dance Floor" are okay, but they're full of nothing special.
Actually, some of the fast songs really COULD have been left behind, like "Girls Gone Wild" and  "Car Show" (featuring Big Boi). And one truly uninspiring song is the obligatory Jazze Pha song "They Ain't JE", and its remix is included as a bonus track (and that's not very exciting either).
Like I said before, the slow songs are where things REALLY impress, like on the title track and "I Don't Wanna". But even those songs only show a little bit of how JE can deliver, especially when measured against past ballads like "Promise", "Gotta Be" or "Let's Get Married". This album is okay, but it seems weak compared to their other stuff. It looks like Jagged have lost their Edge.
Anthony Rupert

And he continues this with Doctor's Advocate.

As everyone knows by now, Game was in the G-Unit camp for a time (which in turn meant that he was on Aftermath), and Dr. Dre was set to produce his new album. But after a highly publicized beef with 50 Cent, Game left the label and instead released the album on Geffen. But you'd never know that he isn't still on Aftermath because not only does the album's title refer to Dre, but he mentions Dre's name at least twice in every song except "Wouldn't Get Far" and "Scream on `Em". He even brings up Dre in songs that otherwise have nothing to do with other rappers (a rarity for Game), like on the filler track "Ol' English". And Scott Storch's beat on "Let's Ride", although good, feels Dre-inspired.

If you can look past all that, there are some good selections to be found, like "Remedy" as well as the creative subject matter in the aforementioned "Wouldn't Get Far" (could that song be about Karrine Steffans?). But what could be the best track is the posse cut "California Vacation", where Snoop and Xzibit help tear it up like it was the Up in Smoke tour all over again. However, immediately following that track is "Bang" with Daz and Kurupt. Daz sounds fine, Game is tolerable, and Kurupt's style feels more dated than classic.

There are also a few more errors. Some songs are ruined by the choruses, like the continuous repetition of "gangsta boogie" in "Compton"; but worse is the two-in-a-row of "Scream on `Em" and "One Night". The former's chorus is boring screaming over various DMX samples (way to go, Swizz), while the latter is an otherwise decent song that falters by a terrible interpolation of the Deele's "Two Occasions". And the nine-minute album closer "Why You Hate the Game" (featuring Nas and Marsha Ambrosius) feels better suited for a concert performance, especially since producer Just Blaze spends the last four minutes of the song giving shout-outs. Also, only the third verse is about haters while the first and second verses aren't really about anything; but the third verse also ends with Game saying "I ain't Pac", which contradicts what he said earlier on the album in "It's Okay (One Blood)".

And that song is also what stretched the album out to 73 minutes. While Doctor's Advocate isn't a bad album per se, to me it just shows that Game is a little too cocky for someone who does a lot of name-dropping and not much else. People that liked his first album will probably also like THIS, but I prefer a little more substance over style.

Anthony Rupert

Input: This Finnish producer cranks out albums about as frequently as anyone in recent memory, four in the past year alone. He's also the rare talent that can back up the output with critically lauded performances. Under his Delay name, "Entain" explored the fractured dub aesthetic, the Luomo alias put out the house gem "Vocalcity," a live-ish laptop-techno album as Uusitalo, and now Anima.
Anima weaves a combination of his various guises, a sixty minute experiment of sonic dub and his ever-present waves of drone. Recorded as one track, noises peak out corners and tickle the edge of hearing, all coated in echo and reverb effects. It's a hypnotic beatscape journey that challenges your attention, seemingly determined to hide content in the background.
Delay's dogged determination to reinterpret territory he's mined before pays off as an artistic endeavor.  Since it conceptually remixes his prior work, though, it serves more as coda to a successful 2000 than a piece that can stand beside Entain or Vocalcity.

Input: Angel's "White hot" from 1977 might be regarded as an embryo to the later pop-metal style played by bands like Bon Jovi. The music is rather polished and in a way harmless, but that doesn't mean it's worthless by any means. Even if Angel doesn't manage to go all the way, it's certainly very catchy from time to time, especially shown in the choruses to "Ain't gonna eat out my heart anymore" and "Hold me, squeeze me". "Don't leave me lonely" is quite alright, and a song like "Over and over" could be much less popish with a different production, while "Under suspicion" is in fact rather hard rocking. I would love to hear Rick Medlocke and Blackfoot doing a cover of "Got love if you want it" - I'm sure they would treat the song right. In "Stick like glue", the verse have  obvious connection to 1950/1960's melodic rock approach while the chorus is very similar to the chorus in Kiss' "Ladies room". But there's also really cheesy moments and both "Flying with broken wings" and "The winter song" could be enough reason for critics to write this band off as nothing but a image driven sickly-sweet bunch of record company marionettes.

Input: The Rolling Stones are arguably the best Rock & Roll band that ever was, and several of their individual albums are definitive rock classics. Forty Licks as a comprehensive anthology, however, fails to deliver. Part of the fault lies in the fact that the Rolling Stones's career cannot be adequately showcased in two CD's. The limitations of space make the job an impossible one. The other fault, however, lies in the poor execution of the compilation. The songs are not chronological, which is not in itself fatal, but they are jumbled seemingly at random. There is no theme or flow to the material. Song selection is not bad on disc one, although I would have substituted Time Is On My Side for She's a Rainbow myself, but disk two is quite poorly selected. The four new songs should have been on one of those bonus discs that are so popular these days to make room for four more classics, or maybe the full length versions of Emotional Rescue and It's Only Rock & Roll. There are too many mid 80's to 90's cuts on disk 2 as well. There are numerous songs like Bitch, She's So Cold, Waiting on a Friend, Star Star etc. that are better than Undercover of the Night or Has Anybody Seen My Baby. On the plus side, however,is the fact that Forty Licks features excellent remastering of the original songs.  Disc one was sourced from the new ABKCO remasters of the 60's material, and disc two benefits from new remastering of the Virgin Records material from the 70's to the present.  Songs like Brown Sugar and Miss You sound quite a bit better than the 1994 vintage CD's. If you are completely new to the Rolling Stones, this is the only compilation that has songs from both the 60's and the post 60's eras and offers a reasonably good offering of their best material.

Input: At the time of the release of the 2 best-selling albums of Sinatra's career, the Duets albums from the mid-'90s, I was elated. Many of us simply didn't want to believe, in fact rejected the unthinkable, i.e. that Sinatra was finished, so these latter-day gifts were sufficient cause for celebration.  And for the first month or two after each of the two releases, I played them repeatedly.  But soon the novelty wore off, and I had no interest in these concoctions, especially with the vast Columbia catalog, the priceless Capitol recordings with Nelson Riddle, the final extended chapter of his Reprise years all beckoning to be revisited.  Apparently, others felt much the same (recently, I've seen either disc going for a buck or two used).

The Bennett Duets are less "tricked-up" than the Sinatra ones, which involved long-distance, call-in performances by his partners.  Moreover, Tony sounds almost as good as ever, much more vibrant physically and in control musically than Ole Blue was after 1990.  Moreover, the program comprises winning songs from the Great American Songbook, with Tony so confident and secure that, rather than being "carried" by any of his younger, more vigorous, partners, he's the one who makes up for their deficiencies with this material.

Perhaps the track with the greatest interest will be "Body and Soul" with Amy Winehouse.  It's the most recorded popular tune in music history (check out the numbers at jazzstandards.com or allmusic.com), partly because much of its satisfaction comes from the challenge of executing it--difficult but ingenious and logical chords, unforgettable melody, mediocre lyrics--but Bennett and Winehouse (who sounds mature lightyears beyond her actual age) pull it off quite nicely.  Listening to Amy's first album--"Frank," the one before her hugely popular "Back to Black"--it soon became clear that the very young girl at this time knew jazz phrasing and could swing. Once she finished the daunting "Moody's Mood for Love," you knew right then that she was capable of delivering the goods in more than one style or genre.

The one thing that may be slightly off-putting is Amy's attempt to sound rougher, more blas, even a bit inebriated (stoned--or an affectation?), than either she or the song requires.  The same could be said about Lady Gaga's otherwise sparkling performance on "The Lady Is a Tramp" (what a travesty this number becomes when certain latter-day singers substitute "champ," which not only wastes Lorenz Hart's clever, subtly ironic, lyrics but actually destroys the non-conformist, free and independent spirit of the lady portrayed in the song).  But Lady Gaga sings the song and the word "Tramp" with the most assured conviction (it's Tony who almost messes it up by (only once) substituting what sounds like "champ").  Though she could do without a couple of "growls," Gaga proves that she's more than some sort of insubstantial hoax, one-trick pony, or year-round Halloween media creature.  Like Tiny Tim (whose musicianship won me over after the initial shock wore off), the person who plays the role of "Lady Gaga" is a wonderful "straight"performer, perhaps even a first-rate musician.  Sounds like she's listened to Sinatra.)

The duets with Michael Buble, Natalie Cole and Dana Evans (Queen Latifah) are predictably right in Tony's wheelhouse.  He could easily make an entire album of arresting performances with any one of these musicians, who have jazz sensibilities similar to Tony's.

The rest of the album will score big with some listeners, especially those who responded favorably to Michael Bolton singing with Pavarotti.  But to my ears the album tends to get a bit thick and mushy, even "injured" by musicians who simply can not swing.  I appreciated Merle Haggard's lengthy interview in the NY Times shortly after his "jazz" album.  Whatever one might think of the result, there was no question that Merle knew he was in unfamiliar territory, over his head and studying up as hard and fast as he could about the elocution, phrasing, and timing required to deliver a classic Gershwin ballad or swing tune and do it justice. Willie Nelson keeps revisiting the "American Songbook," but I have yet to hear him adapt to its standards.)

Bocelli and Groban contribute to the schmaltzy quality weighing down stretches of the album (The solo version of Tony's early signature song, "Stranger in Paradise," is far superior to this new version.  Inexplicably, Aretha goes after a song that was one of the highlights of the first Duets album, "How Do You Keep the Music Playing."  My advice: revisit the first version with Tony and George Michael or simply forget about it.  Aretha is one of the all-time great soul singers (starting out as a jazz singer, despite the popularity of her dad's recorded sermons), and she was delightful on the Sinatra Duets album, providing much needed life.  But here she takes on a freely structured song that goes no where unless the singer is able to take it somewhere.  She's in good voice but the effect on this listener is: "Been there, done that."

As for the others, if you prefer a duet for Harold Arlen's wrist-slasher, "One for My Baby," make it any Sinatra version, or even the Kurt Elling-John Pizzarelli meeting.  On this occasion, the song, which is a musical soliloquy, or a Robert Browning dramatic monologue addressed to a silent auditor, and moreover a haunting cry of despair (one of Sinatra's greatest "suicide songs"), was a mistake from the very beginning (I can imagine the Arlen estate even being offended by this insult to the the memory of Harold Arlen and lyricist Johnny Mercer).  Performed as a duet by Tony and his youthful counterpart, it comes off as little more than slightly mischievous and lightweight albeit pleasant musical conversation.  In fact, there's a bit too much pleasant, pretty music on the album--nice-sounding voices, thick layers of sweet-sounding strings.

But for Tony and the highlights on the album, the result, on balance, still amounts to a winner: 3 stars, a definite thumbs-up  though certainly not a high-five.  This time I'm not as quick to pull the trigger as was the case with the so-so (in retrospect) Sinatra Duets.  I could readily list (and produce from my collection) a dozen albums by Tony that trump both Duets dates--timeless performances, some with just Tony and the piano of Bill Evans, or Tony with Flanagan's or Sharon's trio, or Tony with Count Basie.  The man unquestionably knows the routine (to quote from the aforementioned Arlen song), and on a number of his solo recordings, he's gone beyond and above it--way above it, reaching artistic heights  on the level of the best by Armstrong, Astaire, Garland, Holiday, Crosby, and even Frank, singing his heart out just for the joy of it (and not a fiddler in sight).

Input: This CD is a crap shoot at best, so as the saying goes, "Caveat Emptor" ('Buyer Beware'!).

This show was apparently taken from an FM Broadcast from October 1, 1975 in Vancouver. That being said, the sound quality is iffy throughout a lot of the show. There are rare times when it shines, but most of the time it is somewhat painful to get through, due to over-modulated vocals, music brown-outs (where the sound seems to go from 2 channel stereo to a bad audience recording), and just a mess of a recording in general.
It truly sounds like the original recording used to make these discs was a badly deteriorating set of tapes that were about to literally disintegrate. I know because I have a lot of live shows in my cassette collection that have like 1 or 2 good listens to them before they will self-destruct (I try to play them once, and on that one play, convert it to digital for posterity). The tape that made these discs must have literally been in tatters, and you can tell how bad it is at times when it's just a swirl of good to bad sound and then back again, much like many of my old cassette tapes.
It's too bad that the people who released this could have made at least an attempt to clean up the sound and inconsistencies when making the digital master. However it sounds like they simply used the bad tapes to make this copy, add some reasonably nice packaging, and release it for sale to the masses. If Frank were alive, he'd no doubt grab this one for another round of the 'Beat the Boots' series to simply re-route the cash flow back to his own pockets.

That being said, the content is nevertheless interesting. This show is sort of the mid-seventies pseudo-Mothers show (Roy Estrada is still playing in the band) but with one great exception, Terry Bozzio is on the skins, and that alone makes for an interesting show, especially this early on in his performance relationship with Frank. Napoleon Murphy Brock as always keeps it entertaining, and the band is rounded out by Andre Lewis and (of course) Frank.

After I listened to the first disc, I felt kind of ripped off because the sound was annoying, and even during instrumental sections like 'Chunga's Revenge', it was a mixed bag of good and bad sound. The highlights for me on Disc 1 is a really nice version of Carolina Hardcore Ecstasy and a much slower Illinois Enema Bandit, two songs just finding their way in these early workouts by Frank. Other than that, it's a crap shoot.

However my appreciation for this release (and why I now feel like it is worth buying, at least for me) was after listening to Disc 2. Sure the sound is still at times all over the place, but this disc is worth buying for the series of songs that go into each other that fills the majority of Disc 2: Canadian Customs Routine (which is hilarious!) > T'Mershi Duween > Zoot Allures > Sleep Dirt > Black Napkins. These 5 tracks alone make this disc worth buying. The sound stays relatively static during this set of songs, and it is not bad at all. I love Zoot Allures here because it is performed a bit differently than what eventually gets released on the album of the same name, and Frank makes some sweat sounds during this one, very smooth, mesmerizing, almost trance-like. The horns are absolutely wonderful on T'Mershi Duween and Sleep Dirt, and the Black Napkins (also still in experimental phase) is phenomenal, nothing short of brilliant. Adding Terry Bozzio on drums was one of Frank's smartest moves in the mid 1970's and this version of Black Napkins drives that point home. It's just a very nice sequence of songs, I can't say enough of how much I enjoy listening to this chunk of music on this disc. Of course, the last 2 songs after it, which are the encores, the sound goes back to being crap (the 'Advance Romance' is cut at the beginning and although the 'I am the Slime' is a great version, the vocals are drowned out in the background).

So as I said previously, 'Buyer Beware' but for you die hard Zappa fans like me (who is always looking for more live shows that the Zappa Family Trust is not releasing), it's worth picking up. Historically it is worth owning, and the price (at least when I purchased it) did not break the bank.

Input: In short: An enjoyable album, but somewhat less than impressive.

Having waited for seven years since Enya's last release, I suppose was hoping for something more grand. That is not to say Dark Sky Island is not good, it certainly is. Still, I was left wanting. I certainly was not hoping for any significant changes in her musical style, and I rejoiced that the overall production remained true to the "Enya sound." However, I felt a bit disappointed by a perceived lack of reach or growth. In short, after waiting for seven years, the new album sounds almost indistinguishable from her earlier works. Perhaps it is best not to tamper with the tried and true formula, but I suppose I was hoping for more and am left wondering "what might have been."

Oh, and speaking of tried and true formulas... One final comment on the packaging. Yuck.

This album apparently marks Enya's departure from the traditional plastic "crystal" CD case package, in favor of the lighter, much cheaper (read: more profitable) cardboard sleeve. Beautifully done, to be sure, but the purpose of the case is, after all, to protect the disc. This one failed miserably. The disc arrived coverd with countless tiny scratches on its playing surface. So much so, that the disc looked "hazy." Indeed, it looked like a used CD purchased at a swap meet. Really? After paying full price for a product, it it unreasonable to expect that it be in excellent condition? Perhaps this is how they plan to force people to migrate from physical discs to digital files. (I enjoy and use both, by the way.) Look, I want to save the planet as much as anybody, but let's be honest here. This is about profit margin, not the environment.

End of sermon.

Input: Despite it's significant commercial success, "The River" is without doubt Bruce Springsteen's weakest recording with the E Street band. Perhaps due to incessant critical pampering, perhaps due simply to a creative lull, "The River"  for the first and ONLY time in his career, sees Springsteen sounding uninspired and repetitive. The first record is definitely the stronger of the two with the pop smarts of "Hungry Heart", the moving father/son ballad"Independence Day" and the sorrowful lamentation of the title track, displaying Springsteen in top form . For the most part however, he is caught in mediocrity, chugging out bland rockers and cheesy, overwrought  ballads, many of which would not be out of place on a Bon Jovi album.(see "Crush on You," "Drive all night"  ). Furthermore, the production is a mess with the vocals often being swamped by  muddy and irritating guitars and Weinberg's drumming slipshod at best. Critics of "The River" have often queried why Springsteen felt the need to record a  double record and certainly a more strict culling process  would have made this a more coherent release if nothing else. My personal contention however relates to the songs Springsteen left off the record. "Roulette","Where the bands are" and "Held up without a gun" were all recorded during "The River" sessions and are far superior to much of the pedestrian  material on the actual release. Of course this is obviously opinion and Bruce probably sees the whole thing in a different light. All the same, I'm pretty sure I'm right.

Input: David Sylvian has been as of late full of surprises.  2003's "Blemish" found Sylvian experimenting with minimalism, electronic noise, feedback, and loops, a brilliant and personal album.  His latest effort, a collaboration with brother Steve Jansen and Burnt Friedman under the name Nine Horses, is quite the opposite.

In many ways, "Snow Borne Sorrow" is as much a logical successor to "Secrets of the Beehive" as "Dead Bees on a Cake".  Or perhaps better still, it feels like the child of the unreleased "Little Girls With 99 Lives" material (some of which saw the light of day as b-sides to 'Dead Bees' singles) and 'Beehive'-- keeping the jazz-tinged sound and textures of the former but eschewing lush textures in favor of a '99 Lives'-like modern noir sound.  In better words, its sort of like a modern, loose take on Sylvian's jazz-infected composition.

At its best, the pieces have an unnatural energy to them, from the loping bass of opener "Wonderful World" to the guitar-driven "Darkest Birds" or the bizarrely folky-filtered through Miles Davis "The Day the Earth Stole Heaven".  But at times, the album seems to overreach, primarily in a couple overlong pieces as the title track and closer "The Librarian", neither of which particularly go anywhere.  But on the other hand, something like "Atom and Cell" feels like a lifeless harmony-laden pop song that somehow manages to wholly captivate.

All in all, I find this a pretty mixed record-- at times satisfying, at times I lost interest.  Then again, I didn't get "Blemish" at first, so maybe I'll change my mind in a dozen more listens.  There's enough here to keep me coming back, but not enough to get me raving about it.

Input: This 1987 CD from the now-defunct Conifer label marked the first commercial recording by the City of Birmingham Symphony Chorus (CBSO Chorus), under the direction of their long-time chorus master Simon Halsey. One work from Elgar is featured, the original version of his op. 27 "Scenes from the Bavarian Highlands", with words "imitated from Bavarian Volkslieder and 'Schnadahuepfler' by Caroline Elgar, wife of Edward Elgar. The work is generally lightweight in tone, which the solo piano accompaniment would be expected to emphasize, compared to the version for chorus and orchestra.

The first of the Holst selections, "Dirge and Hymneal", is a 1915 setting of a poem by Thomas Lovell Beddoes, reported here as the world premiere recording. Even though the notes give this away, it's still a bit of an aural surprise to hear melodic material in a choral work that wound up later in "Saturn, the Bringer of Old Age" from Holst's "The Planets". Holst's op. 43 Two Motets, from 1924-1925, set poems by Henry Vaughan ("The Evening Watch") and Digby Mackworth Dolben ("Sing me the men").

The final work on the album, the Five Partsongs, op. 12, actually has the most complicated preparation history behind it. Holst composed the op. 12 in 1902-1903. However, only 3 of these songs were published at first, No. 1 ("Dream Tryst" by Francis Thompson), No. 2 ("Ye Little Birds" by Thomas Heywood) and No. 4 (the anonymous 16th century poem "Now is the month of Maying"). Holst did not complete No. 3, the first verse of "Her eyes the glow-worm lend thee" by Robert Herrick, but Imogen Holst, Gustav Holst's daughter, edited this setting towards the end of her life. No. 5 is a setting of "Come to me" by Christina Rosetti, although the notes don't indicate who was responsible for editing this setting. In any case, this recording was thus the first recording of the complete op. 12.

The CBSO Chorus does a good job throughout, clearly well trained by Simon Halsey. Where things fall short is in the recording quality, where the sound seems rather recessed and the chorus comes off as sounding rather small-scale. The piano is reasonably well blended with the chorus, with Richard Markham doing a good job. But again, the overall sonoroties seem rather diminished, if that makes sense. There is also a small issue of presentation where the timings of the selections are nowhere to be found in the booklet. The timings of each of the tracks are given on the CD itself, but that's the only place where the timings are indicated. The whole CD runs 53:09.

Overall, this CD would seem aimed at aficionados of English choral music, and admirers of the CBSO Chorus and Simon Halsey, primarily. It's an OK, if not necessarily earth-shattering or mind-blowing album.

Just because non-punk fans like it doesn't make it a bad song, guys.
The rest, however is nothing that puts any strut in my step. "Death is a Star" and "Sean Flynn" are okay, but just okay. The rest I can't summon the energy to comment on, and "Overpowered by Funk" is the single most irritating song this side of "Shiny Happy People". I get the whole playing with reggae deal, but this song wears out its welcome in a hurry. IT JUST WON'T END. Instead, the Clash did. Just goes to show you: experimentation is a fine thing, but trying to pretend you're something you're not is not what kept the Ramones going all those years...

Input: I must admit, I was somewhat disappointed with this CD.  It's true, it has some wonderful tracks by relatively obscure composers (Marcello, Locatelli, Corrette), although these particular selections often appear in Baroque compilations.  Some of the renditions on this album lack subtlety.  Bach's "Air on a G-String" is appropriately slow, but shows no variation in dynamics, and the piece lacks its characteristic depth.  The Mouret Rondeau (the infamous "Masterpiece Theater" theme) is overblown and bombastic in this recording, possessing none of the dignity for which the piece is so well known.  Curiously, both the first and last track are Pachebel's Canon: upon first listening, I thought perhaps they would have a different version at the end of the album.  No.  They just have the exact same track twice, a somewhat ungainly version with the organ replacing the double bass, and again, no sensitivity with dynamics.  The booklet claims these classics are "memorably performed by some of the world's finest artists", but fails to name any performers!  This low budget disc contains no documentation with information about the pieces, the composers, or the performances.  For the connoisseur seeking definitive recordings, this CD should not even be a thought.  For some who doesn't know anything about Baroque music and simply doesn't know where to start, I wouldn't recommend starting here.  Start learning about Baroque music with Bach's Brandenburg Concertos, not with this odd compilation.

Input: It's been eleven years since the last Aerosmith studio album, 2001's Just Push Play (and there's also been the 2004 covers album Honkin' On Bobo) which was really a product of its time with the band collaborating with producers that gave them a clean modern pop sound. This time around they brought back producer Jack Douglas who worked on some of the band's best albums in the 1970's. With the inner problems in the band and the near breakup, Steven Tyler doing American Idol fans were beginning to wonder if there was any recording going. It took a long time but Aerosmith's 15th studio album, Music From Another Dimension is here. Initially the band said it would be a throwback to Toys in the Attics (1975) and Rocks (1976) and there are glimpses of that, but there's also glimpses of the 80's and 90's Aerosmith too and a LOT of ballads. It's as if all eras of the band are blended in one album and that's their sound in 2012.  I got to hand it to them, for a band of men in their 60's there's some pretty rocking material here, and I find that the band does vocals harmonies quite a lot this time around(actually they sound like they wouldn't be out of place on a Def Leppard album). There's some good but to me it's an overall underwhelming Aerosmith album.

The ups with MFAD are the strong rock track. In fact the album starts off rather with a string of three solid rock songs. "LUV XXX" starts out with a spoken intro before kicking it into high gear, I wish the entire album was like this, it's genuinely one of the best Aerosmith songs that's been done since the 1970's. It has that vibe from Toys/Rock era and it's fantastic. "Beautiful" is commercial Aerosmith at its best, it's catchy, the vocal harmonies are excellent and the songs is very likeable as a whole. " Legendary Cild"  is a Grip a Grip era song that never saw the light of day. I was intrigued at first and when I listened to it I thought to myself "this could work", and it does it rocks and it's catchy enough I really like this one. "Can't Stop Loving You" with Carrie Underwood is puzzling, having her on an Aerosmith album is obviously not going to well with some of the fans and it's just not that good of a duet. "This Could Have Been Love" was chosen as the single and no surprise, it's a ballad.  I actually like this one, even if it's a 1990's Aero ballad rehash sounding or cheesy or sappy, I can acknowledge all of this but it still works for what is. "Street Jesus" has more of a classic rock edge to it, with even some jamming parts and the result is a longer, more vintage sounding track that works fairly well, it's one of those the hardcore fans will enjoy the most. The Joe Perry sung track "Freedom Fighter" is one of the best songs on this album for me, it's got a good Perry riff and even thought his voice isn't particularly great the song manages to rocks. "Another Last Goodbye" is a fitting ballad to end the album, it's a good one but it's overshadowed by the fact that there are too many ballads on MFAD to truly stand out.

The first half of the album, I have generally good things to say about and it sounds promising and it makes you think that yes, maybe Aerosmith has some of the old rock sound we love back and it's going to be an entire album like this. Then there's the second side, filled with ballads and it really breaks the album's flow. A big part of the problem is that the album suffers from the too much ballads syndrome that was present on albums like Get A Grip, and they sound mostly like 1990's Aerosmith ballads. Six/seven (depending on who you ask) ballads on an album is just too much, and I like ballads but these are for the most part just sappy and rehashed songs that they've already done, except not as good or passionate. There's just no overlooking that many ballads is overkill. The worst part is a duet with Carrie Underwood, no offense but what's she doing on an Aerosmith album? Especially one which was reported as "back to their roots".  I found some of the lyrics here to be the band's most juvenile yet, which is rather humorous coming from men in their sixties. Then again the album has 15 tracks, maybe a little too much and if they removed some of the ballads and Diane Warren songs (still using outside writers it seems) it would have come across as a tighter effort, it comes across as a modern version of Get A Grip (some good rock songs, plenty of ballads and it has over 14 songs and an outtake from that album as well) . Most of those ballads sound like they're trying to be part II of "Amazing", "Crying" or "Don't Wanna Miss A Thing". 15 songs may just be a little too much, if they cut some of it down it would have made for a shorter, tighter more Rock album, that's my take on it.

Like many fans, it's hard for me to hide my disappointment. Still better than Just Push Play that's for sure, but I expected more from the hype Aerosmith had around this release. There are things to like but there's some that bring down the experience ultimately. I listened to it a few times by now and I can honestly say my rating is a 2  out of 5. Some of the Rock tracks are reminiscent of classic Aerosmith and energy charged tunes but overall it comes off as an album that didn't know what direction it wanted to take. There have been some great releases by Classic bands this year, but sadly Aerosmith's is not one of them I'm afraid.

Input: Before writing this, i read the 80 or so reviews of this cd first. Before that, i listened to this cd mutiple times after buying it on vinyl and the Walmart version with the different cover as well as the regular BB edition with the extra dvd and my overall question to the other reviewers is  -  What are you people listening to?????? Sure it's better than current Metallica or 95 % of anything else out now that's heavy. So What!
It isn't any good. The best song, Bible Black, wouldn't make any Sabbath lp thru Born Again with Ian Gillan and would be a minor cut on the Tony Martin albums! Look, I love Iommi; as a current live rock guitarist right now, he is still the best out there. I've seen him live 25 times. For writing new material, it's over and has been for a while. I don't know if having Geezer write the lyrics would have helped this effort, probably not, but this sounds like another Dio record. And i don't think an innovative producer would have made any difference either. You only have so many good riffs in you and Iommi has had more than anyone ever. Did you ever wonder why the classic rockers cannot do anything NEW that rocks when they get past a certain age? Iommi, Townshend, Clapton, Blackmore, Beck, Richards to name a few. And yet live, they play the old stuff the best they ever did. It's because they're 2 entirely different aptitudes. Still, i give Iommi credit for trying to continue compared to someone like Jimmy Page who's had nothing to offer for almost 30 years after plagiarizing old black blues artists the previous ten years. The biggest hoax ever put over the rock world was Led Zeppelins "supposed" superiority over Black Sabbath. Well, right now compare the Iommi/Ozzy canon of work over the last 40 years with Page /Plant and tell me which is more influential, which is superior?

One final test. Listen to TDYK and then listen Sabbath's 1978 lp, "Never Say Die" probably their least acclaimed work ever. It absolutely kills this new effort. When i wanna rock, I'll listen to NSD, you can waste your time with this drivel.

Input: Everyone likes to think that their favorite artist can't be best-of'd, because, "Man, the ALBUMS, man."  But in reality, most folks enjoy Pink Floyd and Radiohead compilations, even if fans and critics pull out their hair, wondering how such an injustice can be contained in a small piece of plastic.  So I'm well aware that complaining about compilations is not fresh territory.

But when I first listened to Canon - already owning all songs on the first disc - I was nonetheless shocked.  It just didn't go together, it was wildly uneven, and songs that should've made it were omitted in favor of songs that really only made sense as a part of their respective albums.  Out of Range, one of Ani's best and certainly her most accessible album, is only represented by two songs.  Many albums have none.  Not a Pretty Girl has four, and, though I can't begrudge it that, I CAN take issue with the four picked.  ("Coming Up" over "This Bouquet"?  Really?)  In all, it's a hodgepodge that doesn't represent its artist well.  At all.  And the rerecorded songs are just plain awful.

If you insist on getting a physical, store-bought representation of (almost) her entire career, this is, unfortunately, your only choice.  However, if you just want to get some good Ani DiFranco, skip this and get Out of Range.  If you like that, get Not a Pretty Girl.  Then Like I Said.  Then maybe Dilate or Little Plastic Castle or something like that.  MAYBE Living in Clip or another live album, although, like most live albums, what's gained is less than what's lost.  (It doesn't help that's it's a double-album; a little Ani goes a long way.)  Or just get the album with the song you like, or even just the song, or have a friend make a mix; it's almost certain to have a better selection of songs than this.

Input: Listening to these songs makes me physically uncomfortable.  It's not Rage and it's not Soundgarden.  The vocals and the instrumentals just don't mesh very well.  Throughout the entire album I felt like Chris Cornell and Tom Morello were each doing their own thing, without 'speaking' to each other.  Cornell's prolonged yells just don't suit the music very well at all.  It's obvious that Tom Morello is still brilliant, but some of the riffs sound recycled, and the rhythm section plays an uncharacteristically low-key role.  The tempo of the CD is unRagely slow -- mostly because Cornell's vocals are somewhat sluggish.  He certainly doesn't have Zack's agility.
On a different note, I looked at the Audioslave (the name's a little weak isn't it?) website.  Though the band attempts to keep one foot in politics, the content and selections just don't have the personalized, hand-picked feel that Zack's material had.
In a nutshell, it feels like both parties deviated from their extremes in an attempt to accomodate each other, and the result is a watery Frankenstein monster.

Input: Hope of the States' The Lost Riots comes with no small amount of instant mythmaking.  Signature guitarist James Lawrence killed himself before the completion of this debut.  Instead of packing it in, the remaining members have soldiered on, releasing their debut to much acclaim in Europe.  A pre-release gig in L.A. confirmed their ramshackle potential - they put on a sloppy, passionate show.  But The Lost Riots, as a recorded experience, is lackluster.  It's epic songwriting - not so modern as Radiohead; more like progressive icons Genesis or Yes or Jethro Tull - that falls flat as lead singer Sam Herlihy's voice.  (Which I don't understand - live he was excellent.  Here, he can't hit a note to save his life.)  What interest the CD holds is in the musicality of violinist Mike Siddell and a generally simplistic, sincere approach to the epic form.  And I would gladly listen to tracks like "Enemies/Friends" and "Nehemiah" - the best ones here - if Herlihy wasn't singing.  It's one thing in rock to have a bad voice - that's legion - but something else to have one that's uninteresting.

Input: I distinctly remember the day that I brought this disc home & listened to it for the first time.  As track after track played I thought "what the (bleep) has happened to one of my favorite singers?"  I tossed the disc on my 'never to be listened to again' pile and promptly forgot that I even had it in my collection.

Fast forward 8 years and I had a mini Chante Moore-athon and decided to give it a 2nd try.  I really had to suspend my memories of Chante's previous albums so that I could listen to this without any prejudice & comparisons to those brilliant first 2 albums.  Overally I truly understand the bind that music artists faced around this time, particularly African-American females in the r&b field.  It was the dawn of the 'hip pop' era and EVERY artist was being forced to work with rappers and add elements of hip hop to what was traditional r&b/soul music.  This collection was too drastic of a change for me as a Chante fan and to this day, I still can't recommend it to anyone.

Input: I think what made Blake Lewis so interesting in American Idol was the fact that each week we could not wait to see which hit song he would take and put a cool spin on it. He would take classic hits as well as more present hits and switch them up and make them different and fun. That being said - his set of original songs are quite boring and bland. The majority of them sound the same therefore they all kind of blend together. He sounds like a cheap knock off of his favorite band: Maroon 5. I bought this CD knowing that he does not have the best vocals but knowing that he had an ear for production and originality. I am quite disappointed here as nothing really jumps out and grabs my attention on this set.
There are a few songs that are fun and catchy. "She's Makin Me Lose It" is by far my favorite song on here. It has an old school Prince like sound to it from the beat to Blake's screeching vocals. A good song. Another ok song on here is "Gots To Get Her" which takes the melody from the classic "Puttin On The Ritz". That's about the only 2 standout songs for me. The rest are just weak considering seeing him do his thing on AI.
If you are a Blake fan I would seriously consider  purchasing his EP of songs that he did on American Idol and maybe sampling this before purchasing it.

~~~~~ JAC  07'

Input: Starsailor brings up an image of something peaceful yet exciting, an interesting band that is one of those that is really good but never gets any airplay.  The name alone is almost enough to sell this group's debut album, Love Is Here.  As it turns out, the name is deceptive as to just what is contained on this disc.  To explain: imagine Coldplay (those guys that brought us "Yellow"), give them a bad, perpetually whiny singer singer, muddy up the sound so it sounds like they're playing live from your sister's room, call it Britpop, and you've got Starsailor.
The saddest part is that the musicians - James Stelfox on bass, Barry Westhead on keyboards, and Ben Byrne on drums - are overflowing with talent.  But the mixing job and the singer, James Walsh, has an almost constant whining gets begins to grate after a few songs.  The combination of excellent musicianship, bad mixing and sub-par vocals soon inspires only frustration.  Two songs, "Fever" and "Good Souls," are exempt from this lethal combination and are truly excellent, and it's a shame that these two are lost in a sea of mud and whine.
It's difficult not to want to like these guys, ...

Input: OK - I understand the concept.  Rock songs like all others have a basic music construction that lends itself to other arrangements, other styles - blues, swing, pop.  But there just seems to be something here that isn't quite right. Like a dream that may be pleasant but is also skewed so that a new reality is the only way that the dream can work.

Paul Anka swinging to Van Halen's Jump?  Paul Anka turning Cobain into - what? - Sinatra?  Certainly this is nothing new - an aging pop star decides to record standards to keep his fan base happy and connected (like Rod Stewart).  Nothing wrong with that necessarily. And Anka has a nice voice, a good style and certainly can still sing.  But this conversion of several rock standards to another format just doesn't quite measure up.  What does this mean for the future?  An aging David Lee Roth singing Cole Porter?

It's not that the rock standards are so sacred that new arrangements cannot be made.  Maybe if the listener had never heard these songs before it would work.  But the original of several of these haunts Anka's version and almost gives mind to a "Weird Al Yankovic" for the geriatric set (of which I am quickly becoming one) to the point where the version seems almost hilarious.

There are some nice attempts on here.  For example, "Eyes Without a Face" comes across almost as a Sinatra-esque late night at a saloon type song.  But the overall effect just doesn't quite live  up to the concept.

Input: I read the previous listener review and was curious to check out this music as I had honestly never before seen this album.  The review had me interested but cautious because of some of the word choices and phrases used to describe the mood created.  In addition, songs like "Classical Gas" didn't seem like "snuggling" music to me.  I chose to check out an online site that has 30 second clips per song to review the music prior to buying this cd -- I'm glad that I did.
This is not Barry White music.  It has no smoky, sultry sound.  Not the gentle, emotional guitar touch that Chet is capable of.  (If you're looking for that I might recommend "Sails" or either of the Chester and Lester CD's--although none of these are quite "snuggling" music either)  You would have to enjoy "Swanee River", "The Streak" or maybe "Convoy" as lovemaking accompaniment to consider this music as "lower the lights after dinner and snuggle" music.  This could only be romantic music for people who like feather boa laden women calling them "Big Boy" in a nasal tone -- GOT THE PICTURE?  Again, CLASSICAL GAS?  Electronic sounding drums.  Bad, shrilly 80's sounding keyboard tone.  Mood Music?  I don't think so.  It's more reminiscent of grammar school kids marching to an assembly.
I felt compelled to steer away those of you who might, like me, have been searching out that warm, soothing music that we think might exist out there but that we're unaware of.  Needless to say, this is not that album.  If you want that sultry, subtle, warm, non-generic smooth jazz sound I might recommend Earl Klugh "Late Night Guitar"(nylon string guitar with soft string accompaniment, some light percussion) or Ben Webster "Jazz 'Round Midnight"(Tenor sax with soft piano, some very light drums).  I think you will be real happy with these albums for that after dinner mood music, or with a nice candle lit dinner, for that matter.
No feather boas.  No Ray Stevens.

Input: This is a rewrite and reappraisal of my previous review of this album. I've now listened to this album about a dozen times, wanting to have it grow on me and trying to give every opportunity for the music to impress me; It has failed to do so.

I have mixed emotions about this album from Transatlantic. I'll start by saying that the technical ablility of the individual musicians is beyond reproach. None of the musicians have anything to prove and they don't use this platform as a showcase for thier individual glorification; they work together nicely as a band. Indeed, this album has a couple great moments but hardly any instances of pure musical brilliance. Some of the transitional passages are akward, others so hackneyed as to be laughable. There is one sound, (I'd call it noise), in the first track that sounds like a dentists' drill to me. I'm not sure what they were going for there, but I find it irritating to the point of distraction each time I hear it. Overall, the performances are competent enough but the music is not well written.

Another problem I have with this album is with the vocal presentation of the lyrics. The solo singing voice is fine, but the lyrics seem to lack any sense of phrasing or rhythm, as though no thought at all was given to the cadence for the performance. He may as well be reading a technical manual. I found the lyrics themeselves largely uniteresting and, in spots banal. The backing vocals are dodgey, at best; in some instances they are downright bad.

If this album was purely instrumental, I might have given it 3 stars, but as it is I can't go that high. This isn't any better a performance than the first Transatlantic album, and I don't find it as satisfying as the works from the four bands represented here. In the future, I'll spend my money on Dream Theater, Marillion and the rest, leaving Transatlantic on the shelf.

Input: After the monster success of their first three albums, Pearl Jam did the time honored tradition of recording a self indulgent, non-commercial album that's more for themselves than their audience.  The band is to be applauded for branching out and stretching themselves, but as with most bands, they would have been better off sticking to what they do best.  The band is influenced by Neil Young, especially his work with Crazy Horse.  The band tries to ape the sound of Mr. Young's work from Rust Never Sleeps on "Red Mosquito" and "Smile" but they come across as bad imitations.  They go curiously into a world beat sound on the "Who You Are" (flip flopping the title of another major influence, The Who's "Who Are You") and "In My Tree".  The latter song is particular bad.  Stone Gossard steps in front of the microphone to sing "Mankind" and he shows why he is the band's lead guitarist.  The album is not without its merits. "Hail Hail" ranks as one the band's all-time best songs with its driving guitars and powerful Eddie Vedder vocals and "Lukin" is another strong rocker.  Many people love this album for its eclectic nature and the fact that it doesn't sound like anything else the band has ever done.  That's the problem No Code suffers from, it doesn't sound like a Pearl Jam record.

Input: After the long string of the single greatest albums of Pink Floyd's career, it had to come to a head eventually. From Dark Side Of The Moon to The Wall, they seemingly could do no wrong. Then came The Final Cut. A HUGE disappointment. For one thing, David Gilmour and Nick Mason had almost no influence on the album. Second, Rick Wright isn't there. Third, Roger Waters has this idea that people want to hear him ramble on about politics with few actual musical sections. He'd take this idea into his solo career. Meanwhile, for the last Floyd album featuring him, we got The Final Cut.

This is a pretty bad album overall. I love the message behind it but I listen to music for... well... music. However, there are four songs that make this album worthwhile. "Your Possible Pasts", "The Gunner's Dream", "The Fletcher Memorial Home", and "Not Now John".

"Your Possible Pasts" - A Wall outtake which is probably why it's so much better than most songs on this album. The main attraction here is that Gilmour lays down a hell of a guitar solo.

"The Gunner's Dream" - One of the most beautiful songs I've ever heard in my life. God, this song is just so great. One of the best songs ever in the Pink Floyd discography. The piano, the sax, the vocals. Perfect.

"The Fletcher Memorial Home" - The vocals on this one are slightly annoying but the guitar solo makes up for it.

"Not Now John" - The second best track on the album. The only one with any real David Gilmour influence as well. David sings on this one and also plays a solo which turns out great. This sounds like a Wall song frankly. It's great.

Everything else you can pretty much skip. "The Gunner's Dream" is easily worth the price alone.

But what tends to ring out are the lyrics that convey and reveal much about betrayal and misunderstandings and the eventual chanting and giving all the secrets away.

Input: Eddie and Alex VH are on fire! Many of the casual fans of VH never understood what VH is all about and the magic of VH live. Hint: It's never been DLR's vocals. So, if you're buying this live album to hear great vocals, please go buy Journey, Captured. But, if you're looking for a TRUE LIVE ALBUM THAT ROCKS...this is the one!! Bands today wouldn't have the courage to put a live album like this out without massive production, touch ups and showing all the warts. VH is good enough live to do just that and I think it's incredible!! Oh, and for those complaining about Michael Anthony no longer being in the band, just STOP IT!! First, if it was your kid, you would do the exact same thing! Second, Michael Anthony was an OK bass player with OK backing vocals, which in the big picture, doesn't matter anymore. VAN HALEN is and always WILL be the power duo of Eddie and Alex VH, not freakin' Michael Anthony. For anyone to say that VH is not VH without Michael Anthony is just plain ridiculous, ludicrous and asinine!

Input: This particular version of band is my favorite, when both Pigpen and Keith Godchaux played keyboards, organ and piano respectively. When Jerry played a strat and Bill was the only drummer. At the time of the Europe '72 tour the Grateful Dead hadn't quite reached the levels of jazzy exploration found in late '73 through '74. Instead they played the songs with a bounce and a swagger they never surpassed in later years and jammed with a new found grace that added quite a bit of subtlety to their more psychedelic interludes.

The Grateful Dead came ready to play on this the second date of the Europe '72 tour and second date at Wembley Empire Pool. Every song is very well played, with Cumberland Blues ending up on the original Europe '72 live album. It's clear that Bob Weir, Phil Lesh and all are on for this show. But what sets 04/08 at the Wembley Empire Pool apart from most of the other shows of this very fine tour is the monstrous Dark Star>Sugar Magnolia>Caution suite. For me the gold standard Dark Stars are the "original" one found on Live Dead and the surreal and exploratory one played at the Fillmore on 02/13/70. This one at Wembley is just as good if not better. The Dead go places they'd never before explored in part because of the efforts of then new piano player Keith Godchaux and the sense of jazzy exploration he brought. The Dead's amazing group mind improvisational skills are very much in evidence. After the excursion into the cosmos that is Dark Star, the band segues brilliantly into Sugar Magnolia which provides a welcome bit of sunshine. Following Sugar Magnolia is the most fiercely jammed out Caution of the tour and perhaps of all time. Jerry is on fire spitting out tart notes like a musical machine gun and the rest of the band are right there with him.

Pick this album up you won't be sorry. It's a keeper. The playing is exceptional, the mix is good, everybody's audible and the recording quality is excellent. That group mind thing I talked about is evident on every song, oh and there's Jerry's sublime pedal steel on Looks Like Rain. For me this concert is one of the best of the Europe '72 tour, top five at least.

Other exceptional shows from the Europe '72 tour: 04/11 at Newcastle, 04/14 at Tivoli Concert Hall, 05/03 at Olympia Theatre (my vote for best show of the tour), and the run at the Lyceum Theatre in England. 05/26 being the debatable best. The show on 05/11 at Rotterdam has another amazing Dark Star>Sugar Mag>Caution suite. Bickershaw on 05/07 is also great with Pigpen wailing on organ throughout and is the only show of the tour that has both the Other One and Dark Star. Speaking of Other Ones, the 05/10 show at the Amsterdam Concertgebouw has the best of the tour.

Input: This compilation is most of Powell's recordings for Vanguard, plus one for Capitol. The latter is from 1947, while the others are from 1953 through 1956,

Since this page has sound samples you can get a good idea of both the musical territory this album covers, as well as the sound quality. I have gone through this album a few times and am still hearing new things on each listen.

Like most of the compilations from this label you get a lot of value, but very little documentation. I have tracked down the source albums and personnel for each and am providing them below. One thing that I love is even though the albums are randomly scattered among the track list, they are out of print, so this is one way to get a large part of Powell's body of work as a leader. And since this is an MP3 album, you can easily reorder the tracks and group them according to album.

Here is what you get:

Tracks 1, 2 and 4 are all but one track from the 1947 album titled Classics In Jazz. The front line is comprised of Jake Porter on trumpet and Bumps Myers on tenor sax. Powell leads the rhythm section that is also comprised of Red Callender on bass and Lee Young on drums. The missing track is There's A Small Hotel.

Tracks 3, 5, 8, 10 through 12, 18, 28, 30, 34, 39, 40 and 41 are the album titled Out on a Limb from 1956. There are two ensembles in this album For tracks 3, 28, 30, 34 and 39 the line up is Ruby Braff fronts on trumpet, backed by Powell, Skeeter Best on guitar, Oscar Pettiford on bass and Bobby Donaldson on drums. The remaining tracks for Out on a Limb feature Al Mattaliano on trumpet, Nick Calazza on tenor sax and Peanuts Hucko on clarinet. The rhythm section is Powell on piano, Tommy Kay on guitar, Arnold Fishkin on bass and Bobby Donaldson on drums.

Tracks 6, 16, 19, 22, 23, 27, 32 and 35 are the 1955 album titled Thigamagig. This is an interesting and unique line up comprised of Ruby Braff on trumpet, Powell on piano and Bobby Donaldson on drums.

Tracks 7, 8, 13, 14 and 41 are the album titled Mel Powell Septet from 1953. The front line is Buck Clayton on trumpet, Henderson Chambers on trombone and Edmund Hall on clarinet. The rhythm section is Powell, Steve Jordan on guitar, Walter Page on bass and Jimmy Crawford on drums.

Tracks 9, 26, 29, 31, 33, 37 and 38 are the 1954 album titled Borderline with another unique trio format featuring Paul Quinichette on tenor sax, Powell on piano and Bobby Donaldson on drums.

Tracks 15, 17, 20, 21, 24, 25 and 36 are the 1956 album titled The Mel Powell Bandstand. The front line is Johnny Glasel on trumpet, Jimmy Buffington on French horn and Chuck Russo on alto and baritone sax, clarinet and bass clarinet. Powell leads the rhythm section comprised of Mundell Lowe on guitar, Joe Kay on bass and Eddie Phyfe on drums. The vocalist is Joan Wile.

Input: This is indie chart staple that some would and do say has been done to death, but it is ruddy great. Opening track `Wreckin bar rar, ra , ra', is a 90 second homage to The Ramones and what a great way to kick off such a joyous album.

All of the tracks could be singles, and sometimes that can be annoying, but they are all so good that it just makes this one album that you don't feel you need to fast forward any tracks at all. The obvious pithy wit, irony and verve that is `Post break up sex' is probably the most stand out track, but only just, a real crowd pleaser and floor filler. Track 5 `Wetsuit'; is slower but still has enough momentum to hook you and take you along for the ride. Personal favourite is `A lack of understanding', as it seems to be about me and I like it when you can instantly empathise with a song. The vocals are great too and are all delivered so clear that a lyric sheet is not needed. I have had this a couple of weeks now and during that time three of my fave bands have brought out new albums; this however has been a constant on my MP3 despite all the other music I have been getting. It just feels like summer, sex, angst and fun all rolled up in a great package that you can dance to (but in my case - not very well).

There is a twelfth track `Somebody else's child that is tucked at the end of track 11 and not available on download, this is the slowest and most reflective number and makes the album approach as opposed to download, probably the better option.

Also not my typical genre, but for indie rock fans who like their music accessible, upbeat, with great lyrics tight playing and some heartfelt humour, then this is indie heaven.
