Input: This is a new purchase so I can only comment on my initial impressions and offer a tip on usage. I will update after I've used it for a while.

The overall build quality, fit and finish seem good. The instructions are only so-so.

The first issue I ran into was adding air as instructed. Both YouTube videos and the printed instructions say to inflate to 150 psi. This is relatively straight-forward using a shock pump (required). What nobody explains is how to remove the pump without losing all of the air you just added. There is an unboxing review on YouTube by Seth's Bike Hacks where he says to put more than 150 psi (the seatpost is rated for up to 250) and "take it off really quick".  Here's how I finally got that to work. First I only screw the pump hose on as far as needed to seal in preparation for minimal turning to remove. Pump it up and then unscrew it slowly until it starts to hiss. Tighten it a quarter turn at a time until the hissing stops.

Now inflate to just shy of 250 psi. If the inner post retracts, squeeze the release mechanism and pull it all the way out and continue inflating. The "trick" to removing quickly is to place the hose nut into something stable so you don't have to hold the pump. I put it loosely into a Panavise. I made it just tight enough that it wouldn't fall out, but didn't crank down on it so as not to deform anything. Place your right forearm on top of the left with fingers pointing at the opposite elbows. One palm should face up and the other should face down hands overlapping with the heels of your hands aligned. This is similar to the "I dream of Jeanie" pose for those who remember that. Put the body of the seatpost between the heels of your hands with the clamp end pointed away from you. As quickly as you can, pull your hands away from your elbows while maintaining pressure against the post. This should rapidly rotate the large diameter part of the seatpost thus unscrewing it from the pump hose. This worked like a charm, but air will still escape until you screw the cap provided over the Schrader valve.

Input: I bought this in person somewhere a few years back.

I do not recommend that you waste your time and money on this. Even if you are going for a budget knife and you don't have the kind of money to buy a higher priced one, you are seriously better off saving up for a long time and getting something at the very least around $30 and up.

Would this knife be useful in a self defense scenario? ABSOLUTELY! That serrated portion could do a ton of damage and is very sharp. Plus there is an intimidation factor as visually, it looks pretty dangerous.

Is it practical for use as an actual knife? ABSOLUTELY NOT! Do not buy this thinking it will be a good survival knife. The handle is total crap, its cheap hollow plastic and mine over the years has developed a sticky residue (though that could have been from something spilled on it or due to heat, I decided to wrap mine). The serrations, while sharp and intimidating are very poor for cutting through cordage or for use as a saw, even for smaller branches. Could it cut through some branches and rope, sure. But it would definitely not hold up to that much abuse for very long.

In short, I would choose this knife as a last resort. It would NOT be in my bug out bag or sit alongside my other knives or tools. I could find much better survival tools to occupy the space this would take in my bag.

It would probably be pretty decent for the impending zombie apocalypse though.

Input: The main defect of this seat is what is being sold as a feature, but to me is definitely a bug.  That is, the swiveling of the seat.  Every time you pedal, pushing with your leg, the seat swivels backwards in the opposite direction leaving you nothing to push back upon.  This steals the pushing force from your pedal stroke and also makes riding with the seat unstable because the seat keeps moving away from behind you every time you make a stroke pedaling .

To clarify, you naturally push from your rear when you pedal, pushing down and forward with your leg.  However, the seat swivels and "disappears" behind your rear, giving you nothing to push back on.  A normal stationary seat gives you something to push back against, giving you force in the other direction against the pedals.

Imagine your have your hands up vertically in a Patty cake position, placed against the the hands of another person facing you similarly.  You press against the persons hands while the other person holds their hands stationary.  This force would provide you propulsion and movement in the opposite direction.  That's what happens when you pedal with your legs.  Now imagine that when you push against the other person's hands that instead of holding them stationary, they just let them go back loosely.  You get no opposing force because you have nothing to push against, and you have the feeling of falling, uncontrolled movement.  That's what happens with this seat.  It neutralizes your movement, causing you to lose pedaling force, destabilizing you with its swivel.

In order to compensate for the movement of the seat I have to adopt an awkward, unnatural style of pedaling to make up for the saddle moving all the time.

What's frustrating is that otherwise the seat is nicely engineered and machined.  It's comfortably padded to sit still on.  If the seat was simply stationary instead of wobby, it would be a perfect seat.

I don't get what the designer was trying to accomplish with the wobbling.  The problem with saddles with noses is the nose.  It's not that they are stationary.  A solid stationary platform is necessary for efficient and stable cycling.  The product description claims that the swiveling makes the seat "comfortable and safe for delicate nerves and arteries".  I don't see this.  If anything it makes it less comfortable and dangerous for the rest of you because of the instability.

This saddle fixes one problem but needlessly adds another.  It's as if the designer felt they had to add some feature to the seat so that it could qualify as unique in order to obtain a patent.  Sorry, as they say in software, it's not a feature, it's a bug.

Input: I am notoriously anti-Brita, since all of their products always seem to break or not work well rather easily.  This bottle is no exception--it was so awful I had to toss it.  The screw-on top of the first bottle I got shattered into pieces after a fall from about a foot--classic Brita craftsmanship.  Amazon quickly replaced the week-old bottle and the newer one went on to suck for almost a year until I chucked it out of disgust.

Pros:

Filters water.

Cons:

Everything else.

1) Not remotely leak/spill-proof.  The screw-on top barely has a seal, so if this happens to tilt or fall over in your work bag, water is going everywhere (not ideal especially if you happen to have a laptop in the same bag).  It also leaks when full and at a small angle--for instance, when you're simply walking and holding it with a finger by the loop.  It leaks constantly while in motion, so you're the dummy leaving a trail of water everywhere.

2) It makes very strange noises when you first try to suck water through the flip-up straw.  Perfect for when you're thirsty in the middle of a meeting and you want everyone to look at you like you just passed gas.

3) As such, not ideal for an office environment.  My main reason for buying this was to have a device that could contain and filter water for consumption throughout my office work day.  Not only does it make untimely straw noises, but you feel like you're using an adult sippy cup.

4) As for outdoors, I cannot imagine this cheap piece of plastic managing any rugged activity (let alone holding any water in).  Again, my first bottle broke after a very short fall onto a carpeted floor.

I recently switched to a Camelbak Chute and couldn't be happier (I fill it with filtered water).  As far as Brita products, I am done forever.  I had so many bad experiences with their pitchers that I switched to Mavea (their pitchers rock, for what it's worth).  This water bottle was no different--cheap parts and ill-conceived design.  That it filters water on the fly does not outweigh the awful experience of having to actually use it.

Input: He started baseball's famous streak That's got us all aglow He's just a man and not a freak, Joltin' Joe DiMaggio. Joe, Joe DiMaggio We want you on our side The song "Joltin'" Joe DiMaggio was penned in 1941 by Ben Homer and Alan Courtney for the Les Brown Orchestra, where it was sung by Betty Bonney. Of course the reference is to the 56-game hitting streak that began on May 15 when DiMaggio went 1-for-4 with a run batted in against the Chicago White Sox. It would end 56 gmes later on July 16, the day before third basemen Ken Keltner of the Cleveland Indians made two terrific backhanded stops to rob DiMaggio of hits. During the streak DiMaggio had 91 hits in 223 at bats to hit .409, to go along with 56 runs, 16 doubles, 4 triples, 15 home runs, and 55 runs batted in. DiMaggio's 56-game hitting streak is one of the greatest individual achievements in baseball history. It might not be as impossible as record to break as Cy Young's marks for career wins (511), career losses (316), and complete games (749), and no one is going to come close to Jack Chesbro's 41 wins. But in terms of single season achievements in the realm of hitting the only other marks that seem equally unassailable are Earl Webb's 67 doubles, Babe Ruth's 177 runs scored (or Billy Hamilton's 192 runs if you want to go pre-1900), and Hack Wilson's 191 RBIs. But none of those have the cache of DiMaggio's hitting streak. What is nice about this Cooperstown Series 4 action figure of Joe DiMaggion in the pinstripped uniform of the New York Yankees is that it is clearly based on one of the best known photographs of the Yankee Clipper, sold on Amazon as The Swing, Washington, D.C., 1941, Joe DiMaggio Photographic Poster Print, 11x14. Was the photo taken during the streak? When the Yankees went to Washington in late May (27-29) those were only games 12-14 in DiMaggio's streak. He went 4-5, 1-4 and 1-3 during the series, with the Yankees winning the first two games and tying the third. So if the photograph was indeed taken during that period it was not because photographers were focuing on the streak. I rounded up on this figure because they did a great job of capturing DiMaggio's distinctive hitting approach, even if they did add a lot of dirt on his pants legs and were rather inconsistent on drawing the pinstrips. But I also like the details that you can just tell DiMaggio is wearing a blue t-shirt underneath his uniform, and that the pine tar goes a third of the way up the bat where the signature is for "Joseph DiMaggio." The sculpt of the face is pretty good, but more from the profiles than from the front. There is no articulation for the figure and you have to add the right foot to the figure to complete it. The most significant change is the knob of the bat comes already attached to the figure's left hand. In the beginning we had to cut open the hands of a batter (e.g., Jason Giambi) to put the bat in position, and then they did it so the knob came off and you could slide the bat into position (e.g., Hideki Matsui), and hope the knob did not fly off and disappear. So this is a great improvement (although I did spend a couple of minutes looking for the knob on my desk or on the ground when I opened the package and found it was not on the end of the bat. The Yankee Clipper played in 139 games in 1941, getting 193 hits in 541 time at bat for a .357 batting average (of course, that was the same year that Ted Williams batted .406). DiMaggio scored 122 runs and drove in 125 while hitting 43 doubles, 11 triples, and 30 home runs while only striking out 13 times, and winning the second of his three American League Most Valuable Player awards. It is quite appropriate that joining DiMaggio in the Cooperstown Series 4 are Ted Williams  completing his swing at Fenway Park for the Red Sox (with road variation), along with Roger Maris of the New York Yankees (clearly based on the photograph of him hitting his home run #61 in 1961, which makes the Cardinal variant somehwat odd), Johnny Bench of the Cincinnati Reds diving over the short fence in front of the dugout at Riverfront Stadium to catch a ball, Steve Carlton about to deliver the ball on the road for the Philadelphia Philies (or at home), and an upside down Ozzie Smith doing his pattented opening day back flip in St. Louis for the Cardinals. With DiMaggio (#5, first worn by Bob Meusel) and Maris (#9) getting McFarlane figures this season, along with Derek Jeter (#2), Babe Ruth (#3), Mickey Mantle (#7, first worn by Leo Durocher), and Yogi Berra (#8), we have two thirds of the Yankee single digit uniform numbers, all of which have been retired except for Jeter (for now). Sooner or later there has to be one of Lou Gehrig (#4), and then the question is whether they will ever do a figure of Billy Martin (#1, first worn by Earle Combs) and Bill Dickey (also #8, although he started wearing #10). Phil Rizzuto wore #10 in case you were wondering (#6 was first worn by Tony Lazzeri, and there are also McFarlane figures of Don Mattingly(#23), and Reggie Jackson (#44) when it comes to retired Yankee numbers, which can include #42, retired now for Jackie Robinson but also in the future for Mariano Rivera. I assume the day will come for Thurman Munson (#15), Whitey Ford (#16), Elston Howard (#32), Casey Stengel (#37), and Ron Guidry (#40), because it seems like McFarlane comes out with a couple of Yankees, past and present, every single year. As soon as I get my updated Bobby Abreu, the new Robinson Cano and the second Johnny Damon figures later this summer, I will have all nine of this year's Yankee starters in Yankees uniforms (Yes, I know, I have to put Giambi at first base instead of DH to do this because there is not a Doug Mientkiewicz action figure, at least, not yet...). Input: I'm an ultra-distance runner and I like to track my runs with an app on my phone. I also use the phone for listening to audiobooks or music while on 10-30 hour runs.  On supported races, I prefer not to wear a backpack, but I still need some place to put my phone.  In the past, I've tucked the phone into my compression shorts, but it tends to fall out slowly, need constant adjusting, etc.  I hate armband phone holders that always end up sitting in my elbow and bouncing around.

So I decided to try the Running Buddy.  IT'S PERFECT.  It snaps into place easily and doesn't bounce at all.  It just sits there, holding my phone, doing exactly what I need.  GPS works great, my tracking app works great, and my phone is right there (I did text my crew a couple times to let them know I was coming in - so it was nice to be able to grab the phone out, use it, and tuck it back in - takes a few seconds only).  I used the Running Buddy during a 50-mile race during a massive rain storm (8" of rain during the race) with near freezing (sub-40 degree temps the whole time, with lots of mud and river crossings.  Phone was perfectly well protected in the water resistant pouch, and I never had to think about it.

The caveat, however, is that you do need to tie the string in your shorts.  If you don't tie it well, you will feel your shorts slipping because of the weight - I use a Samsung S5, in an otterbox case (so... quite heavy already!), and the RunningBuddy itself isn't super light, so the combination does require tying that string nicely.  Normally I don't tie the string at all, so that is something to note.  You don't need to make the shorts tight, you just need them tight enough not to fall down, but I did use a "shoe lace double knot the bows" (whatever you call that) knot to keep the knot from coming undone.

Since there's two pockets on the inside and I knew I'd want to take the phone out from time to time, I put my ID and some cash in the smaller pocket, and the phone in the outer.  I love it and it's going to be on all my runs from now on!

Input: Precor recently dropped their prices on their entry-level ellipticals, so I took the plunge and purchased one (my first elliptical). Of course, their entry-level ellipticals are still more expensive than the top of the line models from most other manufacturers, so it was with some trepidation that I ordered it from Amazon (how do you repack and ship out a 200 pound elliptical if you decide to return it?) Anyway, I'm pleased to say that the Precor was everything I hoped for.

Assembly was straightforward, but you definitely want some help to get it out of the 7 foot box and to put it together (having a dolly was a lifesaver since I had to turn the damn thing around when I found out it was facing the wrong direction). There are no wheels, so you are basically lifting and moving extremely heavy pieces. Precor includes all the tools you'll need, and all the parts fit very nicely together (which is a major major plus if you've ever dealt with the maddening experience of building Ikea furniture).

The elliptical itself is sturdy and exudes quality. The motion is extremely smooth - with my eyes closed it would be hard to tell the difference from the club-quality Precors. Where you really come to realize how this is Precor's budget line is in the feature set. You have to program all your info (weight, etc) each time you start. There are only a few programs built-in (if you crave a lot of variety, you'll need to pony up the extra bucks for the 5.25 or higher). The incline adjustment is manual and can't be adjusted on the fly. And as one previous reviewer noted, the power switch is in the most inconvenient location near the bottom of the machine, at the rear.

However, if you know all these issues up front and just want a high-quality machine to get a great workout, this is definitely the model for you. Note: you can save about $400 and get the 5.21 if you don't need the moving arms.

Input: Usually I roll my eyes at made in China -esque knives on amazon as I look for name brand like Benchmade and CRKT and get disappointed in their steep prices. Nothing against these companies, theyve built a reputation for reliable and great knives, its only fair they charge more for it. But while I have my higher end knives for field use, I needed something smaller and more discrete/reasonable to have at work that wouldnt break the bank. To me it seems pointless to drop near $100 on a smaller knife that just won't see the level of abuse the manufacturer guarantees it can handle. So this time I didn't ignore the amazon blue light specials and I have to say Im pretty happy for it.

In the last year or so the made in china knife industry has really overhauled their quality output, and this Kubey is no exception. Other than the ponderous name (unisex) its a very serious little knife. What I love is for a $20ish option it only says Kubey and D2, no made in China. It doesnt have assisted opening but depressing the flipper will immediately spring the blade out and locked. Lockup feels amazing, despite being a liner lock. Aesthetics are actually pretty decent, simple slim profile with sufficient texture for grip. The blade is decently thick and out of the box was sharp enough to shave arm hair. For my purposes, it outperforms at work.

This is a knife that if stamped CRKT or SOG or Benchmade, people would want to know the model name to buy one. As it is, Ive just found a new source for great edged presents for friends/family, and will not overlook the cheap amazon listings again. If there was a way to incorporate the auto axis design that other next gen made in china knives have copied (Ganzos) I would happily pay x2 the price for this one.

Smells great.  Even the wifey doesn't object.

Input: I can't believe I used bleach and iodine pills for so long! I waited a while for the best price on the Sawyer Mini, but the truth is the price doesn't fluctuate that much and it's well worth the price.

I ended up with a pink filter due to lowest price, which I'm not wild about, but it -does- make it easier to find in my pack and when I'm backpacking with a group of friends I never end up in the argument about whose blue filter is whose.

The filter works so smoothly I don't think the back flushing syringe is a necessary bring along unless you're going to be out for a long time in a place with particularly scummy water. In most instances using a smart water bottle with the tapered drinking nozzle works in place of the syringe and saves you a little bit of weight. That being said, it's nice to have something to thoroughly clean the system when you get home.

Also make sure you get -all- of the water out of it before it gets anywhere approaching freezing. If you're going backpacking in the winter/cold temps it's not a bad idea to tuck your sawyer filter in your sleeping bag with you, as the filter freezing is the easiest way to bust one.

I particularly recommend setting this filter up as an inline system, especially for anyone annoyed with slow flow rates.

Input: I bought this system about a year and a half ago. I was excited at the prospect of not having to scoop because I had always had a regular box.
Initially, the system worked ok. The rake frequently got stuck and many times, there ended up being a bunch of litter underneath the box that captures the waste.
I was also not happy about the smell level and did not find that this system did a very good job at smell control. I was changing the bag up to 3-4 times a week.
One other problem was the amount of litter that got stuck behind the rake.
I tried taking it apart multiple times and cleaning it out but continued to have problems.
It was difficult for me to justify throwing out an expensive piece of equipment so I kept hoping it would get better.
Then about a month ago, the motor burnt out. The motor kept running but the rake would not go. Again, I cleaned it out and replaced everything but that did nothing.
Finally, I ended up throwing it away as it was not functional anymore.
I briefly went back to a regular box but now I am the proud owner of the Scoopfree automatic litter system.
My fingers are crossed and I am still cautiously optimistic but this system is already 1000% better than the Purrforma.
No odor, easy to put together, better functioning (rake goes both ways), and just overall a better product.
I suggest to anyone having an issue with their Purrforma to check into this other system.

And if there are already problems not a month into use, I can't wait to find out how much worse it's going to get while I still have warranty, let alone when warranty actually runs out.

Now aside from the above, this treadmill is actually pretty sturdy...moving up the stairs was no easy feat since the "easy fold" mechanism causes the bottom bars to automatically fold down when you lift the treadmill...and it's quite a heavy treadmill. Input: I purchased two of these as I walk and hike outside often. The temperatures in Klein/Spring Texas, where I live, have been hotter than I've ever felt them, with day upon day of 100 degrees F air temperatures. I had first used some kind of "cooling cloth" which just used evaporative cooling via water, but that didn't help at all. I then researched the reviews for cold-pack cooling neck wraps and I decided on these. In 100 to 105 degrees F temperatures, the item helps a little, but not enough. I guess it would work if one considered the 80s to 95 degrees F temperature range to be "hot," but, if it's hotter, then this item doesn't really have enough of a cooling effect. Also, at least in the temperatures in which I walk and hike, the cold pack strip starts to thaw and it turns into a collection of liquid in about under an hour. In addition, I have to tighten the neck wrap so much, so that the wrap is flush with my skin, that it feels like I'm choking -- if the wrap is not tight then it doesn't work very well.

So, minus one star for melting/thawing in under an hour and minus one star for not having a great enough cooling effect and minus half a star for having to tighten the item so much.

I'd still recommend this item, but if you're in 100+ degrees F temperatures, then I suggest you invest in an actively cooled cooling vest, or, maybe a space suit :P

UPDATE : The cold-packs that slip into the neck wrap are now leaking in two places. I'm going to have to look for a better quality product. With all the problems, I do not recommend that anyone buy this item.

Input: This product promised a great deal of fun during the snowy months. However, it was not meant to be.
I purchased it in October but did not get a chance to put it together for at least another month. Once I set it up, I had a hard time getting the break component working. I contacted Tacx but no response except an automated email saying not to send too many emails or they will tag my emails as junk mail! I waited for my son, who is more tech savvy than me, to try and set it up during the christmas holidays. But he could not get it working either. Still no response from Tacx.
I finally contacted Amazon and the company I bought the item from. Bike-a-mile. They were wonderful and have great costumer service. They responded quickly and tried to help me set it up. They suggested that there maybe a wire loose and with pictures showed me how to connect it. Once I did and plugged it in, I heard and saw a puff of smoke. Bike-a-mile people quickly sent me another break motor module and I replaced it. It worked for a short period but kept heating up and shutting down at speeds over 30mph. After the 5th ride the familiar puff of smoke appeared and the thing died again. I am still waiting to hear back. I assume I got a lemon because there are those who have had it and has worked fine for them.
I give the item two stars because of the potential of how good it could be and believe me, I thoroughly enjoyed the few rides I had on it. The other reason was because of great service from people at bike-a-mile.
Do not expect any useful response from Tacx company. When they eventually responded to my email, they referred me to FAQ to resolve the issues I may have!

Input: For the price, this is a decent bike.
I bought it (in white) for my 9yr old daughter. It is her first "big kid's" bike.
The white with pink accented decals fits the "girl" style fine.. though I don't know why the listing says "boys".
The drop-style top tube allows for easy on and off.

I'd give it 5 starts except..
The brakes and shifters needed to be reinstalled to work properly. Shifters were upside down on wrong ends of the bar. That force brake levers way too far down to work with smaller hands.

Be prepared to take this bike to a shop and have a once over before you put your kid on it and find out the hard way that some things may not be in tune.. And that may not be cheap.

Also.. this is a 24" wheel bike.. By definition it is designed for smaller bodies. Why Mongoose puts a full reach handle bar stem on this.. and a full size grownup's-butt seat on it.. is beyond me. This forces a smaller person to have to reach WAY out to get hands in position and its an uncomfortable (and unsafe) position to ride in.. more akin to a track bike or a triathletes lower "aero" position.

A full size adult might fit the seat to handlebar distance.. but a full size adult would go to a 26" wheel (or larger) frame.

Mongoose is not the only company that makes this mistake.. Have seen it on many mid to low end bikes.
Simply not thought thru well enough. And yet the answers so simple.

So I swapped the handle bar stem for a much shorter reach one I had in my spare parts box and I reversed the seat clamp mount.
That shortened the overall reach by about 6"(1) and now my 9yr old rides comfortably and safely.

Summary. Great kids bike in terms of build and components in terms of price.. but will need considerable work to work safely and properly, and that balances out any price savings.

Input: I've been using this rack for about a month, and so far have pretty mixed feelings. I like the narrow design of the rack, as I just want something to clip on to and don't need a lot of surface area in the back. Riding a bike without mounting points on top, I needed something that would hook behind the brake like this as well.

I do have mounting points above my rear axle, but the rack instructions online recommended just mounting through the rear axle of the wheel so I initially did that. However, this puts the rack dangerously close to the tire. The nuts securing the flat metal piece on top were maybe a centimeter or less from the tire. Wheel sizes are standard, so I'm a little confused as to why they would design this rack to sit so close to the tire, as other reviews here have mentioned. Granted, it shouldn't budge while moving, but it's still pretty scary. Over the course of using the rack with a ~15 lb bag every day, the rack sort of 'settled down' another few mm (because remember, the bottom mounting points are on this extension, meaning they can 'roll back' causing the rack to drop down). Now I had maybe 4mm of clearance from the nut to the tire, which left me super uncomfortable.

I recently remounted the rack to use my rear-fork eyelets instead of the wheel axle, which propped everything up 2-3 inches and now I have ample room. I did have to force the rack to fit into that mounting point, as it is a little narrower than using the axle mount, but it seems secure and I don't think will cause future problems. This also caused me to adjust the flat metal piece that secures to the brake, and this introduced yet another problem. This metal piece slides right underneath the top of the rack (down the middle of the spine, so to speak). Well, I had to slide the piece back a bit more than I had before so it went up to the first metal cross piece (maybe 'ladder rung' makes more sense, if looking down at the rack?). My bag could no longer clip on, because the clip was blocked by the metal piece and I didn't have enough length on the rack to shift over a segment. I then had to push that metal piece back so I had enough room for a clip.

I'm going to continue using the rack, as once you have it set up it works great, but there could be some serious design improvement here. If they want to advertise mounting to the rear axle, this rack should be 2 inches taller than it is. Also, the metal bar on top shouldn't inhibit from clipping in. Either set it lower down, make it narrower, make it shorter, etc. but it vastly reduces the amount of clippable real-estate you have on the rack.

Input: I race sailboats actively on San Francisco Bay, and travel around the country and the world for racing when I can.  I've been through a lot of watches.  Until recently, there were not many sailing specific watches.  The Sunto was too expensive, and the old Ronstan was laughably large, though iconic.  It was great to see so many new introductions this past winter (eg. Ronstan, Freestyle, Gill)  What I've never figured out is why none of the great sailing companies can make a sport specific sailing watch that is even nearly as good as a Timex Ironman.  This new Ronstan is a case in point.

The good.  First, the display is fantastic.  Big numbers centered on the face, with the bonus of still being able to see the time of day at the bottom.  Second, the race timer is top-notch with its ease of use and the great sync feature which allows easy correction of a missed start signal by letting you easily with one button reset a missed 5 minute gun at the 4 minute horn.  That is the most important feature.

The bad.  Nothing is intuitive.  For example, the "Set" button doesn't set the time - it just sets the alarm.  To set the time you hold "Sync", and then press it again to advance the numbers.  Even using the watch every week, I still need don't remember how to switch from race timer mode to clock mode (hold "mode" and then press "sync"). Forget about switching from 5 minute countdown standard race mode to 10 minute match race mode, or adjusting the 3rd user programmable race mode. I have to keep a copy of the watch's instructions in my gear bag.  Compare - I don't even know if an Ironman comes with instructions.  It is perfectly intuitive.

The worst.  The band.  Great on the outside of a spray top for dingy sailing.  Against skin it is definitely not comfortable.  That's forgivable, not all watches can be comfortable for all people.  What is truly awful is that you can't replace the band.  I'm sure someone had a good reason for this design, but all I can say is try it on before you buy it.

I got this Ronstan as a holiday gift, and I'll keep trying it this season, but right now I'm expecting it won't make the cut.  For me, I really like The Band on my Ironman. http://smile.amazon.com/Chums-Band-20mm-Watch/dp/B001AQTKEA/ref=sr_1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1402092850&sr=8-2&keywords=the+band+watch+band

Input: PROS:

- Intense workout

- Stores in a small space (I live in NYC)

- Kinda fun when you get the hang of it

- Easier on my knees than running

- Different and pretty fun

CONS:

- Hard to balance at first (could be dangerous for some)

- Surface not slippery enough out of the box

- User needs reasonable ice skating experience

(hockey skating is best)

- No illustrations in directions to show you best usage

- Slightly overpriced

As the directions suggest as an option, I sprayed some furniture polish on the plastic surface so I could slide better. And then I realized why they don't have a marketing partnership with Pledge... it gets DAMN slippery! They probably have a few lawsuits on hand (I almost fell once). I found without the furniture polish, it wasn't very fun and it really didn't work.

Make sure you WEAR SNEAKERS under your booties. Even if you have small feet that probably means you need the small booties (did I just type the word booties?). Wearing sneakers improves your balance and protects your feet from the contact with the end bumpers.

My girlfriend, who was at one point a serious figure skater, had a lot of trouble with it in the first 5 minutes. I had a much easier time because I use hockey skates and this is very similar in motion.

So, this is a pretty good item but I think you could make the same thing at home with some linoleum and a 2 X 4. the booties are just cheap nylon. Doing it yourself would probably cost under $20 as opposed to well over $100.  It's definitely not a rip-off but in my opinion it should retail under $100.

If you can't ice skate, DO NOT buy this.  If you haver poor balance DO NOT buy this.  Also, I would not recommend this item for older folks who may get hurt if falling down.

Overall, this is a nice departure from the normal exercise routine and I'm getting a great workout in my NYC apartment while having a little fun. If you get it, try holding hand weights while using it.  That makes for an even more intense workout.

There were no reviews when I purchased so I hope this helps you!

Input: I bought this watch 7 weeks ago and have been using it extensively in outdoors 10k runs and in gym activities (spinning & weightlifting).  I wore the HRM strap throughout.

* Setup instructions were quite clear and the initial setup was smooth.

* Coming from the Polar camp (S625X) I had some doubts if the HRM strap would be comfortable. It is.

* The watch looks nice, and it's not too thick.

* The display is good, except one flaw: most athletes are interested in the % of the max HR, not in the bpm. Yet the display shows large bpm digits and small % of the max HR, and there is no function to reverse the order (large %, small bpm).

* PC link: tried it once and it worked OK.

* Charging works well, but be careful with the special USB cord  if it gets damaged, you may not be able to get a new one (see below).

* Water resistance: sweat and very light rain seem to cause no damage.

* GPS function: cold start on a clear, sunny day on the beach, outside temperature 14C (57F)  lock in about 90 seconds. This is OK, somewhat below average (comparing to other GPS watches). GPS accuracy: consistent 1.5% error (1000m are measured by the watch as 985m). Acceptable.

* HRM function: signal is lost quite a bit. I double-checked HRM is On, pairing completed successfully, strap battery is fresh, watch fully charged  and yet the signal sometimes is lost, for minutes (or more) at a time. Unacceptable.

* Calorie counting: starts at rest (60 bpm), unlike Polar which starts at 95 bpm. Polar is preferable  you want to measure the intensity of your training, not your normal breathing  Worse still, kcal/min is roughly linear relative to bpm: at 76-80% of the max HR the watch measures 8 kcal/min; at 81-85%: 9 kcal/min; at 86-90% 10 kcal/min. This is VERY different from Polar, and also from the counters in the Precor gym equipment (treadmill, cross-trainer and stationary bike)  they rise slowly in low HR and quickly at high HR, pushing you toward intensive training.

I asked Pyle about their calorie counting algorithm  they didn't bother to respond.

Other functions (compass, waypoints) - untested.

Bottom line: this is an inexpensive, somewhat inaccurate sports watch, from a non-responsive company. Yet its quite functional for the non-demanding athlete. 3 stars.

Input: I have been reading Entertainment Weekly since issue #1. While I do agree with some reviewers that state that the mag we used to get was better than what they offer now, I still think its the best entertainment magazine out there. I would like to see them return to the irreverent magazine it was when it 1st hit the news stands. But there is still good reason why this magazine is still top of the heap for me. It does not sink to levels of tabloid reporting like many so called 'entertainment' magazines. I used to read TV Guide for their fall previews but have long since given up on reading TV Guide for anything other than what is on tonight. Entertainment Weekly provides me with a detailed analysis of the new shows (or the new music or the new movies) so I can make a more informed decision on what I am going to spend my time on. It has pointed me in the direction of a good TV show or an artist that I have not heard of more times than I can count. Its one of the few magazines I actually read cover to cover--and not just flip through. Entertainment Weekly fills an otherwise entertainment void in decent magazines.

I like the auto renewal...unlike other magazines that hassle and call you a year before your subscription runs out, Entertainment Weekly never bugs you about that stuff at all. Too bad other magazines do not realize that sometimes its better to stop reading their publication than to get woken up too early on a Saturday to be asked 'hows that subscription coming along, are you getting it week?'. With Entertainment Weekly, I found then never reminded me that my subscription was running out so auto renewal is king. Frankly, even that is classy.

Hopefully Entertainment Weekly will keep on producing informative, interesting issues and leave the crap to US Weekly and the Inquirer. I like my entertainment just fine with ET.

Input: Admittedly, I am slightly older than the "Relevant" demographic.  But I'm not 40 yet!  So there are a number of things here that do have some appeal to me.  And I applaud the magazine for attempting to address culturally important issues.

Still, the magazine suffers from it's unrelenting fawning over the whole post-modern vibe and it's own sense of self-importance as a beacon for charismatic hipness. ("Hey, look out, world!  We Jesus Freaks have iPods too!") Usually, the more something or someone sweats to proclaim their own relevance, the more danger there is that they can become irrelevant.

So, like it's spiritual cousin "Charisma," this magazine suffers from a somewhat shallow perspective on life and culture.  It trumpets its ability to ask "the tough questions," even as it follows a relatively safe, politically correct post-mod/charismatic/hipster wannabe party line.

I mean, their idea of being cutting edge was to put Bono on  the cover.  If you want to be cutting edge, put the libertine Adam Clayton on the cover and ask him about Bono's faith.  Now, I would read that article!  (I am a major U2 and Bono fan.  I'm not knocking him; just the lack of imagination at "Relevant".)

There's also way too much emulation of the world's perspective on generational heritage. "Hey, we're young, and we're smart, and we don't need to do anything the way our geezer parents did it."  I guess having a little gray hair or wrinkles doesn't cut it in today's Paris Hilton culture, but I'd like to think that it might be a little different in a culture shaped by biblical values.  Actually, "Relevant" seems to be a little afraid to say what "biblical values" are (beyond the obvious politically expedient ones); it all seems amorphous here.

I've never been a fan of the whole "what's hot/what's not" ethos.  And, I'd like to give a little more respect to today's Christian young people to think they could handle something that didn't fall into that same faddish trap.

I am hopeful that they may get it right yet with "Relevant".  At times, they seem tantilizingly close.  But it takes more than a slick hairdo, male earrings, chin stubble, idolization of youth, culture icon quotations, and psycobabble "cool dude" theological lingo to make one relevant.

Input: Update on March 10, 2017:  Once again I'm changing my rating, this time to 2 stars.  Also I cancelled my subscription a few months ago.  Political bias (anti-Trump, pro-Clinton) is obvious in at least 2 issues of RD:  July/Aug 2016, p. 96-100, "Which Way Do I Vote?"; Nov 2016, p. 102-111, "Who They Really Are."

Update on Jan 25, 2016:  I'm changing my rating of Reader's Digest (again) because I no longer feel that it deserves 5 stars.  I'm torn between 3 and 4 stars, but will be generous (for now) and give it a 4 stars because it continues to feature some good articles and I like its handy size.

What is downgrading the magazine for me is the proliferation of ads and articles for diet books written by RD editor-in-chief, Liz Vaccariello.  Liz Vaccariello has written a multitude of diet books and cookbooks in recent years--at least 7 diet books and at least 5 cookbooks. (If you think I'm exaggerating the number of her books, look her up on Amazon.) What I don't like is that she regularly promotes her books in Reader's Digest, with frequent ads and articles.  Apparently she did the same thing when she was editor of Prevention Magazine, but I was never a regular reader of that magazine, so I don't know much about that.  Also Prevention is a diet and exercise magazine, unlike RD.

The Feb 2016 issue of RD features an article on Liz's latest diet book.  There were also 3 ads for same book in that issue--1 inside the article, another elsewhere in the magazine, and the other on the back of the mailing address card.  I wouldn't complain about this if it were a rare event, but it's not:  Liz's diet books are regularly promoted and advertised in RD.  Being the editor of a high-circulation magazine gives her a great advertising advantage, no doubt.  It's a sweet deal for her, but I find her continuous self-promotion to be annoying (and obviously very biased).

By the way, is there any evidence that her diet books work long-term?  I'd love to see an article in Reader's Digest titled "Secrets Diet Book Authors Won't Tell You", but I won't hold my breath on that.  I don't care how much weight Liz or her staff and friends claim they lost on her latest diet after following it for days, weeks, or a few months.  I won't be impressed until there is proof that the weight loss is being maintained long-term by many.  As we have all heard countless times, strong evidence indicates that the great majority of people regain whatever weight they lost on any given diet within 1-5 years.  And their health often declines in the process.  And it's not their fault, either:  Diets (including those promoted as simple, easy, and healthy) are generally complicated, unpleasant (for the dieter and their families), costly, and are not realistically sustainable long-term.  But regardless of the quality or effectiveness or lack thereof, I am simply tired of seeing Liz's diets promoted so often.

As someone else mentioned:  Since my 2014 update, RD went back to 10 issues per year.  The decrease in issues doesn't bother me as long as the expiration dates don't mysteriously change as they did a few years ago.  On a positive note, RD is now including digital access with each subscription.  While I don't plan to take advantage of that myself, it's an added value which I expect will be popular with many readers.

Update on Aug 18, 2014:  My original review below was written almost 2 years ago.  I'm happy to say that there have been many improvements since then, so I now need to update my review and change my rating from 1 star to 5 stars. Everything I complained about in my original review has been corrected!  The magazine continues to publish occasional "mature" jokes, but on a mild level--nothing offensive like that dirty joke about the Easter Bunny.  There are now 12 issues per year (1 per month) with no more confusing and changeable expiration dates.  Another improvement:  the number of ads was actually reduced.  Also the quality of the magazine's paper has improved.  No more thin, slippery paper; now the paper is thicker and whiter, which makes it easy on the eyes as well as easy to turn the pages.  Best of all, the articles have significantly improved! Lately every issue has been full of interesting, informative, and heartwarming articles. My congratulations and thanks to editor Liz Vaccariello and the other staff for all these great improvements.  I very happily resubscribed to Reader's Digest!

Original Review (Nov. 15, 2012):  Until recently Reader's Digest had all-clean jokes.  You could read all the jokes out loud to your children or grandchildren of any age.  No more.  Page 110 of the September 2012 issued featured a joke about the Easter Bunny having sex with a chicken.  Isn't that a great joke for your children and grandchildren?  This joke didn't accidentally sneak into the magazine.  They knew the joke was dirty, which is why it was titled "Favorite joke I can't share with my kid."  In another comedy section on page 121 of the same issue, you get to see an x-ray of a man that has sunglasses up his rectum (due to accidentally sitting on them).  Not exactly family-friendly humor.

Many customers (myself included) wrote to editor Liz Vaccariello (she became editor in 2011) to complain. In the Letters section of the November 2012 issue, Ms. Vaccariello apologized for the "off-color joke" about the Easter Bunny (which she calls "a rabbit") and said, "Please know it won't happen again."  Yet in that very same November issue there are additional off-color jokes.  For example, on page 160, there's a joke about a woman who punches her husband for "25 years of bad sex" and he punches her back for "knowing the difference."

I'll mention something else new (in the past couple of years) that I don't like about the magazine:  the expiration dates keep changing.  Occasionally they put out what they call a "special" issue, which they count as 2 issues.  When this happens, your expiration date automatically changes.  If at first it expires in May, then it's changed to April, then to March.  On and on it goes and it's even more annoying when it involves a gift subscription.  Let's say you give a subscription to a friend for a Christmas gift.  You paid for "one year" and expect your friend to receive issues from Jan 2013 through Dec 2013.  Well, that won't happen because there will probably be 2 "special" issues during 2013.  In that event, your friend's subscription will automatically be changed to expire with the Oct 2013 issue.  Of course, Reader's Digest will start bugging you to renew your gift subscription well before it expires.  So around June, they will try to get you to renew what's supposed to be a Christmas gift.  If you renew it that year, come the following year, the new expiration will likely have been changed to August.  Have fun trying to keep up with Christmas gifts when you have to renew them in the summer.  Reader's Digest pulls the same expiration date stunt on all the wonderful Reiman magazines (Reminisce, Country, Birds & Blooms, etc.).  The Reiman magazines are still high quality, thanks to having good editors, however Reader's Digest has made some unwelcome changes to them, as well--most regrettably, the addition of ads in these formerly ad-free publications.

Well, that's it for me.  Today (after subscribing for about 30 years) I cancelled my subscription to Reader's Digest.

Input: ...instead of "American Girl", it needs to be "All-American Girl", because that's the only type of girl that most of this magazine's content will appeal to. There are a few sections that address serious problems that young girls face, such as "Help!" (an advice column of sorts), but the majority is hand-crafted for girls who are cute, popular, and have perfect, nuclear families that sensibly and neatly work out problems together.

Every single issue has a huge amount of pages dedicated to throwing parties. Although I'm sure these parties would be very fun for girls who had tons of friends who got along perfectly, plus incredibly wealthy families, they don't make sense for the majority of American girls. They all require a huge amount of time, money, and people. Given today's busy, hectic lifestyle in which both kids and parents are overscheduled, it simply doesn't add up.

Also included in each magazine is a number of short stories that, while sometimes creative plot-wise, are all obviously designed to preach cookie-cutter morals. For a magazine that's supposed to be empowering and inspiring young girls, content like these stories too often seems to be insulting their intelligence.

To be fair, the mag isn't completely fluffy and worthless. There are always a couple of nice real-life stories and such. However, overall the whole thing is too dumbed-down, too cutesy, and not nearly diverse enough. Unless you come from an upper-class family and have a daughter with dozens of friends, plus at least one parent who can constantly be with her to supervise crafts, parties, and activities, skip this and buy her some books instead.

Input: I am only reviewing issues from 1 to 30 of Nintendo Power. Back then, I do remember them as I subscribed to the magazine every year for a few years. Then, I lost interest because the magazine was making a transition from NES to SNES. The biggest positive feature about the magazine is how colorful the artwork (at times, became too much while the actual screenshots of the games were too little) was. The worst feature of it was the paucity of information I was getting about the games that I actually played on. Let's not forget back then that NES games were too expensive to buy, even with the lowered salaries our parents actually earned. There were too many games mentioned in Nintendo Power that it was impossible for any average kid to own many of them. Needless to say, Nintendo Power became a huge shameless marketing tool to try to persuade the kid readers to succumb to their temptations and get their parents to give in to buy the games for them. Now, after 20 years, I've finally a look at the old issues and see what I currently think of them. First off, the writers did very well in explaining the basic moves for certain games. However, they didn't reveal very much about advanced moves. Sometimes, they didn't bother showing the readers other features of the game. It was just a load of irrelevant artwork. For example, in Super Mario Bros. 2, there was no illustration of using coins to pull the lever for slot machine at the end of each stage. Looking at the first issue, they did a very good job in explaining a lot of details and including a full scale of maps of each level so you can see what comes next throughout. But, why did they stop covering any more after a certain level and never look at the final two or three stages? A great example is Issue 1 where they covered Super Mario Bros. 2 from worlds 1-1 to 2-3 and just abruptly stopped thereafter. Same thing goes for Gauntlet where there were 100 rooms to explore, but only three were covered in Nintendo Power. In Issue 10 which was among the worst, there was so little information about Batman and Double Dragon 2 that the coverages became a joke. They didn't even try to explain what happens during a fight with Bosses. And there was nothing about the late stages of the games. Come on, that's all they got? Contra got absolutely weak coverage too despite its popularity. There is a lot of times that this happens, and it makes me to think that the writers actually never got that far or have not beaten these games. Moreover, the writers have exaggerated a lot about the features of the games (many of them were in fact terrible) which supports the notion that there was a clear bias involved. Looking at Nintendo advertisement where you use the Powerline to the Pros by calling them and then noticing in the table of contents where it says, "Our pros can get you out of any video jam." why establish the phone line already when it should be published in the magazine? Is that the magazine's goal to help you out on that because you paid for the subscription to it? Bah...they want to make more money off from the readers. On page 54 of Issue 1, what a weak advice about how to beat Mike Tyson. They can do better than that. Reading a lot of the advices elsewhere, Nintendo Power seems to be more interested in giving out cheat codes rather than instructing the readers in how to beat a game the pure way. Why was there information about movies, music, and celebrities who happen to play Nintendo? The magazine was supposed to be about the games of NINTENDO! What a waste of space. Then, there is a silly page of NES ACHIEVERS where players were recognized for their highest scores per game (um...Game Genie, yes? Of course, it came out in early 1990, making cheating very plausible; plus Nintendo Power never endorsed it due to supposed copyright infringement). Really, beating the game was, and still is today, always the ultimate goal, and nobody cared about points. Even a worse embarrassment was the recognition of achievements by "Power Players."  Time to get out of the house and smell the roses. What's with this Nester and the smug Howard Phillips? Get rid of them already! Why do they show crappy made up stories too? Can we stick with strategies of NES games? Every time I pick up an issue, it's always Zelda, Super Mario 2, Zelda, Metroid, Zelda, Super Mario 3, MegaMan, Super Mario 2, Super Mario 3, Zelda, Super Mario 3, etc. These games got the most coverage of any. Most unfair of them all, there was a 85 page issue (number 13) that was entirely devoted to Super Mario 3. Some of the other games received so little of coverage, and the rest had none (I was really surprised about the lack of coverage for The Simpsons: Bart vs. the Space Mutants) at all. You were out of luck if you were playing any of them because you were trying to figure out how to get past a certain point. Most likely, whichever the company paid the magazine the most got the most coverage. I still can't get over the sight of the dork in white jersey titled Nintendo Power every time I see him and his goofy hair. Damn, issue 5, pg. 19. features what may be the worst accessory of all time in NES history...the Power Glove (That commercial was very convincing. By the way, what happened to the review of the Super Glove Ball game in Nintendo Power?). Let us not forget the wonderful toy called U-Force. They really made it sound so good. The shameless promotion of crappy NES accessories was embarrassing; it would have been nicer if they could have admitted the truth that these accessories were in fact unworkable. However and interestingly, both of the accessories including some others were never mentioned again in future issues (sort of got swept under the rug quietly). Elsewhere, the PowerMeter was the most biased and worthless feature of the magazine because all of the games were thought of so highly and possessed no negative marks, but we all know after getting them, we recognized how truly crappy these games were. Some of the advices the "counselors" (what a ridiculous title) gave for certain games have been questionable at best, and there are certainly far easier solutions than them. One of the "counselors" claimed to have beaten Contra with one life left by using a Power Glove (either it is true or that guy needed a life). Looking at the work done for Mission: Impossible, I am 100% certain that nobody at Nintendo Power had ever beaten the game because they did a rubbish layout of the stages without going much into details. The whole coverage was entirely devoid of any strategy. For the game, I had already written a good review of it that included way, way more helpful tips in trying to beat it than they could do in those wasted pages. Looking at the letters of Mailbox, at least half of them had kids crying and begging to become a "counselor" while majority of them was bragging about their NES achievements. Hmm...so tell me...how many hours a day did these kids waste playing NES games (believe me, they take a very, very long time to master), and how much of that should have been put into homework from school? I love the endless pumping by the writers of the magazine, making sure people were directed to buy whatever the writers were pushing such as call line, cleaning products, technical repair, strategy guides, SNES, Game Boy, etc. Gosh, that Nester character was so annoying that he needed to be entirely cut out of the magazine. The comics were so boring, and they became page wasters. In the later issues, the layout of maps had improved considerably, and that alone will make Nintendo Power worth looking at. However, it was still limited to certain games. Rarely ever the writers will choose the most challenging NES games for greater coverage probably because their "counselors" probably couldn't advance further in the levels, let alone beating them. Hence, lots of cheat codes were provided in every issue. The biggest mistake of the magazine was the combination of NES and Game Boy, and then eventually SNES, coverages into one magazine. The result? Less and less exposure, then eventually extinction, for NES games which is a shame since we all know that the NES console is arguably the greatest console ever in Video Game history. Now I think of it: that was probably the biggest reason why I stopped bothering with Nintendo Power. The simple solution? They should have had separate magazines for each console. Thus, a lot of games could have been given more exposure, say 15 to 20 NES games per issue with 5 to 10 pages per. Also, get rid of the irrelevant art work and boring details about something else that are totally unrelated with NES games. Stick with the maps, strategies, and walkthroughs. Then, the writers would have been sitting on a goldmine. They never bothered with NES games made before Nintendo Power first came out which is another shame. All in all, Nintendo Power is truly a joke of a magazine, and we've discovered how thoroughly excellent gamefaqs and youtube of the games are today.
